stimuli.title: Seven persons facing south, with home cities
stimuli.content:
Seven persons Abhiraj, Charvi, Hriday, Kesha, Navya, Rishit and Tanmay sit in a straight row, all facing south. Each of them is from a different city among Agra, Bhopal, Indore, Kochi, Madurai, Patna and Surat. (For a person facing south, the right is towards the west and the left is towards the east.)

- Abhiraj sits exactly in the middle of the row.
- Charvi sits second to the left of Abhiraj.
- The person from Bhopal sits immediately to the left of Charvi.
- Navya sits immediately to the right of Abhiraj.
- Kesha sits at one of the extreme ends of the row, but she is not from Bhopal.
- Tanmay sits immediately to the left of Abhiraj.
- Rishit is not from Bhopal.
- The person from Surat sits at the extreme right end of the row.
- Navya is from Kochi, and the person from Patna sits immediately to the left of Navya.
- Only one person sits between the persons from Agra and Kochi.
- Charvi is not from Indore.
stimuli.solution:
Number the seats 1 to 7 from the west end. Facing south, 'to the right' means a lower seat number and 'to the left' a higher one.
Step 1: Abhiraj = 4. Charvi is second to his left: 6. Navya is immediately to his right: 3, and Tanmay immediately to his left: 5.
Step 2: Bhopal is immediately to Charvi's left: seat 7. Kesha is at an end but not from Bhopal, so Kesha = 1.
Step 3: Seats 2 and 7 remain for Hriday and Rishit. Rishit is not from Bhopal (seat 7), so Rishit = 2 and Hriday = 7 (Bhopal).
Step 4: The extreme right end is the west end, seat 1: Kesha is from Surat. Navya (3) is from Kochi, and Patna is immediately to her left, seat 4: Abhiraj.
Step 5: Agra is two seats from Kochi (3): seat 1 or 5; seat 1 is Surat, so Agra = 5 (Tanmay). Indore and Madurai remain for Rishit and Charvi; Charvi is not from Indore, so Charvi is from Madurai and Rishit from Indore.

| Seat (from west) | Person | City |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Kesha | Surat |
| 2 | Rishit | Indore |
| 3 | Navya | Kochi |
| 4 | Abhiraj | Patna |
| 5 | Tanmay | Agra |
| 6 | Charvi | Madurai |
| 7 | Hriday | Bhopal |

stimuli.title: Eight persons facing north or south, with languages
stimuli.content:
Eight persons Advait, Bhairavi, Dhruv, Gargee, Jivesh, Kalyani, Paras and Sumedha sit in a straight row. Some of them face north and the others face south. Each of them is learning a different language among Bengali, French, German, Japanese, Korean, Russian, Spanish and Tamil. (For a person facing north, the right is towards the east; for a person facing south, the right is towards the west.)

- Sumedha learns German. She sits fourth from the west end of the row and faces north.
- Dhruv sits third to the right of Sumedha.
- Kalyani sits at one of the extreme ends of the row, and Dhruv sits immediately to her right.
- Paras sits at the other extreme end and faces the same direction as Kalyani.
- Bhairavi sits second to the right of Kalyani.
- Both persons sitting immediately next to Bhairavi face north, but Bhairavi does not.
- Jivesh sits immediately to the right of Sumedha.
- Advait sits second to the left of Jivesh.
- Gargee faces the same direction as Sumedha.
- Exactly four persons face north.
- Bhairavi learns Bengali. The person who learns Russian sits at an extreme end, and only one person sits between the Russian learner and Bhairavi.
- The Spanish learner sits immediately to the right of the German learner.
- Dhruv learns Japanese, and the French learner sits at an extreme end of the row.
- The Korean learner faces south.
stimuli.solution:
Number the seats 1 to 8 from the west end.
Step 1: Sumedha = 4, facing north, German. Dhruv is third to her right (east): 7.
Step 2: Dhruv is immediately to the right of Kalyani, who is at an end. Kalyani = 8 facing south (her right is west, seat 7) works; Kalyani = 1 cannot have seat 7 next to her. Paras = 1, facing south.
Step 3: Bhairavi is second to Kalyani's right: 8 − 2 = 6. Her neighbours (5 and 7) face north and she faces south, so Dhruv faces north.
Step 4: Jivesh is immediately to Sumedha's right: 5 (so he faces north). Jivesh faces north, so his left is west: Advait = 5 − 2 = 3, and Gargee takes seat 2.
Step 5: Gargee faces north like Sumedha. North-facing so far: Sumedha, Dhruv, Jivesh, Gargee = four, so Advait faces south.
Step 6: Russian is at an end two seats from Bhairavi (6): seat 8, Kalyani. Spanish is immediately right of German (seat 4, facing north): seat 5, Jivesh. Dhruv learns Japanese; French is at an end: seat 1, Paras.
Step 7: Korean and Tamil remain for Gargee (north) and Advait (south). The Korean learner faces south: Advait learns Korean and Gargee Tamil.

| Seat (from west) | Person | Faces | Language |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Paras | south | French |
| 2 | Gargee | north | Tamil |
| 3 | Advait | south | Korean |
| 4 | Sumedha | north | German |
| 5 | Jivesh | north | Spanish |
| 6 | Bhairavi | south | Bengali |
| 7 | Dhruv | north | Japanese |
| 8 | Kalyani | south | Russian |

stimuli.title: A south-facing row of unknown length
stimuli.content:
Some persons sit in a straight row, all facing south. (For a person facing south, the right is towards the west and the left is towards the east.) The number of persons in the row is not given. Ojasvi, Pratyush, Ranjana, Shailesh, Uditi and Varenya are among them.

- Ranjana sits fifth from the right end of the row.
- Shailesh sits sixth to the left of Ranjana.
- Only three persons sit between Shailesh and Uditi, and Uditi sits to the left of Shailesh.
- Varenya sits exactly midway between Ranjana and Uditi.
- Ojasvi sits second to the right of Varenya.
- Pratyush sits at the extreme left end of the row, and as many persons sit between Uditi and Pratyush as sit between Ranjana and Ojasvi.
stimuli.solution:
Count positions from the right end of the row (the west end, since everyone faces south). Moving 'to the left' of someone increases this count.
Step 1: Ranjana = 5th from the right. Shailesh is sixth to her left: 5 + 6 = 11th.
Step 2: Three persons sit between Shailesh and Uditi, Uditi on his left: 11 + 4 = 15th.
Step 3: Varenya is midway between 5th and 15th: 10th. Ojasvi is second to Varenya's right: 10 − 2 = 8th.
Step 4: Between Ranjana (5th) and Ojasvi (8th) sit two persons, so two persons sit between Uditi (15th) and Pratyush, who is at the left end: Pratyush = 15 + 3 = 18th from the right. The row has 18 persons.

| Person | From the right end | From the left end |
|---|---|---|
| Ranjana | 5th | 14th |
| Ojasvi | 8th | 11th |
| Varenya | 10th | 9th |
| Shailesh | 11th | 8th |
| Uditi | 15th | 4th |
| Pratyush | 18th | 1st |

stimuli.title: Six floors and six favourite colours
stimuli.content:
Six persons Kavin, Lajja, Mrinalini, Nimit, Pooja and Suhas live on the six floors of a building, one on each floor. Floor 1 is the lowermost and floor 6 the topmost. Each of them likes a different colour among Blue, Green, Orange, Pink, Purple and Yellow.

- Kavin lives on floor 3.
- Only one person lives between Kavin and Lajja, and Lajja lives above Kavin.
- Mrinalini lives immediately above Lajja.
- The person who likes Green lives immediately below Lajja.
- Suhas lives above Pooja, and Nimit does not live on an even-numbered floor.
- The person who likes Pink lives on the topmost floor.
- The person who likes Purple lives immediately below the person who likes Green.
- Pooja likes Blue.
- The person who likes Yellow lives on an odd-numbered floor below Kavin.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Kavin = 3, Lajja = 5, Mrinalini = 6.
Step 2: Floors 1, 2 and 4 remain for Nimit, Pooja and Suhas. Nimit is on an odd floor: 1. Suhas is above Pooja: Pooja = 2, Suhas = 4.
Step 3: Green is immediately below Lajja: floor 4 (Suhas). Purple is immediately below Green: floor 3 (Kavin). Pink is on floor 6 (Mrinalini). Pooja likes Blue.
Step 4: Yellow is on an odd floor below Kavin: floor 1 (Nimit). Orange is left for Lajja.

| Floor | Person | Colour |
|---|---|---|
| 6 | Mrinalini | Pink |
| 5 | Lajja | Orange |
| 4 | Suhas | Green |
| 3 | Kavin | Purple |
| 2 | Pooja | Blue |
| 1 | Nimit | Yellow |

stimuli.title: Seven floors and seven family sizes
stimuli.content:
Seven persons Jairam, Kumud, Madhav, Oorja, Pawan, Rachit and Shruti live on the seven floors of a building, one on each floor (floor 1 is the lowermost, floor 7 the topmost). Their families have 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8 members, a different number for each person.

- Shruti lives on floor 4, and Pawan lives immediately below her. Shruti's family has twice as many members as Pawan's.
- Madhav lives on the topmost floor, and his family has one member more than Pawan's.
- Only one person lives between Madhav and Jairam, and Jairam's family is the smallest of all.
- Oorja lives immediately below Madhav. Her family has as many members as Jairam's and Rachit's families together.
- Kumud lives above Rachit.
- The family on floor 2 is the largest of all.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Shruti = 4, Pawan = 3, Madhav = 7, Oorja = 6. Jairam is two floors from Madhav: 5. Kumud and Rachit take floors 2 and 1; Kumud is above Rachit, so Kumud = 2, Rachit = 1.
Step 2: Jairam's family is the smallest: 2. Kumud (floor 2) has the largest family: 8.
Step 3: Shruti = 2 × Pawan and Madhav = Pawan + 1. From 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 the only doubling pair is 3 and 6, so Pawan = 3, Shruti = 6, Madhav = 4.
Step 4: 5 and 7 remain for Oorja and Rachit, and Oorja = 2 + Rachit: Rachit = 5, Oorja = 7.

| Floor | Person | Family members |
|---|---|---|
| 7 | Madhav | 4 |
| 6 | Oorja | 7 |
| 5 | Jairam | 2 |
| 4 | Shruti | 6 |
| 3 | Pawan | 3 |
| 2 | Kumud | 8 |
| 1 | Rachit | 5 |

stimuli.title: Eight floors, eight professions and eight home cities
stimuli.content:
Eight persons Amolika, Bhargav, Chandan, Damayanti, Girish, Hamida, Jignesh and Kalpesh live on the eight floors of a building, one on each floor (floor 1 is the lowermost, floor 8 the topmost). Each has a different profession among Architect, Banker, Chef, Dentist, Engineer, Lawyer, Pilot and Teacher, and each is from a different city among Gaya, Jaipur, Kanpur, Mysuru, Nagpur, Pune, Ranchi and Shimla.

- The Architect lives on the lowermost floor, and exactly three persons live between the Architect and the Lawyer.
- The person from Jaipur lives immediately below the Lawyer.
- Girish lives on the topmost floor and is the Pilot. The Pilot lives two floors above the Chef.
- Hamida lives immediately below Girish, and the Dentist is from Shimla.
- Kalpesh lives immediately below Damayanti, and Damayanti lives on an odd-numbered floor.
- The Engineer lives on an odd-numbered floor, immediately below the Teacher.
- Chandan lives immediately above the Architect and is from Kanpur.
- Amolika is from Mysuru, and the person from Gaya lives somewhere below her.
- The person from Pune lives above the person from Shimla, and the person from Nagpur lives on an even-numbered floor.
- Bhargav is not the Architect.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Architect = 1, Lawyer = 5, Jaipur = 4. Girish = 8 and is the Pilot, so the Chef is on floor 6. Hamida = 7. Chandan = 2 (above the Architect), from Kanpur.
Step 2: Damayanti is on an odd floor with Kalpesh immediately below. Floor 1 has nothing below, floor 3 would need Kalpesh on Chandan's floor 2, and floor 7 is Hamida's, so Damayanti = 5 (Lawyer) and Kalpesh = 4 (Jaipur).
Step 3: The Engineer is on an odd floor immediately below the Teacher: floor 1 is the Architect and floor 7 would need the Teacher on the Pilot's floor 8, so Engineer = 3 and Teacher = 4 (Kalpesh).
Step 4: Banker and Dentist remain for floors 2 and 7. The Dentist is from Shimla, but floor 2 is Kanpur, so Dentist = 7 (Hamida, Shimla) and Banker = 2 (Chandan). Pune is above Shimla: floor 8.
Step 5: Amolika, Bhargav and Jignesh take floors 1, 3 and 6; Gaya, Mysuru, Nagpur and Ranchi go to floors 1, 3, 5 and 6. Nagpur is on an even floor: 6. Amolika is from Mysuru with Gaya below her, so she is not on 1 or 6: Amolika = 3 (Mysuru), Gaya = 1 and Ranchi = 5. Bhargav is not the Architect: Bhargav = 6, Jignesh = 1.

| Floor | Person | Profession | City |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8 | Girish | Pilot | Pune |
| 7 | Hamida | Dentist | Shimla |
| 6 | Bhargav | Chef | Nagpur |
| 5 | Damayanti | Lawyer | Ranchi |
| 4 | Kalpesh | Teacher | Jaipur |
| 3 | Amolika | Engineer | Mysuru |
| 2 | Chandan | Banker | Kanpur |
| 1 | Jignesh | Architect | Gaya |

stimuli.title: Seven boxes with weights and colours
stimuli.content:
Seven boxes C, G, K, N, Q, U and Z are kept one above another in a single stack (position 1 is the bottom and 7 the top). Their weights are 12, 15, 18, 22, 26, 30 and 35 kg, and their colours are Black, Brown, Cream, Gold, Maroon, Silver and Violet, one weight and one colour per box.

- Box C is kept exactly in the middle of the stack, and Box Q is kept immediately above Box C.
- Box N is kept at the top. It is 4 kg heavier than Box C.
- Exactly three boxes are kept between Box N and Box Z.
- Box Z is the heaviest box, and its colour is Gold.
- Box K is kept immediately below Box Z and is the lightest box.
- Box U is kept below Box G.
- Box Q is twice as heavy as Box G.
- The Silver box is kept at the bottom, and it weighs 26 kg.
- The Black box is the lightest box.
- The Violet box is kept immediately between the Gold box and the Brown box.
- The Cream box is lighter than the Maroon box.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: C = 4, Q = 5, N = 7. Three boxes lie between N and Z: Z = 3 (Gold, 35 kg). K = 2 (12 kg, so Black).
Step 2: Positions 1 and 6 remain for U and G; U is below G: U = 1, G = 6. The Silver box is at the bottom and weighs 26 kg: U.
Step 3: Weights left: 15, 18, 22, 30 for C, G, N, Q. N = C + 4 gives 18 and 22; Q = 2 × G gives 15 and 30. So C = 18, N = 22, G = 15, Q = 30.
Step 4: Violet lies between Gold (3) and Brown with one box between them, so Brown = 5 (Q) and Violet = 4 (C). Cream and Maroon remain for G (15 kg) and N (22 kg); Cream is lighter: G Cream, N Maroon.

| Position | Box | Weight (kg) | Colour |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7 | N | 22 | Maroon |
| 6 | G | 15 | Cream |
| 5 | Q | 30 | Brown |
| 4 | C | 18 | Violet |
| 3 | Z | 35 | Gold |
| 2 | K | 12 | Black |
| 1 | U | 26 | Silver |

stimuli.title: Nine boxes in a three-by-three rack
stimuli.content:
A rack has three shelves (top, middle and bottom), and each shelf has three compartments (left, middle and right, as seen from the front). Nine boxes D, E, G, I, M, O, R, U and W are kept in the rack, one in each compartment. 'Directly above/below' means in the same column on the next shelf.

- Box U is kept in the centre compartment of the rack (middle shelf, middle column).
- Box M is kept directly below Box U.
- Box E is kept immediately to the right of Box M, on the same shelf.
- Box I is kept directly above Box E.
- Box G is kept immediately to the left of Box O, on the same shelf.
- Box D is kept directly below Box W.
- Box R is kept on the bottom shelf.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: U = middle shelf, middle. M is directly below: bottom, middle. E is to M's right: bottom, right. I is directly above E: middle, right.
Step 2: Free compartments: bottom-left, middle-left and the whole top shelf. R is on the bottom shelf: bottom-left.
Step 3: D is directly below W, and only the left column has two free compartments one above the other (middle-left and top-left): D = middle-left, W = top-left.
Step 4: G and O take the top-middle and top-right compartments, G on the left.

| Shelf | Left | Middle | Right |
|---|---|---|---|
| Top | W | G | O |
| Middle | D | U | I |
| Bottom | R | M | E |

stimuli.title: Eight boxes and the sums of their weights
stimuli.content:
Eight boxes F, J, K, P, S, T, V and Y are kept one above another in a single stack (position 1 is the bottom and 8 the top). Their weights are 6, 9, 11, 14, 17, 20, 23 and 27 kg, one weight per box.

- Box S is kept fifth from the bottom.
- The heaviest box is kept two places below Box S, and the lightest box is kept immediately below Box S.
- Exactly three boxes are kept between Box P and the heaviest box, and Box P is kept above it.
- Box K is kept between Box S and Box P.
- Box V is kept at the top, and its weight equals the combined weight of Box F and Box P.
- Box K weighs as much as Box S and Box J together.
- Box J is kept immediately above Box T, and Box T is lighter than Box Y.
- The two bottom boxes together weigh 29 kg.
- Box P is lighter than Box V but heavier than Box J.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: S = 5. The heaviest box (27 kg) is at 3 and the lightest (6 kg) at 4. P is four places above the heaviest: P = 7. K lies between S and P: K = 6. V = 8. F, J, T and Y take positions 1 to 4.
Step 2: 9, 11, 14, 17, 20 and 23 kg are left for positions 1, 2, 5, 6, 7 and 8. The two bottom boxes weigh 29 kg together: only 9 + 20 works, so positions 1 and 2 hold 9 and 20 kg, and S, K, P, V share 11, 14, 17, 23.
Step 3: K = S + J, where J is one of the bottom four (9, 20, 27 or 6 kg). The possibilities are 14 + 9 = 23 or 11 + 6 = 17 or 17 + 6 = 23. V = F + P with P lighter than V uses the other two weights: (a) S 14, J 9, K 23 ⇒ V 17, P 11, F 6; (b) S 11, J 6, K 17 ⇒ V 23, P 14, F 9; (c) S 17, J 6, K 23 ⇒ V 14, P 11, F 3 ✗.
Step 4: In (b) J (6 kg) is at 4, so T is at 3 with 27 kg and Y would be lighter than T ✗. So (a): F = 4 (6 kg); J (9 kg) is in the bottom pair and is immediately above T: T = 1 (20 kg), J = 2, and Y = 3 (27 kg). P (11) is heavier than J (9) and lighter than V (17), as required.

| Position | Box | Weight (kg) |
|---|---|---|
| 8 | V | 17 |
| 7 | P | 11 |
| 6 | K | 23 |
| 5 | S | 14 |
| 4 | F | 6 |
| 3 | Y | 27 |
| 2 | J | 9 |
| 1 | T | 20 |

stimuli.title: Five arrow symbols for comparisons
stimuli.content:
In the questions of this set, arrows are used between two letters with these meanings:
'A ↑ B' means 'A is greater than B'; 'A ↓ B' means 'A is smaller than B'; 'A ⇑ B' means 'A is not smaller than B'; 'A ⇓ B' means 'A is not greater than B'; 'A ↔ B' means 'A is equal to B'.
Assuming the statements to be true, find which of the conclusions I and II is/are definitely true.
stimuli.solution: Decode: ↑ means >, ↓ means <, ⇑ means ≥ ('not smaller than'), ⇓ means ≤ ('not greater than') and ↔ means =. Rewrite every statement with ordinary signs, join them into one chain and test each conclusion along it.

stimuli.title: Six morning runners and their distances
stimuli.content:
Six friends Amol, Binita, Chirag, Deepti, Eshan and Gargi each ran a different distance on a Sunday morning.

- Deepti ran farther than Chirag but less than Gargi.
- Amol ran less than Chirag.
- Eshan ran farther than Gargi.
- Binita ran farther than Amol but less than Chirag.
stimuli.solution: Chirag < Deepti < Gargi < Eshan, and Amol < Binita < Chirag. Joined: Eshan > Gargi > Deepti > Chirag > Binita > Amol.

stimuli.title: Seven bank officers: designations and review days
stimuli.content:
Seven officers Ansh, Bina, Chhavi, Darsh, Eshita, Faisal and Gita of a bank hold seven different designations. In decreasing order of seniority these are: General Manager, Deputy General Manager, Assistant General Manager, Chief Manager, Senior Manager, Manager and Officer. Each officer conducts a review on a different day of one week, from Monday to Sunday.

- The General Manager's review is on Thursday.
- Darsh is the Assistant General Manager, and his review is on the day immediately after the Officer's review.
- Exactly two reviews are held between Bina's review and the General Manager's review, and Bina is junior to Darsh.
- Faisal's review is on Sunday. Faisal is senior to Chhavi but junior to Eshita.
- The Manager's review is on Monday.
- Gita's review is on the day immediately before Ansh's review, and Gita is senior to Ansh.
- Exactly one review is held between Ansh's review and Faisal's review.
- Ansh is senior to Eshita.
- Chhavi's review is earlier in the week than Darsh's review.
stimuli.solution:
Bina is three days away from the General Manager's Thursday: Monday or Sunday; Faisal has Sunday, so Bina is on Monday and, as the Monday reviewer, is the Manager. One review between Ansh and Faisal (Sunday) puts Ansh on Friday and Gita on Thursday, so Gita is the General Manager. Tuesday, Wednesday and Saturday remain for Chhavi, Darsh and Eshita. Darsh comes the day after the Officer: Darsh on Saturday would make Ansh (Friday) the Officer, but Ansh is senior to Eshita; Darsh on Tuesday would make the Monday Manager the Officer. So Darsh is on Wednesday and the Officer on Tuesday; Chhavi is earlier than Darsh, so Chhavi is on Tuesday (Officer) and Eshita on Saturday. Ranks left 2, 4, 5: Ansh > Eshita > Faisal gives Ansh DGM, Eshita Chief Manager, Faisal Senior Manager.

Mon Bina (Manager), Tue Chhavi (Officer), Wed Darsh (AGM), Thu Gita (GM), Fri Ansh (DGM), Sat Eshita (Chief Manager), Sun Faisal (Senior Manager).

stimuli.title: Digit codes for relations
stimuli.solution: Decode each expression pair by pair from the left, draw the small tree, and read the asked relation off it. A child of a married person is taken to be the child of the couple.

stimuli.title: A family of eight with three couples
stimuli.content:
A family has eight members: Anand, Bharati, Chinmay, Damini, Ekansh, Fatima, Gopal and Hema. There are exactly three married couples, and every married person's spouse is a member of the family. Anand is male.

- Anand and Bharati are married to each other and have exactly three children, of whom only one is a daughter.
- Damini is the daughter of Bharati and is unmarried.
- Ekansh, a boy, is the only grandchild of Anand, and Hema is Ekansh's mother.
- Chinmay is a son of Anand.
- Fatima is the wife of one of Ekansh's uncles.
- Gopal is not an uncle of Ekansh.
stimuli.solution:
Anand's children are Damini and two sons. Ekansh's mother Hema must be married to a son of Anand (Damini is unmarried). The only males left are Chinmay, Ekansh and Gopal, and Ekansh is a grandchild, so Anand's sons are Chinmay and Gopal. Gopal is not Ekansh's uncle, so he is Ekansh's father and Hema's husband; Fatima is then Chinmay's wife.
Tree: Anand + Bharati → Chinmay (+ Fatima), Damini, Gopal (+ Hema) → Ekansh.

stimuli.title: Six places in a small town
stimuli.content:
Six places in a small town are located as follows.

- The temple is 12 km north of the market.
- The school is 5 km east of the temple.
- The hospital is 5 km west of the market.
- The post office is 6 km south of the temple.
- The library is 1 km east of the hospital.
stimuli.solution: Put the market at (0, 0), east and north positive: temple (0, 12), school (5, 12), hospital (−5, 0), post office (0, 6), library (−4, 0).

stimuli.title: Four coded sentences about a train
stimuli.content:
In a certain code language:
'train leaves early today' is written as 've ko ra mi'
'today platform is crowded' is written as 'tu mi ne sa'
'night train arrives today' is written as 'le zo mi ra'
'platform leaves at night' is written as 'pu sa zo ko'
(The codes of the words in a sentence may be in any order.)
stimuli.solution: today = mi (sentences 1, 2 and 3); train = ra (1 and 3); leaves = ko (1 and 4); platform = sa (2 and 4); night = zo (3 and 4). Leftovers: early = ve, arrives = le, at = pu. 'is' and 'crowded' appear only in sentence 2, so they share 'tu' and 'ne' in some order.

stimuli.content:
Study the following arrangement of letters, numbers and symbols and answer the question.

G 4 & P 7 U © 3 M L 8 % E 2 F 6 # W 9 A T 5
stimuli.solution: Number the elements 1 to 22 from the left; the k-th element from the right is the (23 − k)-th from the left.

Study the following arrangement of letters, numbers and symbols and answer the question.

7 K # 2 E R 9 @ D 4 U £ 6 H Q 1 $ I 8 B * 3 Z O 5 % N 6
stimuli.solution: Number the elements 1 to 28 from the left (k-th from the right = (29 − k)-th from the left). Vowels: E, U, I, O. When elements are removed or moved, write out the new arrangement before counting.

stimuli.title: Seven persons and their weights
stimuli.content:
Seven persons Abha, Bimal, Charu, Dhruv, Ekta, Farhan and Gopi have different weights.

- Only two persons are heavier than Abha.
- Dhruv is heavier than Farhan but lighter than Charu.
- Exactly two persons have weights between those of Charu and Ekta.
- Charu is heavier than Ekta.
- Gopi is lighter than Farhan.
- Bimal is heavier than Dhruv, but Bimal is not the heaviest.
stimuli.solution: Abha is the 3rd heaviest. Gopi < Farhan < Dhruv < Charu, so Charu is at least 4th from the bottom, and Ekta is exactly three places below Charu. If Charu were 4th from the bottom, Ekta would be the lightest, but Gopi, Farhan and Dhruv must fill the three places below Charu. If Charu were 2nd heaviest, Ekta would be 5th heaviest, Dhruv 4th heaviest, and Bimal (heavier than Dhruv, not the heaviest) would have no place. So Charu is the heaviest, Ekta 4th, Bimal 2nd, and Dhruv, Farhan, Gopi follow. Heaviest to lightest: Charu, Bimal, Abha, Ekta, Dhruv, Farhan, Gopi.

stimuli.title: Machine: most consonants to the right end
stimuli.content:
A word arrangement machine rearranges a line of words step by step. In each step it takes, among the words not yet arranged, the word with the most consonants (letters other than a, e, i, o and u); if two such words have the same number of consonants, it takes the one that comes first in alphabetical order. It places that word at the right end, immediately to the left of the words already arranged there (in Step I, at the extreme right). The other words keep their order. The machine stops when the arrangement is complete.

Input: glints planet aroma stream oasis branch idea
stimuli.solution:
Consonants: planet 4, stream 4, oasis 2, branch 5, idea 1, glints 5, aroma 2. Order of selection: branch, glints, planet, stream, aroma, oasis, idea.

Step I: glints planet aroma stream oasis idea branch
Step II: planet aroma stream oasis idea glints branch
Step III: aroma stream oasis idea planet glints branch
Step IV: aroma oasis idea stream planet glints branch
Step V: oasis idea aroma stream planet glints branch
Step VI: idea oasis aroma stream planet glints branch

stimuli.title: Machine: numbers read backwards
stimuli.content:
A number arrangement machine rearranges a line of two-digit numbers step by step. In each step it takes, among the numbers not yet arranged, the one whose value is the smallest when its digits are read in reverse order, writes it with its digits reversed, and places it immediately to the right of the numbers already arranged at the left end (in Step I, at the extreme left). The other numbers keep their order. The machine stops when every number has been arranged.

Input: 62 38 81 47 15 93

stimuli.title: Machine: swapped letters and units-digit numbers
stimuli.content:
A word and number arrangement machine rearranges a line step by step. In each step it makes two moves: (1) among the words not yet arranged, it takes the word with the fewest vowels (a, e, i, o, u; if two words have the same number of vowels, the one that comes first in alphabetical order), interchanges its first two letters, and places it at the left end, immediately to the right of the words already placed there; (2) among the numbers not yet arranged, it takes the one with the largest units digit, adds its units digit to it, and places the result at the right end, immediately to the left of the numbers already placed there. All other elements keep their order. The machine stops when every element has been arranged.

Input: garden 37 kite 54 brush 89 apron 62 stick 45
stimuli.solution:
Words: brush (1 vowel), stick (1), then apron, garden, kite (2 each) → rbush, tsick, paron, agrden, ikte. Numbers by units digit: 89, 37, 45, 54, 62 → 98, 44, 50, 58, 64.

Step I: rbush garden 37 kite 54 apron 62 stick 45 98
Step II: rbush tsick garden kite 54 apron 62 45 44 98
Step III: rbush tsick paron garden kite 54 62 50 44 98
Step IV: rbush tsick paron agrden kite 62 58 50 44 98
Step V: rbush tsick paron agrden ikte 64 58 50 44 98

stimuli.title: A station for the village
stimuli.content:
In a small town on the edge of a dry district, a radio station broadcasts from two rooms above a grocery shop. Its signal reaches only about fifteen kilometres, and most of its presenters are farmers, housewives and students who had never spoken into a microphone before. This is community radio: a low-power station run by and for the people of a small area.

Unlike large commercial channels, which try to attract as many listeners as possible across a city or a state, a community station serves a few villages and speaks in their own dialect. Its programmes are shaped by local needs. A typical day might include a talk by an agriculture officer on pest control, a call-in show on a new pension scheme, folk songs recorded at a wedding and the prices of vegetables at the nearest market.

Supporters say that the greatest strength of such stations is trust. Listeners recognise the voices on air; the person reading out a weather warning may be a neighbour's daughter. During floods and heavy storms, when mobile networks often fail, community stations have kept villages informed about rising water levels, safe shelters and relief camps.

Running a station, however, is not easy. Most are operated by schools, colleges or voluntary organisations with little money. They cannot depend on advertising, since local businesses are small and the stations are allowed to broadcast only a limited amount of it. Equipment breaks down, trained volunteers move away to cities, and licences take a long time to obtain.

Many stations have survived by involving their listeners. Villagers donate small sums, women's groups produce their own programmes, and young people learn to record and edit on cheap phones. As one station manager put it, the station does not belong to its staff; it belongs to the people who keep switching it on.

stimuli.title: Driving blind in the fog
stimuli.content:
Every winter, large parts of northern India disappear under a thick blanket of fog. For railway passengers, the season brings a familiar frustration: trains that run hours, sometimes a whole day, behind schedule. Passengers often blame poor planning, but the main cause is simple. A driver who cannot see the signal ahead cannot safely run his train at full speed.

Railway signals work much like traffic lights. A red light tells the driver to stop, while yellow and green lights tell him how much of the line ahead is clear. In good weather a driver can see a signal from a long distance and adjust his speed calmly. In dense fog, visibility may fall to a few metres, so he may not spot a red signal until it is too late. A heavy train needs a long distance to halt even after the brakes are applied. Rules therefore require trains to slow down sharply when the fog is thick.

Technology has eased the problem without removing it. Many locomotives now carry a small device that uses satellite positioning to tell the driver how far away the next signal is, and sounds an alert as the train approaches it. Drivers say this removes much of the guesswork. Some routes are also being fitted with systems that can apply the brakes automatically if a train passes a red signal or goes faster than the safe speed.

Even so, delays cannot be avoided entirely. One late train holds up the trains behind it on a busy line, and the effect spreads across the network. Railways therefore cancel or shorten some services in the foggiest weeks, so that the remaining trains can run closer to time.

For passengers, the practical lesson is to check the running status of a train before leaving home. For the railways, the challenge is to make winter travel safe first and punctual second, in that order.

stimuli.title: Money that crosses borders
stimuli.content:
Every month, millions of Indians working abroad, in the Gulf, in Europe, in North America and elsewhere, send part of their earnings home. These transfers, known as remittances, have made India the largest recipient of such money in the world. For many families, the monthly transfer from a son or a husband abroad pays for food, school fees and medical bills, and over the years it has built houses, shops and small businesses.

Economists value remittances for reasons that go beyond the family budget. Unlike foreign investment, which may leave a country quickly when conditions turn bad, remittances tend to be steady, and they often rise when the home country faces a disaster, because workers abroad send more to help relatives in trouble. They also bring in foreign currency without creating any debt that must later be repaid.

The benefits, however, come with costs. Sending small sums across borders has long been expensive: once fees and the margin on the exchange rate are added, a worker may lose a noticeable share of what he sends. Many migrants also borrow heavily to pay recruitment agents before they leave, and spend their first years abroad simply clearing that debt. At home, families that depend on a single overseas earner are exposed if he loses his job or falls ill.

Some researchers worry about a subtler effect. Where remittances are large, they argue, young people may come to see migration as the only route to a good life, and invest little effort in local work or study. Others reply that the money often pays for the education that makes the next generation more productive.

Policy has focused on making transfers cheaper and safer. Digital channels have cut fees, and banks have been encouraged to offer accounts and investment products tailored to migrants and their families. The larger challenge is to turn money that is spent mainly on daily needs into savings and investment that can outlast the worker's years abroad.

stimuli.title: Pooling the milk
stimuli.content:
Twice a day, in thousands of Indian villages, a small queue forms outside a room with a tin roof. Farmers, many of them women, arrive carrying steel cans of milk from one or two buffaloes or cows. Each can is weighed, a small sample is tested for fat content, and within minutes the farmer receives a slip showing what she will be paid. This is the village collection centre of a dairy cooperative, and it is the first link in a chain that ends in packets of milk, butter and cheese on shop shelves hundreds of kilometres away.

Before cooperatives spread, a small producer had little choice but to sell to a private trader. With only a few litres to sell and no way of storing milk, which spoils within hours in the heat, she accepted whatever price the trader offered. Traders often paid late, cheated on measurement, or lent money on terms that tied the farmer to them for years.

The cooperative changed the balance of power by pooling the milk of many small producers. Together they could afford chilling plants, trucks and processing units, and could sell in distant cities where prices were higher. Because the members owned the organisation, its surplus returned to them, often as a bonus at the end of the year. Testing every sample also meant that the price depended on quality rather than on the trader's mood, so farmers had a reason to feed and care for their animals better.

The model is not free of problems. In some places, cooperatives have been captured by local politicians who use them to reward their supporters, and elections to their boards are bitterly fought. Private dairies, which now compete for the same milk, sometimes offer higher prices in good seasons, tempting members to sell outside.

Still, the basic idea has proved remarkably durable: when many small sellers act together, they can win terms that none of them could obtain alone.

stimuli.title: When winning means losing
stimuli.content:
Imagine a jar of coins put up for auction in a classroom. Nobody knows exactly how much money it contains, so each student makes a guess and bids accordingly. Some guesses are too low and some too high, and if the class is large, the average guess may be quite close to the true value. Yet the student who wins the auction is, almost by definition, the one whose guess was the most optimistic. Experiments of this kind repeatedly find that the winner pays more than the jar is worth.

Economists call this the winner's curse. It arises whenever many bidders compete for an item whose true value is the same for all of them but uncertain to each, such as the right to drill for oil in a particular field, a licence to use a band of radio frequencies, or a company that has been put up for sale. Every bidder's estimate contains some error. Winning therefore tells a bidder something unwelcome: that everyone else valued the prize less highly, and so her own estimate was probably too high.

The lesson for a careful bidder is counter-intuitive. Rather than bidding what she believes the item is worth, she should bid somewhat less, and shade her bid further as the number of rivals grows, because the more bidders there are, the more extreme the most optimistic estimate is likely to be. A bidder who ignores this may win often and still lose money.

The curse is not inevitable. Experienced bidders in industries with frequent auctions learn to discount their own enthusiasm, and the designers of an auction can reduce the problem by releasing more information about the item, which narrows the spread of estimates. Where bidders are inexperienced, or where pride and publicity reward winning for its own sake, the curse tends to bite hardest.

The idea reaches well beyond auctions. A company that wins a fierce bidding war to take over a rival, a city that outbids others to host a costly sporting event, even a buyer who beats a crowd of others to a house, may each discover that the victory was the most expensive part of the deal.

stimuli.title: When the totals mislead
stimuli.content:
A regional manager comparing two branches of a bank looks at a single figure: the share of loans repaid on time. The town branch recovers 88 per cent of its loans, the hill branch only 79 per cent. The conclusion seems obvious, and the hill branch is told to learn from its neighbour.

A closer look tells a different story. Each branch makes two kinds of loans: crop loans to small farmers, which are riskier because they depend on the weather, and salary loans to government employees, which are almost always repaid. Of the hill branch's 100 loans, 80 are crop loans, of which 60 were repaid, and 20 are salary loans, of which 19 were repaid. The town branch made only 20 crop loans, recovering 14, and 80 salary loans, recovering 74.

Now compare like with like. On crop loans, the hill branch recovers 75 per cent and the town branch 70 per cent. On salary loans, the hill branch recovers 95 per cent and the town branch 92.5 per cent. The hill branch does better in both categories, yet worse overall. It is not a weaker lender; it simply makes far more of the difficult loans.

This reversal is known as Simpson's paradox. It appears whenever the groups being compared differ in their mix of some factor that strongly affects the outcome. A hospital that treats the most serious cases can show a higher death rate than others even if it treats every type of patient better; a school that admits weaker students can post lower pass rates while adding more to each student's learning.

The paradox does not mean that totals are useless, nor that a breakdown always gives the truer picture. Splitting data by the wrong factor can create misleading patterns of its own. What it demands is a question before every comparison: are these groups really alike in the ways that matter? A manager who asked it might reward the hill branch for taking on the farmers whom others avoid, rather than scold it for the arithmetic that follows.

stimuli.title: The pot that keeps water cool
stimuli.content:
In many Indian homes, a round earthen pot still sits in a corner of the kitchen, (1) ______ with drinking water. Even on the hottest summer afternoon, the water inside stays pleasantly cool, although the pot uses no electricity at all and costs only a small sum at the local market.

The secret lies in the clay. Baked clay is full of tiny holes, so a little water slowly (2) ______ through the walls of the pot to its outer surface. There it evaporates, and evaporation carries heat away from the pot, just as sweat cools our skin on a hot day. The drier and (3) ______ the air, the faster the water evaporates and the cooler the pot becomes. In humid coastal weather, when the air is already full of moisture, the effect is much (4) ______.

Potters say that a new pot works best after it has been soaked and used for a few days. They also advise keeping it in a shady, airy place, and (5) ______ it regularly so that its tiny holes are not blocked by dust and by the salts left behind by the water.

In recent years, the earthen pot has found new admirers. Some families who own refrigerators still prefer it, because its water is cool without being icy and is gentler on the throat. Designers have used the same principle to build simple clay coolers for vegetables, which help small farmers and vendors keep their produce fresh for a few extra days. An old object, it seems, still has something to (6) ______ to a modern world that is worried about rising temperatures and electricity bills.

stimuli.title: The vanishing scavengers
stimuli.content:
Not long ago, vultures were a common sight in India, circling high above towns or crowding around the body of a dead cow at the edge of a village. Then, within roughly a decade from the 1990s, the numbers of several species (1) ______ by more than ninety per cent, one of the fastest declines of any bird ever recorded.

For years the cause remained a (2) ______. Scientists suspected disease or poisoning, but the answer turned out to be a common painkiller given to cattle. Vultures that fed on the bodies of animals treated shortly before death absorbed the drug, which (3) ______ their kidneys. Because a single carcass can feed dozens of birds, even a small share of treated animals was enough to kill vast numbers of them.

The loss was not only an ecological one. Vultures had quietly performed a public service, stripping a carcass to the bone within hours. Without them, carcasses lay rotting for days, and the number of stray dogs feeding on them rose. More dogs meant more dog bites and more cases of rabies, a disease that is almost always (4) ______ once its symptoms appear.

The veterinary use of the drug was banned, and breeding centres were set up to raise vultures in captivity and later release them into the wild. Progress has been slow, partly because vultures breed slowly, (5) ______ only one egg a year, and partly because some other painkillers that harm them remain in use.

The story is a reminder that the value of a species is not always obvious until it is gone. Animals that seem (6) ______, even unpleasant, may be holding up parts of the system on which human health depends.

stimuli.title: The trap of the minimum due
stimuli.content:
Every credit card statement shows two figures that matter: the total amount due, and a much smaller 'minimum amount due', usually a small percentage of the balance. Paying the minimum keeps the account in good standing and **(1) avoids** a late-payment fee. Many cardholders therefore treat it as the amount they owe. That is an expensive mistake.

Any part of the balance that is not paid by the due date begins to attract interest, often at rates of thirty to forty per cent a year, far **(2) lower** than the rate on almost any other kind of borrowing. Worse, on many cards the interest-free period on new purchases is lost as long as an old balance is carried forward, so even fresh spending starts attracting interest from the day it is made. A cardholder who pays only the minimum each month may find, after a year of steady payments, that the balance has barely **(3) fallen**.

The design is not accidental. Card issuers earn much of their income from customers who **(4) clear** their balances from month to month, and a low minimum makes this easy to do. In the United States, for example, card statements must show how long it would take to repay the balance through minimum payments alone, and how much would be paid in total along the way; the figures are often **(5) sobering**.

The remedy is simple to state, if not always to follow: treat the card as a convenient way to pay, not as a source of credit, and settle the full amount every month. A cardholder who cannot do so is, in effect, borrowing at one of the highest rates on offer, and would usually be better off **(6) increasing** the card balance with a cheaper personal loan.

stimuli.title: Pseudocode: years for a deposit to grow
stimuli.content:
A trainee writes this pseudocode to find how many years a deposit takes to reach Rs 15,000 at 10% interest compounded yearly:

```
balance = 10000
year = 0
WHILE balance < 15000
    balance = balance + balance * 10 / 100
    year = year + 1
END WHILE
PRINT year, balance
```

All calculations use exact decimal arithmetic unless a question says otherwise.
stimuli.solution: Balance after each pass: 11,000; 12,100; 13,310; 14,641; 16,105.1. The condition is tested 6 times (5 true, 1 false); the program prints 5 and 16105.1.

stimuli.title: Backup schedule of a branch file server
stimuli.content:
A branch file server holds 200 GB of data. A full backup is taken every Sunday at 23:00. On Monday to Saturday a backup is taken at 23:00 every night, under one of two plans:

- Plan X: incremental backups (only data changed since the previous backup of any kind).
- Plan Y: differential backups (all data changed since the last full backup).

New or changed data each day (no data changes twice in the week): Mon 6 GB, Tue 4 GB, Wed 10 GB, Thu 5 GB, Fri 8 GB, Sat 3 GB.

Copies of every backup are kept on tape in a safe at the bank's disaster-recovery site in another city. The server's disks fail on Thursday at 15:00.
stimuli.solution: Plan X restore: Sunday full + Mon, Tue, Wed incrementals (4 sets). Plan Y restore: Sunday full + Wednesday differential (2 sets). Plan Y daily sizes 6, 10, 20, 25, 33, 36 GB (total 130 GB); Plan X total 36 GB. Changes after Wednesday 23:00 (16 hours) are lost.

stimuli.solution: LAN 10.20.30.0/26 = 10.20.30.0-10.20.30.63 (broadcast .63). PC2 (10.20.30.70) is in 10.20.30.64/26, outside the gateway's subnet. PC3 has a self-assigned link-local address (no DHCP lease). 10.20.7.9 matches /16, /8 and /0; the longest, /16, wins.

stimuli.title: Incident timeline at a bank
stimuli.content:
The bank's security operations centre (SOC) reconstructs this incident:

- Day 1, 09:12 - A clerk at Branch 14 receives an email with the attachment Revised_TDS_Rates.docm, opens it and clicks 'Enable Content' when Word asks.
- Day 1, 09:13 onwards - The clerk's PC sends a small HTTPS request to an unknown server abroad every 60 seconds and receives short instructions in reply.
- Day 2 - Using an administrator password stored on the clerk's PC, the attacker logs in to the branch file server and from there to the head-office HR server.
- Day 3, 02:00 - 4 GB of HR records are compressed and uploaded to a cloud-storage account controlled by the attacker.
- Day 3, 11:00 - The SOC computes the SHA-256 hash of the payroll master file and finds it different from the hash recorded at last week's audit, although no authorised change was made.
stimuli.solution: Macro malware (initial access) -> command-and-control beaconing -> lateral movement -> exfiltration; the changed hash shows that the payroll file's integrity has been violated.

stimuli.title: Test report of a fingerprint login system
stimuli.content:
A bank tests a fingerprint login system with 2,000 genuine attempts (real users) and 5,000 impostor attempts (other people's fingers), at three matching thresholds:

| Threshold | Genuine attempts rejected | Impostor attempts accepted |
|---|---|---|
| Low | 20 | 150 |
| Medium | 60 | 25 |
| High | 180 | 5 |

False Acceptance Rate (FAR) = impostor attempts accepted / impostor attempts. False Rejection Rate (FRR) = genuine attempts rejected / genuine attempts.
stimuli.solution: FAR: Low 3%, Medium 0.5%, High 0.1%. FRR: Low 1%, Medium 3%, High 9%. A stricter threshold lowers FAR and raises FRR.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Simplify: ¾ of 168 + 25% of 360 ÷ 6 − 8²

solution.concept: 'Of' (and a percentage of) is worked first, then ÷ and ×, then + and −
solution.explanation: ¾ of 168 = 126 and 25% of 360 = 90. Next the division: 90 ÷ 6 = 15. Then 126 + 15 − 64 = 77.
solution.why_others_wrong: 152 skips the ÷ 6 (126 + 90 − 64); −28 works left to right, dividing 126 + 90 by 6; 125 reads 8² as 2 × 8 = 16.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?)?
6.25 × 0.48 + 0.9 ÷ 0.025 − 2.5² = ?

solution.concept: Clear the decimals: 6.25 = 25/4, and dividing by 0.025 is multiplying by 40
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.35 divides 0.9 by 0.25 instead of 0.025 (3.6); 34 squares 2.5 as 5; 45.25 adds 6.25 instead of subtracting it.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the smallest number by which 2,450 must be divided so that the quotient is a perfect square?

solution.concept: Write the number as a product of primes; divide out every prime that appears an odd number of times
solution.explanation: 2,450 = 2 × 5² × 7². Only the prime 2 has an odd power, so dividing by 2 leaves 5² × 7² = 1,225 = 35².
solution.why_others_wrong: Dividing by 5 gives 490, by 7 gives 350 and by 10 gives 245, none of which is a perfect square (5 and 7 already appear squared).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?)?
45% of 1,240 − ? × 12 = 7/9 of 315 + 11²

solution.concept: Evaluate both sides fully, then isolate the term with ?
solution.why_others_wrong: 77 adds 366 to 558 instead of subtracting; 24.25 takes 11² as 22; 14.5 takes 45% of 1,240 as 540.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Find the value of (256)^0.16 × (16)^0.18.

solution.concept: Write both bases as powers of 2 and add the exponents
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 stops at 2¹ (adding 0.28 + 0.72); 8 is 2³; 16 is 4², mixing the base 4 with the exponent 2.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If x = √5 + 2, what is the value of x − 1/x?

solution.concept: Rationalise 1/x: multiply the numerator and denominator by √5 − 2
solution.why_others_wrong: 2√5 is x + 1/x; √5 − 2 is 1/x itself; 9 + 4√5 is x².

solution.concept: Write everything as a power of 5/3: (3/5)ⁿ = (5/3)⁻ⁿ and (9/25)⁻³ = (25/9)³ = (5/3)⁶
solution.why_others_wrong: 0 takes the right side as (5/3)³; −9 takes it as (5/3)⁻⁶ (forgetting that the negative power flips 9/25); 11/3 treats (3/5)^(x − 4) as (5/3)^(x − 4), giving 3x − 5 = 6.

solution.concept: a⁰ = 1 and a⁻¹ = 1/a; keep the sign of (−1/3)⁻¹ = −3
solution.why_others_wrong: 3/2 drops the minus sign of the numerator; −3/4 takes (−1/3)⁻¹ as +3 (denominator 12); −5/3 takes (0.6)⁰ as 0 (numerator −10).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If √(1 + x/144) = 13/12, what is the value of x?

solution.concept: Square both sides before isolating x
solution.why_others_wrong: 12 forgets to square 13/12 (x/144 = 1/12); 169 is 13², the numerator before subtracting 144; 5 is √25, the square root of the answer.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the square root of 12,34,54,321?

solution.concept: Numbers made of 1s have palindromic squares: 11² = 121, 111² = 12,321, 1,111² = 12,34,321, …
solution.explanation: 12,34,54,321 rises 1-2-3-4-5 and falls back 4-3-2-1, the pattern of 11,111² (five 1s). Check: 11,111² = 12,34,54,321.
steps: Digits rise to 5 and fall back ⇒ five 1s
solution.shortcut: 1…1 (n ones) squared reads 1, 2, …, n, …, 2, 1 for n ≤ 9.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If a = 2.36 and b = 1.64, what is the value of (a³ + b³) ÷ (a² − ab + b²)?

solution.concept: a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²), so the quotient is simply a + b
solution.explanation: Since a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²), the expression equals a + b = 2.36 + 1.64 = 4.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.72 is a − b (the result for a³ − b³ over a² + ab + b²); 3.8704 is ab; 16 is (a + b)².

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

What will come in place of the question mark (?)?

solution.why_others_wrong: 5/6 skips the ÷ 2⅓ (7/12 + 1/4); 29/18 multiplies by 2⅓ instead of dividing; 1/4 forgets the final + ¼.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?)?
8^3.2 × 4^1.8 ÷ 2^? = 32

solution.why_others_wrong: 18.2 adds 5 to 13.2 instead of subtracting; 4.8 writes 8^3.2 as 2^(3 + 3.2); 6.4 writes 4^1.8 as 2^1.8.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If x − 1/x = 3, what is the value of x⁴ + 1/x⁴?

solution.concept: Square twice: (x − 1/x)² = x² + 1/x² − 2, then (x² + 1/x²)² = x⁴ + 1/x⁴ + 2
solution.why_others_wrong: 121 forgets to subtract 2 at the second squaring; 81 is simply 3⁴; 79 forgets to add 2 at the first squaring (9² − 2).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the value of 11² + 12² + 13² + … + 20²?

solution.concept: 1² + 2² + … + n² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6; take the sum up to 20 and subtract the sum up to 10
solution.why_others_wrong: 2,870 forgets to remove 1² to 10²; 2,364 removes 1² to 11² (506), dropping 11² as well; 2,605 averages only the first and last squares (10 × (121 + 400)/2), but squares do not rise evenly.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Which of the following is the largest?

solution.concept: √a − √b = (a − b)/(√a + √b); with the same a − b, the smallest denominator gives the largest value
solution.explanation: Each difference has a − b = 2, so each equals 2 ÷ (√a + √b). The denominator is smallest for √5 + √3 (about 3.97), so √5 − √3 (about 0.504) is the largest; the others are about 0.410, 0.354 and 0.317.
solution.why_others_wrong: √7 − √5, √9 − √7 and √11 − √9 have larger denominators √7 + √5, √9 + √7 and √11 + √9, so they are smaller.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If a = 2.7, b = −1.2 and c = −1.5, what is the value of (a³ + b³ + c³) ÷ abc?

solution.concept: If a + b + c = 0, then a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc
solution.why_others_wrong: −3 slips a sign in abc (which is positive here: 2.7 × −1.2 × −1.5 = 4.86); 0 assumes the cubes also add to zero; 1 assumes a³ + b³ + c³ = abc.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
3, 8, 24, 48, 120, ?

solution.concept: The terms are one less than the squares of the prime numbers 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, …

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
20, 21, 17, 26, 10, 35, ?

solution.concept: The differences are squares with alternating signs: +1², −2², +3², −4², +5², …
solution.why_others_wrong: 71 adds 36 instead of subtracting it; −14 subtracts 7² and skips 6²; 10 subtracts 5² and repeats an earlier term.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
3, 8, 17, 32, 57, ?

solution.concept: Each term is n² + 2ⁿ for n = 1, 2, 3, …
solution.shortcut: Differences 5, 9, 15, 25 have second differences 4, 6, 10 = 2 + 2, 2 + 4, 2 + 8; next 2 + 16 = 18, so the next difference is 43.
solution.why_others_wrong: 92 assumes the differences grow by 10 each time (+35); 89 adds only 2⁵ = 32; 96 assumes the second differences go 4, 6, 10, 14 (+39).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the missing number (?) in the series:
4, 18, ?, 100, 180, 294

solution.concept: Each term is n³ − n² = n²(n − 1) for n = 2, 3, 4, …
solution.why_others_wrong: 64 is 4³ without subtracting 4²; 46 doubles the first difference (18 + 28); 50 is 48 + 2 and does not give 100 by the same rule.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
4.5, 8, 12.5, 18, 24.5, ?

solution.concept: Each term is half of a perfect square: 9/2, 16/2, 25/2, 36/2, 49/2, …
solution.why_others_wrong: 31 adds 6.5 again; 31.5 adds 7; 36 is 6² rather than 8²/2.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the missing number (?) in the series:
1, 2, 6, 16, ?, 120, 328

solution.concept: From the third term on, each term is twice the sum of the two terms before it
solution.why_others_wrong: 48 triples 16 and fails the check 2(16 + 48) = 128 ≠ 120; 42 and 50 also fail the check (116 and 132).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
47, 58, 71, 79, 95, 109, ?

solution.concept: Each term is the previous term plus the sum of its own digits
solution.why_others_wrong: 123 adds 14 again (repeating the last difference); 121 adds 12 (taking the digit sum of 109 as 12); 110 adds 1, the digit sum of 10 only.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
1, 4, 15, 64, 325, ?

solution.concept: Add 1 to each term, then multiply by 2, 3, 4, 5, …
solution.why_others_wrong: 1,950 multiplies 325 by 6 without adding 1 first; 1,630 multiplies by 5 again; 1,951 multiplies first and adds 1 afterwards.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
150, 131, 114, 99, 86, 74, 66

solution.concept: The differences fall by 2 each time: 19, 17, 15, 13, 11, 9
solution.why_others_wrong: 114, 86 and 66 fit the rule; 66 confirms 75, since 75 − 9 = 66.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
29, 31, 37, 41, 43, 49, 53

solution.concept: The terms are consecutive prime numbers
solution.explanation: The primes after 29 are 31, 37, 41, 43, 47, 53. The sixth term should be 47; 49 = 7 × 7 is not prime.
solution.why_others_wrong: 41, 43 and 53 are all primes in the right places.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
5, 7, 13, 25, 44, 75, 117

solution.why_others_wrong: 25, 75 and 117 fit; 75 confirms 45, since 44 + 30 = 74.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
2, 10, 32, 68, 130, 222, 350

solution.concept: Each term is n³ + n for n = 1, 2, 3, …
solution.why_others_wrong: 10, 130 and 222 equal 2³ + 2, 5³ + 5 and 6³ + 6.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
4, 7, 12, 21, 39, 71, 136

solution.concept: Each term is twice the previous term minus 1, 2, 3, 4, …
solution.why_others_wrong: 21, 71 and 136 fit; 71 confirms 38, since 39 × 2 − 5 = 73.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
3, 8, 20, 51, 137, 384, 1,122

solution.concept: Each term is three times the previous term minus 1², 2², 3², …

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
3, 6, 7, 14, 17, 36, 45, 90

solution.concept: The operations alternate: × 2, then + 1², × 2, then + 2², × 2, then + 3², …
solution.why_others_wrong: 7, 36 and 45 fit; 36 confirms 18, since 17 × 2 = 34.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the roots of I and II and choose the relation between x and y that holds for every pair.
I. x² − 3x − 54 = 0
II. y² + 13y + 42 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorise; a root shared by both equations makes the relation non-strict
solution.explanation: I: (x − 9)(x + 6) = 0, so x = 9 or −6. II: (y + 6)(y + 7) = 0, so y = −6 or −7. The smallest x (−6) equals the largest y (−6), and every other pair has x > y. So x ≥ y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y fails for the pair x = y = −6; x < y holds for no pair.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve both quadratics and state how x compares with y.
I. x² − 17x + 72 = 0
II. y² − 21y + 110 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorise each equation; compare the largest x with the smallest y
solution.explanation: I: (x − 8)(x − 9) = 0, so x = 8 or 9. II: (y − 10)(y − 11) = 0, so y = 10 or 11. The largest x (9) is below the smallest y (10), so x < y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y and x ≥ y reverse the comparison; every x is smaller than every y.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Each equation has one positive and one negative root. Find them and decide which relation between x and y, if any, always holds.
I. x² + 2x − 63 = 0
II. y² − 4y − 45 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: When the roots interleave, no single relation holds for every pair
solution.explanation: I: (x + 9)(x − 7) = 0, so x = 7 or −9. II: (y − 9)(y + 5) = 0, so y = 9 or −5. x = 7 is less than y = 9 but greater than y = −5, so no relation holds for every pair.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y fails for 7 and 9; x ≤ y fails for 7 and −5; x < y and x ≥ y fail similarly.
solution.final_answer: Option B: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve the two equations, whose roots are negative, and choose the relation between x and y.
I. 3x² + 20x + 32 = 0
II. 2y² + 9y + 10 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Split the middle term: 20x = 12x + 8x and 9y = 4y + 5y
solution.explanation: I: 3x² + 12x + 8x + 32 = (3x + 8)(x + 4) = 0, so x = −8/3 ≈ −2.67 or −4. II: 2y² + 4y + 5y + 10 = (y + 2)(2y + 5) = 0, so y = −2 or −2.5. The largest x (−2.67) is below the smallest y (−2.5), so x < y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y and x ≥ y compare 8/3 and 4 with 2 and 2.5 without the minus signs.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The roots of both equations below are positive. Solve them and mark the relation between x and y.
I. 5x² − 18x + 9 = 0
II. 20y² − 17y + 3 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorise by splitting the middle term; watch for a common root
solution.explanation: I: 5x² − 15x − 3x + 9 = (5x − 3)(x − 3) = 0, so x = 3 or 0.6. II: 20y² − 12y − 5y + 3 = (5y − 3)(4y − 1) = 0, so y = 0.6 or 0.25. The smallest x (0.6) equals the largest y (0.6), and all other pairs have x > y. So x ≥ y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y fails for the common root 0.6; x < y holds for no pair.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find all the roots of I and II and choose the relation between x and y.
I. 2x² + 11x + 12 = 0
II. 2y² + 19y + 45 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorise both; with negative roots, the larger number is the one nearer zero
solution.explanation: I: (2x + 3)(x + 4) = 0, so x = −1.5 or −4. II: (2y + 9)(y + 5) = 0, so y = −4.5 or −5. The smallest x (−4) is greater than the largest y (−4.5), so x > y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y and x ≤ y treat −4 as smaller than −4.5.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
In equation I, k is a constant, and x = 4 is known to be one root of I. Find the other root of I and the roots of II, then choose the relation between x and y.
I. x² − 9x + k = 0
II. y² − 10y + 21 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: The two roots of x² − 9x + k = 0 add up to 9
solution.explanation: Sum of the roots of I = 9, so the other root is 9 − 4 = 5 (and k = 20). II: (y − 3)(y − 7) = 0, so y = 3 or 7. x = 4 is greater than 3 but less than 7, so no relation holds for every pair.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y fails for x = 4, y = 3; x ≥ y fails for x = 5, y = 7; x > y and x ≤ y fail for the same pairs.
solution.final_answer: Option C: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Both equations have fractional coefficients. Clear the fractions, solve, and choose the relation between x and y.
I. x²/2 − 3x + 4 = 0
II. y²/2 − 9y/2 + 10 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Multiply each equation by 2 first
solution.explanation: I × 2: x² − 6x + 8 = 0, so x = 2 or 4. II × 2: y² − 9y + 20 = 0, so y = 4 or 5. x = y = 4 is possible and every other pair has x < y. So x ≤ y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y fails for x = y = 4; x ≥ y holds only for that one pair.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equation I contains |x|, the absolute value of x. Find every real x and y and choose the relation between them.
I. x² − 4|x| + 3 = 0
II. y² + 8y + 15 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Since x² = |x|², equation I is a quadratic in |x|; each positive |x| gives two values of x
solution.explanation: I: |x|² − 4|x| + 3 = 0, so |x| = 1 or 3, giving x = −3, −1, 1, 3. II: (y + 3)(y + 5) = 0, so y = −3 or −5. The smallest x (−3) equals the largest y (−3), and every other pair has x > y. So x ≥ y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y misses the negative roots of I (x = −3 = y); x ≤ y holds only for that pair.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Three ropes 84 m, 126 m and 210 m long are to be cut into pieces of equal length, with no rope left over. The pieces are to be as long as possible. How many pieces will there be in all?

solution.concept: The longest equal piece that divides every rope is the HCF of the lengths
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 and 30 use 21 m or 14 m pieces, which are common divisors but not the greatest; 42 is the piece length, not the number of pieces.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the largest three-digit number that leaves a remainder of 5 when divided by each of 12, 18 and 21?

solution.concept: Such numbers are 5 more than a multiple of LCM(12, 18, 21)
solution.explanation: LCM(12, 18, 21) = 252. Multiples of 252 below 1,000: 252, 504, 756. The largest required number is 756 + 5 = 761.
solution.why_others_wrong: 756 forgets to add the remainder; 1,013 (1,008 + 5) has four digits; 751 subtracts 5 instead of adding it.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: When a number n is divided by 6, the remainder is 4. What is the remainder when n² + 3n is divided by 6?

solution.concept: Replace n by its remainder: n² + 3n leaves the same remainder as 4² + 3 × 4
solution.explanation: n = 6k + 4, so n² + 3n leaves the same remainder as 16 + 12 = 28 when divided by 6. 28 = 4 × 6 + 4, so the remainder is 4.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 uses 16 + 3 (forgetting to multiply 3 by n); 0 assumes n² + 3n = n(n + 3) must be a multiple of 6, but 4 × 7 = 28 is not; 5 treats 3n as 3 + n (16 + 7 = 23 leaves 5).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the sum of all the factors (divisors) of 360, including 1 and 360?

solution.concept: For n = 2ᵃ × 3ᵇ × 5ᶜ, the sum of divisors is (1 + 2 + … + 2ᵃ)(1 + 3 + … + 3ᵇ)(1 + 5 + … + 5ᶜ)
solution.why_others_wrong: 810 leaves out 360 itself; 24 is the number of divisors, not their sum; 1,080 is three times 360, not a divisor sum.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The LCM of two numbers is 48 times their HCF, and the sum of their HCF and LCM is 1,029. If one of the numbers is 63, what is the other?

solution.concept: HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers
solution.explanation: HCF + 48 × HCF = 49 × HCF = 1,029, so HCF = 21 and LCM = 1,008. The other number = 21 × 1,008 ÷ 63 = 336. Check: HCF(63, 336) = 21 and LCM(63, 336) = 1,008.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1,008 is the LCM, not the second number; 16 is 1,008 ÷ 63, which forgets to multiply by the HCF; 48 is the ratio LCM ÷ HCF.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the highest power of 12 that divides 40! (the product 1 × 2 × 3 × … × 40) exactly?

solution.concept: 12 = 2² × 3: count the 2s and the 3s in 40! and see which runs out first
solution.explanation: Number of 2s in 40! = 20 + 10 + 5 + 2 + 1 = 38, enough for 19 copies of 2². Number of 3s = 13 + 4 + 1 = 18. Each 12 needs one 3, so only 18 copies of 12 divide 40!.
solution.why_others_wrong: 19 counts only the pairs of 2s; 3 counts only the multiples of 12 up to 40; 38 counts the single 2s.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What are the last two digits of 7¹⁰⁰?

solution.concept: 7⁴ = 2,401 ends in 01, and any power of a number ending in 01 also ends in 01
solution.explanation: 7⁴ = 2,401, which ends in 01. 7¹⁰⁰ = (7⁴)²⁵, and numbers ending in 01 multiply to numbers ending in 01, so 7¹⁰⁰ ends in 01.
solution.shortcut: The last two digits of powers of 7 repeat in the cycle 07, 49, 43, 01; 100 is a multiple of 4.
solution.why_others_wrong: 49, 43 and 07 are the last two digits of 7², 7³ and 7¹; 100 is a multiple of 4, so the cycle ends at 01.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A batter scored 110 runs, including 3 sixes and 8 fours. What percentage of his runs did he make by running between the wickets?

solution.concept: Runs from boundaries = 6 × sixes + 4 × fours; the rest came from running
solution.why_others_wrong: 45 5/11% is the boundary share; 60% divides the running runs by 100 instead of 110; 40% subtracts the 50 boundary runs from 100 and divides by 100.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Fresh grapes contain 80% water by weight, while raisins made from them contain 10% water. How many kilograms of raisins can be made from 45 kg of fresh grapes?

solution.concept: Drying removes only water: the solid part stays the same
solution.explanation: Solid in the grapes = 20% of 45 = 9 kg. In the raisins this 9 kg is 90% of the weight, so the raisins weigh 9 ÷ 0.9 = 10 kg.
solution.why_others_wrong: 9 kg is the solid alone, ignoring the 10% water left in the raisins; 4.5 kg is 10% of 45; 11.25 kg divides 9 by 0.8, mixing up the two water percentages.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Meena spends 80% of her income and saves the rest. Her income rises by 15%, but she keeps her savings the same in rupees. By what percentage does her expenditure rise?

solution.concept: All the extra income goes into expenditure; compare that extra with the old expenditure
solution.explanation: Take income = 100: expenditure 80, savings 20. New income = 115 and savings stay 20, so expenditure = 95. Rise = 15 on 80 = 18.75%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15% assumes expenditure grows at the same rate as income; 75% divides the extra 15 by the savings (20) instead of the expenditure (80); 12% takes 80% of the 15% rise in income.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A refrigerator's price includes 18% GST on its pre-tax price. The GST rate is cut to 12% while the pre-tax price does not change. By what percentage does the price paid by the buyer fall (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Final price ∝ (1 + GST rate); compare 1.12 with 1.18
solution.explanation: With a pre-tax price of 100, the buyer paid 118 and now pays 112. The fall is 6 on 118 = 5.08%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6.00% is the cut in percentage points of tax, not the change in price; 5.36% divides 6 by the new price 112; 33.33% is the fall in the tax rate itself (6 on 18).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In a village, the number of men rose by 8% and the number of women by 12% over a year, and the total population rose by 9.6%. What was the ratio of men to women at the start of the year?

solution.concept: The overall rate is a weighted average of the two rates; use alligation
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 : 3 reverses the alligation; 1 : 1 would give 10%; 4 : 3 would give about 9.71%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The angles of a triangle are in the ratio 2 : 3 : 7. What is the largest angle?

solution.concept: The three angles add up to 180°
solution.explanation: 2 + 3 + 7 = 12 parts = 180°, so one part = 15°. Largest angle = 7 × 15° = 105°.
solution.why_others_wrong: 30° and 45° are the other two angles; 70° takes one part as 10°.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The monthly salaries of A and B are in the ratio 5 : 7. If each gets an increment of ₹4,000, the ratio becomes 7 : 9. What is A's present salary?

solution.concept: Let the salaries be 5k and 7k; the increment is added to both
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹14,000 is B's present salary (or A's new salary); ₹8,000 is 4k; ₹18,000 is B's new salary.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If x : y = 3 : 4, what is (4x² − y²) : (x² + y²)?

solution.concept: Put x = 3k and y = 4k; k² cancels
solution.explanation: 4x² − y² = 4 × 9k² − 16k² = 20k² and x² + y² = 9k² + 16k² = 25k². Ratio = 20 : 25 = 4 : 5.
solution.why_others_wrong: 8 : 7 uses x and y without squaring (4 × 3 − 4 : 3 + 4); 4 : 25 takes 4x² − y² as (2x − y)² = 4k²; 5 : 4 inverts the answer.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The present ages of a mother and her daughter are in the ratio 9 : 2, and the mother is 28 years older than the daughter. After how many years will the mother be exactly three times as old as the daughter?

solution.concept: The age gap (7 parts) is fixed at 28 years
solution.explanation: 7 parts = 28 years, so 1 part = 4: mother 36, daughter 8. In n years: 36 + n = 3(8 + n) ⇒ 36 + n = 24 + 3n ⇒ n = 6. Check: 42 = 3 × 14.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 years is one part (k); 8 years is the daughter's present age; 12 years gives 48 and 20, a ratio of 2.4.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: ₹4,200 is shared among 3 men, 4 women and 6 children so that each man gets twice as much as each woman, and each woman gets 1½ times as much as each child. How much does each child get?

solution.concept: Express every share in terms of one child's share c: woman = 1.5c, man = 3c
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹300 and ₹600 are a woman's and a man's shares; ₹323.08 divides 4,200 by the 13 people as if all shares were equal.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If 2, x, y and 54 are in continued proportion, what is the value of x + y?

solution.concept: In continued proportion each term is the previous one times the same ratio r: 2, 2r, 2r², 2r³
solution.why_others_wrong: 56 adds the end terms 2 and 54; 18 is y alone; 36 takes x and y as 9 and 27 (the ratio 3 applied from 3 instead of from 2).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Four years ago, the ages of A and B were in the ratio 5 : 4. The ratio of A's age four years from now to B's age four years ago is 3 : 2. What is the sum of their present ages?

solution.concept: Let A − 4 = 5k and B − 4 = 4k; then A + 4 = 5k + 8
solution.explanation: (5k + 8) ÷ 4k = 3/2 ⇒ 10k + 16 = 12k ⇒ k = 8. So A = 44 and B = 36, and the sum is 80 years.
solution.why_others_wrong: 72 years is the sum four years ago; 88 years is the sum four years from now; 44 years uses A's present age instead of his age four years from now in the second ratio ((5k + 4)/4k = 3/2 gives k = 4).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The monthly cost of running a delivery van is partly fixed and partly proportional to the distance driven. It costs ₹5,600 in a month in which the van covers 600 km and ₹7,700 in a month in which it covers 900 km. What will it cost in a month in which it covers 1,200 km?

solution.concept: The extra cost of the extra distance gives the cost per km; the rest is the fixed part
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹11,200 treats the whole cost as proportional to distance (5,600 × 2); ₹10,500 is 7,700 × 1,200/900, the same mistake from the other month; ₹8,400 forgets the fixed part.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A is 3 years older than B, and B is 5 years older than C. The sum of the present ages of A, B and C is 61 years. How old is A?

solution.concept: Write every age in terms of C's age
solution.explanation: C = c, B = c + 5, A = c + 8. Then 3c + 13 = 61, so c = 16 and A = 24 years.
solution.why_others_wrong: 21 years is B's age; 16 years is C's age; 26 years adds 3 and 5 to B instead of to C.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A man's present age is 125% of what it was 10 years ago, and 83⅓% of what it will be 10 years from now. What is his present age?

solution.concept: 125% = 5/4 and 83⅓% = 5/6; either condition gives the age, and the other checks it
solution.why_others_wrong: 40 years is his age 10 years ago; 60 years is his age 10 years from now; 45 years satisfies neither condition.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The present ages of three sisters are in arithmetic progression (equal gaps). The sum of their ages is 39 years and the product of the youngest and the eldest sisters' ages is 153. What is the eldest sister's age?

solution.concept: Let the ages be m − d, m, m + d; the sum fixes m
solution.explanation: 3m = 39 ⇒ m = 13. Then (13 − d)(13 + d) = 169 − d² = 153 ⇒ d = 4. The ages are 9, 13 and 17, so the eldest is 17.
solution.why_others_wrong: 13 years is the middle sister; 9 years is the youngest; 21 years takes d = 8 (from 169 − 153 = 16 without the square root).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: When Ravi reaches his father's present age, his father will be three times as old as Ravi is now. Ravi's father is 40 years old now. How old is Ravi now?

solution.concept: Ravi reaches 40 after (40 − r) years; the father ages by the same amount
solution.explanation: If Ravi is r now, he reaches 40 after 40 − r years, when his father will be 40 + (40 − r) = 80 − r. So 80 − r = 3r ⇒ r = 20.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 years subtracts the gap from the father's age instead of adding it (40 − r = 3r); 13⅓ years uses the father's present age (40 = 3r); 60 years is the father's age at that future time.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the average of the squares of the first ten natural numbers (1², 2², …, 10²)?

solution.why_others_wrong: 30.25 squares the average of 1 to 10 (5.5²); 35 divides 385 by 11; 55 is the sum of 1 to 10, not of squares.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average of 8 numbers is 25. The average of the smallest three of them is 18 and the average of the largest three is 33. What is the average of the remaining two numbers?

solution.concept: Total of all = 8 × average; subtract the totals of the two groups of three
