steps: Counting from the right (west) end: Ranjana 5th, Ojasvi 8th, Varenya 10th, Shailesh 11th, Uditi 15th, Pratyush 18th (the left end); 18 persons in all
Pratyush = 18th from the right (the left end)
solution.why_others_wrong: 8th is Ojasvi's original position; 17th and 11th are not Pratyush's seat.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Eight persons Bhavin, Chandni, Dipali, Faiz, Hiral, Imran, Juhi and Kunal sit in a straight row, all facing north. Two of them belong to each of four clubs: Chess, Hockey, Kabaddi and Tennis.
- Exactly one person sits between the two Chess players, exactly two persons sit between the two Hockey players, exactly three between the two Kabaddi players and exactly four between the two Tennis players.
- A Tennis player sits at the extreme left end of the row.
- Chandni sits at the extreme right end of the row.
- Faiz and Kunal belong to the same club.
- Imran sits second to the right of Bhavin, and Hiral sits immediately to the left of Imran.
- Dipali and Imran belong to the same club.
- Juhi sits at one of the extreme ends of the row, and Faiz sits somewhere to the left of Kunal.

Who is the other member of Hiral's club?

solution.concept: Fix the club pattern first, then place the names
solution.explanation: With a Tennis player at seat 1 and four persons between the Tennis pair, Tennis = seats 1 and 6. The only way to fit the other gaps in the free seats is Kabaddi 3 & 7, Chess 2 & 4 and Hockey 5 & 8. Placing the names puts Hiral at seat 6 (Tennis), so her club-mate is Juhi at seat 1.
steps: Kabaddi needs a gap of 4 seats among 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8: only 3 & 7 (2 & 6 and 4 & 8 clash with Tennis or leave no room for Hockey) ⇒ free 2, 4, 5, 8
Chandni = 8. Bhavin, Hiral, Imran sit in three consecutive seats from west to east

Juhi is at an end, so Juhi = 1. Imran's club-mate is Dipali: trio 2-3-4 needs Dipali at 2 ✗, trio 3-4-5 needs her at 8 ✗, trio 4-5-6 needs her at 1 ✗ (Juhi), trio 5-6-7 gives Imran = 7 (Kabaddi), Dipali = 3 ✓
Faiz and Kunal take 2 and 4 (both Chess), Faiz to the left: Faiz = 2, Kunal = 4
Hiral = seat 6 (Tennis) ⇒ the other Tennis player is Juhi (seat 1)
solution.why_others_wrong: Chandni and Bhavin play Hockey; Faiz plays Chess.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Eight persons Ishika, Jairaj, Kriti, Nakul, Pihu, Ritvik, Sanvi and Yashas sit in a straight row of eight seats, numbered 1 to 8 from the west end. The persons in seats 1 to 4 face north and those in seats 5 to 8 face south. (Facing north, the right is towards the east; facing south, the right is towards the west.)
- Ritvik sits at one of the extreme ends of the row, and Kriti sits immediately to his right.
- Ishika sits immediately to the right of Yashas, and Jairaj sits third to the right of Yashas.
- Sanvi sits immediately to the left of Jairaj.
- Yashas does not sit at an extreme end of the row, but Nakul does.
- Pihu faces north, but Yashas faces south.

How many persons sit between Nakul and the person who sits immediately to the left of Pihu?

solution.concept: When the facing depends on the seat, check which half each person sits in before moving right or left
solution.explanation: Yashas faces south, so he is in seat 5, 6 or 7, and Ishika and Jairaj are one and three seats west of him. Only Yashas = 6 works, giving (west to east) Nakul, Sanvi, Jairaj, Pihu, Ishika, Yashas, Kriti, Ritvik. Pihu (seat 4) faces north, so her left is west: seat 3, Jairaj. Between Nakul (1) and Jairaj (3) sits one person.
steps: Yashas faces south ⇒ seat 5, 6 or 7; Ishika = Yashas − 1, Jairaj = Yashas − 3
Yashas 5 ⇒ Jairaj 2 (north) ⇒ Sanvi 1, leaving only seat 8 for both Ritvik and Nakul ✗
Yashas 7 ⇒ Ishika 6, Jairaj 4 ⇒ Sanvi 3; Ritvik 8 needs Kriti 7 ✗, Ritvik 1 ⇒ Kriti 2, Nakul 8, Pihu 5 faces south ✗
Yashas 6 ⇒ Ishika 5, Jairaj 3 ⇒ Sanvi 2; Ritvik 1 needs Kriti 2 ✗ ⇒ Ritvik 8, Kriti 7, Nakul 1, Pihu 4 ✓
Pihu (4, north) ⇒ left = west = seat 3 = Jairaj
Between Nakul (1) and Jairaj (3): Sanvi ⇒ one
solution.why_others_wrong: Any other count comes from taking Pihu's left as east or from a case that breaks the clues.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Five friends Aniket, Bhumika, Chaitra, Daman and Eshwar sit at the five corners of a pentagonal table, one at each corner, all facing the centre. (Facing the centre, a person's right is the next seat anticlockwise.)
- Chaitra sits immediately to the right of Aniket.
- Bhumika sits second to the left of Aniket.
- Daman does not sit next to Chaitra.

Who are the immediate neighbours of Eshwar?

solution.concept: Fix one person and place the rest around him
solution.explanation: Going anticlockwise from Aniket: Chaitra (his immediate right), then two seats remain before Bhumika, who is second to Aniket's left. Daman cannot sit next to Chaitra, so the order is Aniket, Chaitra, Eshwar, Bhumika, Daman. Eshwar sits between Chaitra and Bhumika.
steps: Bhumika = second to the left (two seats clockwise) = seat 3
Seats 2 and 4 remain; seat 2 touches Chaitra ⇒ Daman = 4, Eshwar = 2
solution.why_others_wrong: Aniket's neighbours are Chaitra and Daman; Daman sits between Bhumika and Aniket.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Six persons Kamakshi, Manohar, Neha, Omprakash, Prakriti and Rajat sit around a hexagonal table, one at each side, all facing away from the centre. (Facing outside, a person's right is the next seat clockwise.)
- Manohar sits exactly opposite Kamakshi.
- Neha sits immediately to the right of Kamakshi.
- Rajat sits second to the left of Neha.
- Prakriti sits immediately to the left of Rajat.

Who sits second to the right of Omprakash?

solution.concept: Facing outside reverses right and left compared with facing the centre
solution.explanation: Number the seats 0 to 5 anticlockwise from Kamakshi. Manohar = 3 (opposite). Neha is to Kamakshi's right, i.e. clockwise: seat 5. Rajat is second to Neha's left (anticlockwise): seat 1, and Prakriti is immediately to Rajat's left: seat 2. Omprakash takes seat 4. Two seats to his right (clockwise) is seat 2: Prakriti.
solution.why_others_wrong: Neha is second to his left, Rajat third to his right, and Manohar immediately to his right.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Eight persons Ambika, Bhushan, Champa, Devesh, Gaurika, Harbhajan, Indrajit and Jyoti sit around a circular table, equally spaced. Some face the centre and the others face outside, and of any two persons sitting next to each other, one faces the centre and the other faces outside. (Facing the centre, the right is anticlockwise; facing outside, it is clockwise.)
- Ambika faces the centre, and Harbhajan sits exactly opposite her.
- Bhushan sits immediately to the left of Harbhajan.
- Jyoti sits immediately to the right of Bhushan.
- Indrajit faces the centre.
- Devesh is an immediate neighbour of Ambika.
- Gaurika sits second to the left of Champa.

Who sits third to the right of Indrajit?

solution.concept: With alternate facing, every second seat faces the same way
solution.explanation: Number the seats 0 to 7 anticlockwise from Ambika. Ambika faces the centre, so even seats face the centre and odd seats face outside. Harbhajan = 4 (centre); his left is clockwise: Bhushan = 3 (outside). Bhushan's right is clockwise: Jyoti = 2. Indrajit faces the centre: the only even seat left is 6. Devesh, Champa and Gaurika take 1, 5 and 7; Gaurika is second to the left (anticlockwise) of an outside-facing Champa, which works only for Champa = 5, Gaurika = 7, leaving Devesh = 1, next to Ambika. Indrajit (6) faces the centre: three seats anticlockwise is seat 1, Devesh.
steps: Even seats face the centre, odd seats outside
solution.why_others_wrong: Gaurika is immediately to Indrajit's right, Ambika second to his right, and Champa immediately to his left.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Ten persons Anup, Bhanu, Deepika, Gyan, Hiten, Ira, Kanchan, Mihir, Nirmala and Purab sit around a rectangular table, all facing the centre. One person sits at each of the two shorter sides and four persons sit along each of the two longer sides, so that each person on a longer side sits directly opposite a person on the other longer side. (Facing the centre, the right is anticlockwise.)
- Ira and Gyan sit at the two shorter sides.
- Mihir sits second to the right of Ira.
- Purab sits directly opposite Mihir.
- Deepika sits fourth to the left of Purab.
- Kanchan sits immediately between Mihir and Deepika.
- Hiten sits immediately to the left of Ira.
- Nirmala sits immediately to the right of Gyan.
- Bhanu does not sit next to Ira.

Who sits directly opposite Anup?

solution.concept: Number the seats round the table and pair the long-side seats
solution.explanation: Start at Ira's shorter side and number the seats 0 to 9 anticlockwise; Gyan is at seat 5. Seats 1–4 form one longer side and 9–6 the other, so seat s faces seat 10 − s. Mihir = 2, Purab opposite = 8, Deepika four seats clockwise from Purab = 4, Kanchan between them = 3, Hiten = 9 and Nirmala = 6. Bhanu cannot sit next to Ira, so Bhanu = 7 and Anup = 1. Seat 1 faces seat 9: Hiten.
steps: Ira 0, Gyan 5; seat s faces 10 − s
Seats 1, 7 for Anup, Bhanu; Bhanu not next to Ira ⇒ Anup 1
solution.why_others_wrong: Bhanu faces Kanchan, Nirmala faces Deepika, and Purab faces Mihir.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Ten persons Aditi, Bipin, Dhanush, Gautam, Hansraj, Jasmeet, Laboni, Murali, Neelima and Sameer sit around a table shaped like a regular pentagon. Five of them sit at the five corners and face away from the centre; the other five sit at the middle of the five sides and face the centre. Corner and side seats alternate around the table. (Facing the centre, the right is anticlockwise; facing outside, it is clockwise.)
- Aditi sits at a corner, and Murali sits immediately to her left.
- Neelima sits second to the right of Murali.
- Gautam sits immediately to the left of Neelima.
- Sameer sits second to the right of Neelima, and Bipin sits immediately to the left of Sameer.
- Hansraj sits immediately between Aditi and Laboni.
- Dhanush faces the centre.

Who sits third to the right of Laboni?

solution.concept: Corner persons face outside, side persons face the centre: read each clue with the speaker's own facing
solution.explanation: Number the seats 0 to 9 anticlockwise from Aditi (corner); even seats are corners (outside), odd seats sides (centre). Murali, to Aditi's left (anticlockwise), is at 1. Neelima is second to Murali's right (anticlockwise): 3. Gautam, to Neelima's left (clockwise): 2. Sameer, second to Neelima's right: 5, and Bipin, to Sameer's left: 4. Hansraj sits between Aditi and Laboni: seat 1 is taken, so Hansraj = 9 and Laboni = 8. Dhanush faces the centre: 7, and Jasmeet 6. Laboni (8) faces outside, so her right is clockwise: 7, 6, 5 — third to her right is Sameer.
steps: Even seats: corners, facing outside (right = clockwise); odd seats: sides, facing the centre (right = anticlockwise)
Hansraj between Aditi and Laboni ⇒ Hansraj 9, Laboni 8
Laboni 8, facing outside ⇒ right = clockwise: 7, 6, 5 ⇒ Sameer
solution.why_others_wrong: Dhanush is immediately and Jasmeet second to her right; Hansraj is immediately to her left.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Who likes Green?

solution.concept: Placing an attribute relative to a fixed person
solution.explanation: Lajja lives on floor 5, so the person immediately below her, on floor 4, likes Green: Suhas.
steps: Bottom to top: floor 1 Nimit (Yellow), floor 2 Pooja (Blue), floor 3 Kavin (Purple), floor 4 Suhas (Green), floor 5 Lajja (Orange), floor 6 Mrinalini (Pink)

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which colour does Lajja like?

solution.concept: The last colour by elimination
solution.explanation: Pink, Green, Purple, Blue and Yellow go to Mrinalini, Suhas, Kavin, Pooja and Nimit, so Lajja likes Orange.
steps: Bottom to top: floor 1 Nimit (Yellow), floor 2 Pooja (Blue), floor 3 Kavin (Purple), floor 4 Suhas (Green), floor 5 Lajja (Orange), floor 6 Mrinalini (Pink)
solution.why_others_wrong: Pink is Mrinalini's, Yellow Nimit's and Green Suhas's colour.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How many persons live between Pooja and Mrinalini?

solution.concept: Floors strictly between two persons
solution.explanation: Pooja is on floor 2 and Mrinalini on floor 6, so floors 3, 4 and 5 lie between them: three persons.
steps: Bottom to top: floor 1 Nimit (Yellow), floor 2 Pooja (Blue), floor 3 Kavin (Purple), floor 4 Suhas (Green), floor 5 Lajja (Orange), floor 6 Mrinalini (Pink)

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Who lives immediately above the person who likes Purple?

solution.concept: Locate the attribute, then move one floor
solution.explanation: Purple is liked by Kavin on floor 3. Floor 4, immediately above, is Suhas's.
steps: Bottom to top: floor 1 Nimit (Yellow), floor 2 Pooja (Blue), floor 3 Kavin (Purple), floor 4 Suhas (Green), floor 5 Lajja (Orange), floor 6 Mrinalini (Pink)
solution.why_others_wrong: Pooja lives immediately below Kavin; Lajja is two floors above him; Nimit is on floor 1.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Who lives immediately below Bansi?

solution.concept: Reading a neighbour off the floors
solution.explanation: Bansi lives on floor 7; floor 6 is Himani's.
steps: Bottom to top: 1 Falgun, 2 Akhil, 3 Gopi, 4 Eela, 5 Chinu, 6 Himani, 7 Bansi, 8 Darpan

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements:
All herons are storks.
No stork is an egret.

Conclusions:
I. No heron is an egret.
II. Some egrets are herons.

Take the statements as true. Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: Two-statement syllogism (Venn diagram method)
solution.explanation: Every heron lies inside the storks, and the storks lie completely outside the egrets, so no heron can be an egret: I follows. Because no heron is an egret, 'Some egrets are herons' is impossible: II does not follow.
steps: All herons are storks + No stork is an egret ⇒ No heron is an egret (All + No = No)
I follows; II contradicts I, so it does not follow
solution.why_others_wrong: Conclusion II is not forced by the statements (some valid diagram breaks it), so 'Both' and 'Only II' are wrong; I holds in every diagram, so 'Neither' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only conclusion I follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements:
Some tractors are scooters.
Some scooters are jeeps.

Conclusions:
I. Some tractors are jeeps.
II. No tractor is a jeep.

Take the statements as true. Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Either conclusion I or II follows

solution.concept: Two-statement syllogism (Venn diagram method)
solution.explanation: Two 'Some' statements give no definite link between tractors and jeeps, so neither conclusion is certain on its own. But I and II are about the same pair and between them cover every case (either some tractors are jeeps or none is), so exactly one of them must be true: either I or II follows.
steps: I and II: 'Some A are B' and 'No A is B' form a complementary pair
solution.why_others_wrong: Neither conclusion is certain alone, so 'Only I' and 'Only II' are wrong; but in every diagram one of the two holds, so 'Neither' is wrong. ('Either' replaces 'Both' under the four-option rule.)
solution.final_answer: Option D: Either conclusion I or II follows

I. All ladles are graters.
II. Some graters are ladles.

Take the statements as true. Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: 'Only a few' and 'Only' statements
solution.explanation: 'Only a few ladles are sieves' means some ladles are sieves and some are not. The ladles that are sieves are also graters, so some graters are ladles (II). The ladles outside the sieves may or may not be graters, so 'All ladles are graters' is not certain (I).
steps: Ladle ∩ sieve ≠ ∅ and ⊂ graters ⇒ some graters are ladles: II follows
Ladles outside sieves are unrestricted ⇒ I not certain
solution.why_others_wrong: Conclusion I is not forced by the statements (some valid diagram breaks it), so 'Both' and 'Only I' are wrong; II holds in every diagram, so 'Neither' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only conclusion II follows

Conclusions:
I. Some beavers are walruses.
II. All otters being walruses is a possibility.

Take the statements as true. Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: 'Only a few' and 'Only' statements
solution.explanation: 'Only beavers are otters' means every otter is a beaver. The walruses that are otters are therefore beavers, so some beavers are walruses (I). Nothing stops the walrus circle from covering the whole otter circle, so 'All otters being walruses' is possible (II).
steps: Only beavers are otters ⇒ All otters are beavers
Walruses may enclose all otters ⇒ II (possibility) follows
solution.why_others_wrong: Each conclusion holds in every valid diagram, so choosing only one of them, or neither, is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements:
Some daisies are lotuses.
No lotus is a marigold.

Conclusions:
I. All daisies being marigolds is a possibility.
II. Some lotuses being marigolds is a possibility.

Take the statements as true. Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: Possibility conclusions in syllogism
solution.explanation: Some daisies are lotuses, and no lotus can be a marigold, so those daisies can never be marigolds: 'All daisies being marigolds' is impossible (I fails). 'No lotus is a marigold' is definite, so 'Some lotuses being marigolds' is impossible too (II fails).
steps: Daisy ∩ lotus is outside marigolds ⇒ all daisies can never be marigolds: I fails
No lotus is a marigold (given) ⇒ II is impossible
solution.why_others_wrong: Each conclusion fails in at least one valid diagram, so 'Only I', 'Only II' and 'Both' are wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Neither conclusion I nor II follows

steps: Auditor ∩ banker ≠ ∅ and outside traders ⇒ I follows
Cashiers need not touch the auditor–banker overlap ⇒ II not certain

solution.concept: 'Only a few' and 'Only' statements

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements:
Some canals are creeks.

solution.explanation: The canals that are creeks are deltas, and no delta is a fjord, so those canals are not fjords: 'Some canals are not fjords' is definite (II). For the same reason all canals can never be fjords, so the possibility in I fails.
steps: Canal ∩ creek ⊂ deltas, which are outside fjords
⇒ some canals are not fjords: II follows
⇒ 'All canals are fjords' is impossible: I fails
solution.why_others_wrong: Conclusion I is not forced by the statements (some valid diagram breaks it), so 'Both' and 'Only I' are wrong; II holds in every diagram, so 'Neither' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only conclusion II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements:
Only a few vultures are peacocks.
All peacocks are kingfishers.
Some ibises are not kingfishers.

Conclusions:
I. All vultures are kingfishers.
II. All ibises being peacocks is a possibility.

Take the statements as true. Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: Possibility conclusions in syllogism
solution.explanation: The vultures that are not peacocks may lie outside the kingfishers, so 'All vultures are kingfishers' is not certain (I). Some ibises are outside the kingfishers, and every peacock is inside them, so those ibises can never be peacocks: 'All ibises being peacocks' is impossible (II).
steps: Vultures outside peacocks are unrestricted ⇒ I not certain
Ibises outside kingfishers cannot be peacocks (peacocks ⊂ kingfishers) ⇒ II impossible
solution.why_others_wrong: Each conclusion fails in at least one valid diagram, so 'Only I', 'Only II' and 'Both' are wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Neither conclusion I nor II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements:
Only rockets are gliders.
No rocket is a drone.
Some satellites are drones.

Conclusions:
I. No glider is a drone.
II. Some satellites being rockets is a possibility.

Take the statements as true. Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: Possibility conclusions in syllogism
solution.explanation: 'Only rockets are gliders' puts every glider inside the rockets; no rocket is a drone, so no glider is a drone (I). Some satellites are drones, but the other satellites are unrestricted and may overlap the rockets, so 'Some satellites being rockets' is possible (II).
steps: Only rockets are gliders ⇒ gliders ⊂ rockets
Rockets ∩ drones = ∅ ⇒ No glider is a drone: I follows
Satellites outside drones may meet rockets ⇒ II (possibility) follows
solution.why_others_wrong: Each conclusion holds in every valid diagram, so choosing only one of them, or neither, is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements:
All vases are urns.
Only a few urns are pitchers.
No pitcher is a goblet.

Conclusions:
I. Some urns are not goblets.
II. All urns being goblets is a possibility.

Take the statements as true. Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: Possibility conclusions in syllogism
solution.explanation: Some urns are pitchers, and no pitcher is a goblet, so those urns are not goblets: I follows. For the same reason all urns can never be goblets, so the possibility in II fails.
steps: ⇒ some urns are not goblets: I follows
⇒ all urns being goblets is impossible: II fails
solution.why_others_wrong: Conclusion II is not forced by the statements (some valid diagram breaks it), so 'Both' and 'Only II' are wrong; I holds in every diagram, so 'Neither' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only conclusion I follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Conclusions:
I. Some flares are beacons.
II. All beacons being signals is a possibility.

Which one of the following sets of statements, taken to be true, makes both conclusions I and II definitely follow?

options.text: No beacon is a flare. Some flares are signals.
All flares are signals. Some beacons are not signals.
All beacons are flares. No flare is a signal.
Some beacons are flares. All flares are signals.

solution.concept: Reverse syllogism: testing candidate statement sets
solution.explanation: With 'Some beacons are flares. All flares are signals.', some flares are beacons (I), and the beacons not yet placed are free, so all of them may lie inside the signals (II).
steps: Test each set for both conclusions
Set 'Some beacons are flares; All flares are signals': I definite, II possible ⇒ both follow
solution.why_others_wrong: 'All beacons are flares. No flare is a signal.' makes every beacon a non-signal, so II fails. 'No beacon is a flare…' contradicts I. 'All flares are signals. Some beacons are not signals.' gives no definite flare–beacon overlap, so I fails (and II fails too).
solution.final_answer: Option D: Some beacons are flares. All flares are signals.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: K ≥ T > B = R ≥ F < W

Conclusions:
I. K > F
II. W > B

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Both I and II are true

solution.concept: Reading a combined inequality chain
solution.explanation: K ≥ T > B = R ≥ F gives K > F (one strict sign on the way). W and B are on opposite sides of the turn at F (R ≥ F < W), so W > B is not certain.
steps: I: K ≥ T > B = R ≥ F ⇒ K > F, true
II: B = R ≥ F < W: direction turns at F ⇒ no relation
solution.why_others_wrong: II is not definitely true (a valid ordering breaks it), so 'Only II' and 'Both' are wrong; I always holds, so 'Neither' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only I is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: D < Q = L ≥ Z > M ≤ H

Conclusions:
I. D < Z
II. H > Z

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Both I and II are true

solution.concept: Reading a combined inequality chain
solution.explanation: D < Q = L ≥ Z changes direction at L (rising, then falling), so D and Z are unrelated. Z > M ≤ H turns at M, so H and Z are unrelated too.
steps: I: D < Q = L ≥ Z: turn at L ⇒ no relation
II: Z > M ≤ H: turn at M ⇒ no relation
solution.why_others_wrong: Each conclusion fails for some ordering that satisfies the statements, so the other three are wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Neither I nor II is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: V = J ≤ S < N ≥ C > Y

Conclusions:
I. J > C
II. Y < N

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Both I and II are true

solution.concept: Reading a combined inequality chain
solution.explanation: J ≤ S < N ≥ C: the chain turns at N, so J and C are unrelated. Y < C ≤ N gives Y < N.
steps: I: J ≤ S < N ≥ C: turn at N ⇒ no relation
II: N ≥ C > Y ⇒ Y < N, true
solution.why_others_wrong: I is not definitely true (a valid ordering breaks it), so 'Only I' and 'Both' are wrong; II always holds, so 'Neither' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only II is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: P ⇑ R, R ↑ T, T ↔ G, G ⇓ M

Conclusions:
I. P ↑ G
II. M ⇑ T

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Both I and II are true

solution.concept: Decoding symbols, then reading the chain
solution.explanation: Decoded: P ≥ R > T = G ≤ M. P ≥ R > T = G gives P > G (I). M ≥ G = T gives M ≥ T (II).
steps: Decode: P ≥ R, R > T, T = G, G ≤ M
Chain: P ≥ R > T = G ≤ M
solution.why_others_wrong: Each conclusion holds for every ordering that satisfies the statements, so picking one, or neither, is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both I and II are true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: B ↓ H, H ⇓ X, X ↔ E, E ↑ U

Conclusions:
I. H ↓ E
II. H ↔ E

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Either I or II is true

solution.concept: Decoding symbols, then reading the chain
solution.explanation: Decoded: B < H ≤ X = E > U. Only H ≤ E is known, so neither H < E nor H = E is certain alone, but one of them must hold.
steps: Decode: B < H, H ≤ X, X = E, E > U
I: H < E and II: H = E split '≤' ⇒ either
solution.why_others_wrong: Neither conclusion is certain alone, but one of them must hold, so 'Neither' is wrong. ('Either' replaces 'Both' under the four-option rule.)
solution.final_answer: Option D: Either I or II is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: W ↑ F, F ⇑ K, Y ⇓ K, Y ↑ A

Conclusions:
I. F ↑ Y
II. A ⇑ K

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Both I and II are true

solution.concept: Decoding symbols, then reading the chain
solution.explanation: Decoded: W > F ≥ K ≥ Y > A. F ≥ K ≥ Y gives only F ≥ Y, so F > Y is not certain (I). A < Y ≤ K gives A < K, so A ≥ K is false (II).
steps: Decode: W > F, F ≥ K, Y ≤ K (K ≥ Y), Y > A
Chain: W > F ≥ K ≥ Y > A
I: F ≥ Y only ⇒ F > Y not certain
II: A < K ⇒ A ≥ K false
solution.why_others_wrong: Each conclusion fails for some ordering that satisfies the statements, so the other three are wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Neither I nor II is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: J ↔ C, C ⇓ V, V ↓ N, D ⇑ N

Conclusions:
I. J ↑ V
II. D ↑ C

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Both I and II are true

solution.concept: Decoding symbols, then reading the chain
solution.explanation: Decoded: J = C ≤ V < N ≤ D. J = C ≤ V means J > V is false (I). D ≥ N > V ≥ C gives D > C (II).
steps: Decode: J = C, C ≤ V, V < N, D ≥ N
Chain: J = C ≤ V < N ≤ D
I: J ≤ V ⇒ J > V false
II: D ≥ N > V ≥ C ⇒ D > C, true
solution.why_others_wrong: I is not definitely true (a valid ordering breaks it), so 'Only I' and 'Both' are wrong; II always holds, so 'Neither' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only II is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: G > S; S ≥ Z; Z = O; O < I; I ≤ T

Conclusions:
I. G > O
II. T > S

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Both I and II are true

solution.concept: Reading a combined inequality chain
solution.explanation: Combined: G > S ≥ Z = O < I ≤ T. G > S ≥ Z = O gives G > O (I). T and S lie on opposite sides of the turn at O, so T > S is not certain (II).
steps: Chain: G > S ≥ Z = O < I ≤ T
II: S ≥ … O < … T: turn at O ⇒ no relation
solution.why_others_wrong: II is not definitely true (a valid ordering breaks it), so 'Only II' and 'Both' are wrong; I always holds, so 'Neither' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only I is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: U ≤ E; E < Q; Q = W; B ≥ W; R < U

Conclusions:
I. B > U
II. R < Q

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Both I and II are true

solution.concept: Reading a combined inequality chain
solution.explanation: Combined: R < U ≤ E < Q = W ≤ B. Every sign from R to B points the same way, so B > U (I) and R < Q (II).
steps: Chain: R < U ≤ E < Q = W ≤ B
I: B ≥ W = Q > E ≥ U ⇒ B > U, true
II: R < U ≤ E < Q ⇒ R < Q, true
solution.why_others_wrong: Each conclusion holds for every ordering that satisfies the statements, so picking one, or neither, is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both I and II are true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: H ≥ N; N > P; P ≤ Y; Y = F; F < L; K ≥ H

Conclusions:
I. K > Y
II. L > N

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Both I and II are true

solution.concept: Reading a combined inequality chain
solution.explanation: Combined: K ≥ H ≥ N > P ≤ Y = F < L. K and Y, and L and N, are compared across the turn at P (N > P ≤ Y), so neither relation is fixed.
steps: Chain: K ≥ H ≥ N > P ≤ Y = F < L
I: K … N > P ≤ Y: turn at P ⇒ no relation
II: N > P ≤ … L: turn at P ⇒ no relation
solution.why_others_wrong: Each conclusion fails for some ordering that satisfies the statements, so the other three are wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Neither I nor II is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: A ≥ X; X = C; C > V; V ≥ O; M ≤ O; M < S

Conclusions:
I. A > O
II. S > V
III. V ≥ M

Which of the conclusions is/are definitely true?

options.text: Only I and III are true
All I, II and III are true

solution.concept: Three conclusions tested against one chain
solution.explanation: Combined: A ≥ X = C > V ≥ O ≥ M < S. A > O follows (I). S and V are on opposite sides of the turn at M, so S > V is not certain (II). V ≥ O ≥ M gives V ≥ M (III).
steps: Chain: A ≥ X = C > V ≥ O ≥ M < S
II: turn at M ⇒ not certain
III: V ≥ O ≥ M ⇒ V ≥ M, true
solution.why_others_wrong: 'All three' wrongly accepts II; 'Only I' misses III ('≥' conclusions are true when the chain gives ≥); 'Only III' misses I.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only I and III are true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Five colleagues Bhoomi, Chetan, Dilnaz, Ekansh and Farida each take a week's leave in 2027 (not a leap year), in five different months among February, May, June, August and December.
- Chetan's month has the shortest name of the five months.
- Farida's month is the next of these five months after Chetan's.
- Bhoomi's month has 28 days.
- Ekansh's month comes before Dilnaz's.

Who takes leave in August?

solution.concept: Fix the months with a unique property first
solution.explanation: May has the shortest name (3 letters), so Chetan takes May; the next listed month, June, goes to Farida. Only February has 28 days: Bhoomi. August and December remain, and Ekansh is before Dilnaz, so Ekansh takes August.
steps: Ekansh before Dilnaz ⇒ Ekansh August, Dilnaz December
solution.why_others_wrong: Dilnaz takes December, Farida June and Chetan May.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Five persons Gopal, Hetal, Ira, Jatin and Kavya each book a cooking class in the same month, on five different dates among the 6th, 9th, 15th, 16th and 28th.
- Gopal's date is a perfect square greater than 10.
- Hetal's date is 12 days after Gopal's.
- Ira's date is an odd number smaller than 10.
- Jatin's date is earlier than Kavya's.

Whose class is on the date that comes immediately after Ira's?

solution.concept: Number properties of the dates
solution.explanation: Of the five dates, 9 and 16 are perfect squares and only 16 is greater than 10: Gopal. Hetal = 16 + 12 = 28. The odd dates below 10: only 9, so Ira has the 9th. Jatin and Kavya share the 6th and the 15th, and Jatin is earlier: Jatin 6th, Kavya 15th. The date right after the 9th is the 15th: Kavya.
solution.why_others_wrong: Jatin has the 6th (before Ira), Gopal the 16th and Hetal the 28th.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Five cousins Nupur, Om, Pallavi, Rakesh and Sanya were born in five different years among 2008, 2011, 2013, 2016 and 2019. Ages are counted in completed years on their birthdays.
- Nupur and Om were born in leap years, and Nupur is older than Om.
- Pallavi is exactly three years younger than Om.
- Rakesh is older than Sanya.

What is the sum of the ages of Rakesh and Om on their birthdays in 2026?

solution.concept: Leap years are divisible by 4
solution.explanation: Among the five years only 2008 and 2016 are divisible by 4, so Nupur (older) was born in 2008 and Om in 2016. Pallavi = 2016 + 3 = 2019. Rakesh and Sanya share 2011 and 2013, Rakesh older: Rakesh 2011, Sanya 2013. In 2026 Rakesh is 15 and Om 10: 25.
solution.why_others_wrong: 23 adds Sanya's age (13) to Om's; 28 adds Rakesh's and Sanya's; 26 uses Rakesh's age as 16.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Five persons Tanuj, Urmila, Vikrant, Yashika and Zubin each hold an event on the 1st of a different month of 2027. 1 January 2027 is a Friday, and 2027 is not a leap year.
- Tanuj's event falls on a Sunday.
- Urmila's event falls on a Thursday in the first half of the year.
- Vikrant's event falls on the same day of the week as Urmila's.
- Yashika's event falls on a Monday, in a month that has 30 days.
- Zubin's event falls on a Wednesday and comes after Yashika's.

How many of the five events are held in a month that has 31 days?

solution.concept: Weekday of the 1st of each month (odd days)
solution.explanation: A month of 31 days moves the weekday on by 3, a 30-day month by 2 and February (28 days) by 0. From Friday 1 January the 1sts of 2027 fall on: Jan Fri, Feb Mon, Mar Mon, Apr Thu, May Sat, Jun Tue, Jul Thu, Aug Sun, Sep Wed, Oct Fri, Nov Mon, Dec Wed. Tanuj: the only Sunday, August. Urmila: Thursday in the first half, April; Vikrant: the other Thursday, July. Yashika: a Monday in a 30-day month — February and March fail, so November. Zubin: a Wednesday after November, December. The 31-day months are August, July and December: three events.
steps: 1sts: Feb/Mar/Nov Mon, Apr/Jul Thu, Aug Sun, Sep/Dec Wed
Tanuj Aug, Urmila Apr, Vikrant Jul, Yashika Nov, Zubin Dec
solution.why_others_wrong: Two or One leave out some of August, July and December; Four counts April or November, which have 30 days.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
A free health clinic runs once every 9 days in 2027: its first day is Sunday, 3 January, the next is 12 January, and so on. Five persons Prerna, Qadir, Raunak, Seema and Tushar each visit on a different clinic day between January and March 2027 (2027 is not a leap year).
- Prerna visits on the earliest clinic day that falls on a Saturday.
- Qadir visits on a Friday in February.
- Raunak visits exactly four clinic days after Prerna.
- Seema visits on a Tuesday in January.
- Tushar visits on the last clinic day in March.

On which date and day of the week does Tushar visit?

solution.concept: A 9-day cycle moves the weekday on by 2
solution.explanation: Clinic days: 3, 12, 21, 30 January; 8, 17, 26 February; 7, 16, 25 March. Since 9 = 7 + 2, each clinic day falls two weekdays after the previous one: Sun, Tue, Thu, Sat, Mon, Wed, Fri, Sun, Tue, Thu. So the last clinic day in March, 25 March, is a Thursday. (Prerna 30 Jan, Raunak 7 Mar, Seema 12 Jan and Qadir 26 Feb fit the other clues.)
solution.why_others_wrong: 25 March, Friday ignores the 2-day weekday step; 24 March, Wednesday miscounts February as 29 days; 16 March is the second-last clinic day in March.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Five persons Harsh, Ila, Jai, Kriti and Lalit visit a dental clinic on five consecutive days from Thursday to the following Monday, one person per day.
- Kriti visits on Saturday.
- Ila visits on the day immediately before Kriti.
- Jai visits on the last of the five days.
- Lalit visits on a later day than Harsh.

Who visits on Sunday?

solution.concept: Days across a weekend
solution.explanation: Kriti is on Saturday and Ila on Friday. Jai takes the last day, Monday. Thursday and Sunday remain; Lalit is later than Harsh, so Harsh visits on Thursday and Lalit on Sunday.
steps: Kriti Sat, Ila Fri, Jai Mon
Thursday and Sunday left; Harsh before Lalit ⇒ Lalit Sunday
solution.why_others_wrong: Harsh visits on Thursday, Jai on Monday and Ila on Friday.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Five teachers Mehul, Nisha, Omkar, Priti and Rohan work in a college. Four of them hold the posts of Principal, Vice-Principal, Head of Department and Lecturer, one post each, in decreasing order of seniority.
- Mehul is a guest lecturer and holds none of the four posts.
- Priti is the Vice-Principal.
- Rohan holds a post junior to Priti's post but senior to Omkar's.
- Nisha is senior to Omkar.

Who is the Head of Department?

solution.concept: Seniority order of posts
solution.explanation: Mehul holds no post. Priti is the Vice-Principal. Rohan is junior to Priti but senior to Omkar, so Rohan is the Head of Department and Omkar the Lecturer. That leaves Nisha as Principal (senior to Omkar, as required).
steps: Priti > Rohan > Omkar ⇒ Rohan HoD, Omkar Lecturer

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Five teams Amber, Coral, Ivory, Jade and Ruby play a round-robin tournament: every team plays every other team exactly once, and every match has a winner (no draws). At the end, no two teams have won the same number of matches.
- Jade won more matches than Ruby but fewer than Ivory.
- Amber beat Ivory.
- Coral lost to Ruby.

How many matches did Jade win?

solution.concept: Distinct win counts in a round-robin
solution.explanation: There are 10 matches and each team plays 4. Five different win counts adding up to 10 must be 4, 3, 2, 1 and 0. Then the team with 4 wins beat everyone, the team with 3 beat all but the top team, and so on — a strict ladder. Ivory > Jade > Ruby in wins, Ruby beat Coral so Ruby is above Coral, and Amber beat Ivory so Amber is above Ivory. Ladder: Amber 4, Ivory 3, Jade 2, Ruby 1, Coral 0.
steps: 10 matches; distinct counts from 0–4 adding to 10 ⇒ 4, 3, 2, 1, 0
Distinct counts ⇒ higher team beats lower
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 is Ivory's count, 1 Ruby's and 4 Amber's.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Six trainers Gauri, Hemant, Isha, Jairaj, Komal and Lakshay each take one session in a two-week course. Sessions are held only on Monday, Wednesday and Friday of each week (six sessions in all), one trainer per session.
- Isha's session is on the Wednesday of week 2.
- Exactly two sessions are held between Isha's session and Gauri's session.
- Komal's session is on a Friday.
- Hemant's session is in the same week as Komal's, and earlier.
- Lakshay's session is the first of the six.

Whose session is on the Friday of week 1?

solution.concept: Slots in order: Mon, Wed, Fri of week 1, then week 2
solution.explanation: Number the slots 1 to 6. Isha is slot 5; two sessions between Isha and Gauri puts Gauri in slot 2 (slot 8 does not exist). Lakshay is slot 1. Komal is on a Friday (slot 3 or 6) with Hemant earlier in the same week: slot 3 would need Hemant in slot 1 or 2, both taken, so Komal is slot 6 and Hemant slot 4 (slot 5 is Isha's). Jairaj takes the remaining slot 3, the Friday of week 1.
steps: Komal Friday: slot 3 fails (Hemant has no room) ⇒ slot 6
solution.why_others_wrong: Hemant is on Monday of week 2, Gauri on Wednesday of week 1 and Komal on Friday of week 2.

questions.question_text: Whose review is on the day immediately after the Assistant General Manager's review?

solution.explanation: The AGM (Darsh) reviews on Wednesday; Thursday's review is Gita's.
steps: Mon Bina–Manager, Tue Chhavi–Officer, Wed Darsh–AGM, Thu Gita–GM, Fri Ansh–DGM, Sat Eshita–Chief Manager, Sun Faisal–Senior Manager
solution.why_others_wrong: Chhavi is the day before Darsh; Ansh is on Friday and Eshita on Saturday.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Gauri's mother is the only sister of Hemant. Hemant's father is Vinod. How is Vinod related to Gauri?

solution.concept: A mother's father is a grandfather
solution.explanation: Gauri's mother is Hemant's sister, so she is also Vinod's daughter. Vinod is therefore the father of Gauri's mother: Gauri's (maternal) grandfather.
steps: Gauri's mother = Hemant's sister ⇒ Vinod's daughter
solution.why_others_wrong: Father and Uncle put Vinod one generation too low; Father-in-law would need Gauri to be married to Vinod's son.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Nikhil is the only brother of Manoj. Lalita is Manoj's wife, and Ketan is Lalita's son. How is Ketan related to Nikhil?

solution.concept: A brother's son is a nephew
solution.explanation: Ketan is the son of Lalita and her husband Manoj. Manoj is Nikhil's brother, so Ketan is the son of Nikhil's brother: Nikhil's nephew.
solution.why_others_wrong: Ketan's father is Manoj, not Nikhil; Ketan is a generation below Nikhil, so he is neither his brother nor his cousin.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: A is the child of B. B is the only son of C, and D is C's wife. How is D related to A?

solution.concept: The wife of a grandfather is a grandmother
solution.explanation: B is the son of C and his wife D, so D is B's mother. A is B's child, so D is A's grandmother (whether A is a boy or a girl).
steps: A = child of B ⇒ D is A's grandmother
solution.why_others_wrong: Mother is D's relation to B; Aunt would need D to be a sister of A's parent; Mother-in-law would need A to be married to D's child.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Simran's husband is the brother of Tara. Tara's mother is Usha. How is Simran related to Usha?

solution.concept: A son's wife is a daughter-in-law
solution.explanation: Simran's husband is Tara's brother, so he is also Usha's son. Simran, the wife of Usha's son, is Usha's daughter-in-law.
steps: Simran's husband = Tara's brother = Usha's son
solution.why_others_wrong: Simran is not Usha's own child; she is Tara's sister-in-law, not Usha's; a niece is a sibling's daughter.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Deepa's son Arjun is married to Kavita. Mohit is Deepa's husband. How is Mohit related to Kavita?

solution.concept: A husband's father is a father-in-law
solution.explanation: Arjun is the son of Deepa and her husband Mohit. Kavita is Arjun's wife, so Mohit is her husband's father: her father-in-law.
solution.why_others_wrong: Kavita is not Mohit's own child; a brother-in-law would be in Kavita's generation; Grandfather skips a generation.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If 'L 4 M 2 N 3 O', how is L related to O?

solution.concept: Decode pair by pair
solution.explanation: L is M's brother; M is N's daughter, so L is also N's son; N is O's wife, so L is O's son.
steps: L 4 M: L is M's brother
M 2 N: M is N's daughter ⇒ L is N's son
N 3 O: N is O's wife ⇒ L is O's son
solution.why_others_wrong: Brother-in-law and Nephew would need L to be outside O's own children; Grandson skips a generation.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If 'E 5 F 4 G 1 H', how is F related to H?

solution.concept: A father's brother is an uncle
solution.explanation: E is F's mother; F is G's brother, so F and G are both E's children; G is H's father. F, the brother of H's father, is H's uncle (whether H is a boy or a girl).
steps: E 5 F, F 4 G: F and G are siblings
G 1 H: G is H's father ⇒ F is H's uncle
solution.why_others_wrong: H's father is G; F is a generation above H, so neither H's brother nor cousin.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In the expression 'U ? V 2 W', which code should replace ? so that U is definitely the husband of W?

solution.concept: Fix V's parents first
solution.explanation: V is W's daughter. With '1', U is V's father; V has only one father, so W must be V's mother and U, the father of her daughter, is W's husband. With '5', U would be V's mother (W's wife, not husband); with '3' or '4' U is V's wife or brother, which says nothing about U being W's husband.
steps: V 2 W: V is W's daughter
U 1 V: U is V's father ⇒ W is V's mother ⇒ U is W's husband
Test 3, 4, 5: none makes U W's husband
solution.why_others_wrong: '3' makes U V's wife, '4' V's brother and '5' V's mother — none makes U the husband of W.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How is Fatima related to Ekansh?

solution.concept: Fix both couples first
solution.explanation: Ekansh's father is Gopal, and Chinmay is Gopal's brother. Fatima is Chinmay's wife, so she is the wife of Ekansh's paternal uncle: his aunt.
steps: Anand + Bharati → Chinmay (+ Fatima), Damini, Gopal (+ Hema) → Ekansh
Fatima = wife of Chinmay = wife of Ekansh's uncle ⇒ aunt
solution.why_others_wrong: Ekansh's mother is Hema; Fatima is a generation above Ekansh, so she is not his sister; his grandmother is Bharati.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How is Chinmay related to Hema?

solution.concept: Husband's brother = brother-in-law
solution.explanation: Hema is Gopal's wife, and Chinmay is Gopal's brother, so Chinmay is Hema's husband's brother: her brother-in-law.
steps: Anand + Bharati → Chinmay (+ Fatima), Damini, Gopal (+ Hema) → Ekansh
Hema's husband Gopal; Chinmay = Gopal's brother
solution.why_others_wrong: Hema's husband is Gopal; Anand is her father-in-law; Chinmay is not Hema's own brother.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Who is Ekansh's father?

solution.concept: Use the 'not an uncle' clue
solution.explanation: Ekansh's father is a son of Anand, i.e. Chinmay or Gopal. The other son would be Ekansh's uncle, and Gopal is not his uncle, so Gopal is the father.
steps: Gopal is not an uncle ⇒ Gopal is the father
solution.why_others_wrong: Chinmay is Ekansh's uncle (Fatima's husband); Anand is his grandfather; the last clue settles it, so it can be determined.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How many female members are there in the family?

solution.concept: Read each member's gender off the tree
solution.explanation: Bharati (wife of Anand), Damini (a daughter), Fatima (a wife) and Hema (a mother) are female; Anand, Chinmay, Gopal and Ekansh are male. Four females.
steps: Anand + Bharati → Chinmay (+ Fatima), Damini, Gopal (+ Hema) → Ekansh
solution.why_others_wrong: Every member's gender follows from the clues: Chinmay and Gopal are Anand's sons and Ekansh is a boy.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

solution.concept: A parent's sibling's child is a cousin
solution.explanation: R is S's son; S is T's husband, so T is R's mother; T is U's sister, so U is R's maternal uncle or aunt; U is V's parent, so V is the child of R's mother's sibling: R's cousin (whatever the genders of U and V).
steps: R ▲ S ■ T: R is the son of S and T
T ● U: U is a sibling of R's mother
U ◆ V: V is U's child ⇒ cousin
solution.why_others_wrong: Nephew would put V a generation below R; Brother needs the same parents; Uncle a generation above.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Rekha said to Nitin, "Your mother's father-in-law is the only son of my father." How is Rekha related to Nitin?

solution.concept: Collapse the phrase step by step
solution.explanation: Nitin's mother's father-in-law is the father of Nitin's father: Nitin's paternal grandfather. He is the only son of Rekha's father, so he is Rekha's brother. Rekha is therefore the sister of Nitin's grandfather: his grand-aunt.
steps: Only son of Rekha's father = Rekha's brother
solution.why_others_wrong: Aunt would be the sister of Nitin's father; Grandmother would be the grandfather's wife, not his sister; Mother-in-law has no basis.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Grand-aunt (sister of his paternal grandfather)

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain system, every direction is renamed in the same way: south is called east, east is called north and north is called west. What is west called in that system?

solution.concept: Renaming = turning every direction by the same angle
solution.explanation: South → east is a 90° anticlockwise turn, and so are east → north and north → west. Turning west 90° anticlockwise gives south.
steps: Each name is 90° anticlockwise of the true direction
solution.why_others_wrong: North turns west the other way; East reverses it; West would mean no renaming at all.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Harsh drives 14 km towards the east. He turns left and drives 9 km, turns left again and drives 6 km, and then turns left once more and drives 3 km. How far is he now from his starting point, and in which direction?

solution.concept: Net east and net north displacement
solution.explanation: He ends 14 − 6 = 8 km east and 9 − 3 = 6 km north of the start: √(64 + 36) = 10 km, north-east.
steps: Turn left from east ⇒ north: 9 km → (14, 9)
Turn left from north ⇒ west: 6 km → (8, 9)
Turn left from west ⇒ south: 3 km → (8, 6)
solution.why_others_wrong: '10 km, North-West' mixes up east and west; '10 km, South-West' gives the direction of the start from the end point; '14 km, North-East' adds the two components instead of using Pythagoras.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How far is the school from the market, and in which direction?

solution.concept: A 5-12-13 triangle
solution.explanation: The school is 5 km east and 12 km north of the market: √(25 + 144) = 13 km, north-east.
steps: Market (0, 0), temple (0, 12), school (5, 12), hospital (−5, 0), post office (0, 6), library (−4, 0)
solution.why_others_wrong: '13 km, North-West' mixes up east and west; '13 km, South-West' gives the direction of the start from the end point; '17 km, North-East' adds the two components instead of using Pythagoras.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which place lies on the straight road joining the hospital and the school?

solution.concept: Midpoint test
solution.explanation: The hospital is at (−5, 0) and the school at (5, 12). The midpoint of this segment is (0, 6), exactly where the post office is. The library and the market lie on the line y = 0 and the temple at (0, 12), none of them on the segment.
steps: Market (0, 0), temple (0, 12), school (5, 12), hospital (−5, 0), post office (0, 6), library (−4, 0)
Midpoint of hospital and school = (0, 6) = post office
solution.why_others_wrong: The library (−4, 0), the market (0, 0) and the temple (0, 12) are off the hospital–school line.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the straight-line distance between the library and the school, and in which direction is the school from the library?

solution.concept: Difference of two positions
solution.explanation: Library (−4, 0), school (5, 12): the school is 9 km east and 12 km north of the library, √(81 + 144) = 15 km, north-east.
steps: Market (0, 0), temple (0, 12), school (5, 12), hospital (−5, 0), post office (0, 6), library (−4, 0)
solution.why_others_wrong: '15 km, North-West' mixes up east and west; '15 km, South-West' gives the direction of the start from the end point; '21 km, North-East' adds the two components instead of using Pythagoras.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In which direction is the hospital with respect to the temple?

solution.concept: Signs of the two components
solution.explanation: Hospital (−5, 0) minus temple (0, 12) = (−5, −12): west and south, so the hospital is south-west of the temple.
steps: Market (0, 0), temple (0, 12), school (5, 12), hospital (−5, 0), post office (0, 6), library (−4, 0)
solution.why_others_wrong: North-East is the temple's direction from the hospital; South-East takes the hospital as east of the market; West ignores the 12 km north–south gap.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Tina was standing in an open field facing south, and her shadow fell exactly to her right. At what time of the day was this most likely?

options.text: The time cannot be judged from a shadow

solution.concept: A shadow points away from the sun
solution.explanation: Facing south, her right is west, so the shadow pointed west. A shadow points away from the sun, so the sun was in the east: it was morning.
solution.why_others_wrong: In the evening the sun is in the west and the shadow would fall to her left; at noon the shadow is very short and points north (in India), not west; the side of the shadow does tell the time of day.
solution.final_answer: Option C: In the morning, after sunrise

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Vivaan walks 10 m towards the north. He turns right and walks 5 m, turns right again and walks 4 m, and then turns left and walks 3 m. How far must he walk now, and in which direction, to go straight back to his starting point?

solution.concept: The way back is the opposite of the displacement
solution.explanation: He ends 8 m east and 6 m north of the start, 10 m away. To return he must walk 10 m towards the south-west.
steps: Turn right from north ⇒ east: 5 m → (5, 10)
Turn right from east ⇒ south: 4 m → (5, 6)
Turn left from south ⇒ east: 3 m → (8, 6)
Displacement (8, 6): 10 m north-east of the start
solution.why_others_wrong: '10 m, South-East' mixes up east and west; '10 m, North-East' gives the end point's direction from the start; '14 m, South-West' adds the two components instead of using Pythagoras.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Kabir and Laila stand back to back, Kabir facing east. Kabir then turns 135° clockwise, and Laila turns 135° anticlockwise. What is the smaller angle between the directions they now face?

solution.concept: Find each new facing, then compare
solution.explanation: Kabir: east + 135° clockwise = south-west. Laila faces west (back to back with Kabir); west − 135° = south-east. South-west and south-east are 90° apart.
solution.why_others_wrong: 45° and 135° come from turning one of them the wrong way; 180° assumes they still face opposite ways.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: A drone takes off from point O and flies 9 km towards the north. It then turns 45° clockwise and flies 4√2 km, turns 135° clockwise and flies 25 km, and finally turns 90° clockwise and flies 9 km. How far is the drone from O, and in which direction?

solution.concept: A diagonal leg of k√2 moves k along each axis
solution.explanation: North 9 → (0, 9). A 45° clockwise turn points it north-east; 4√2 km moves it 4 km east and 4 km north → (4, 13). Another 135° clockwise makes it face south: 25 km → (4, −12). A 90° clockwise turn makes it face west: 9 km → (−5, −12). Distance √(25 + 144) = 13 km, south-west.
solution.why_others_wrong: '13 km, South-East' mixes up east and west; '13 km, North-East' gives the direction of the start from the end point; '17 km, South-West' adds the two components instead of using Pythagoras.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code language, PRINT is written as MOFKQ. How is GLOBE written in that code language?

solution.concept: Every letter moves back by the same number of places
solution.explanation: P→M, R→O, I→F, N→K, T→Q: every letter moves 3 places back. G→D, L→I, O→L, B→Y (B, A, Z, Y), E→B: DILYB.
solution.why_others_wrong: JORGH moves every letter forward; DILYC moves E back only 2 places; DJLYB moves L back only 2.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, BAT is written as 26 and FUN is written as 44. How is RICE written in that code?

solution.concept: Sum of positions plus the number of letters
solution.explanation: BAT: 2 + 1 + 20 = 23, plus 3 letters = 26. FUN: 6 + 21 + 14 = 41, plus 3 = 44. RICE: 18 + 9 + 3 + 5 = 35, plus 4 letters = 39.
solution.why_others_wrong: 35 leaves out the number of letters; 43 adds 8 (twice the length); 40 adds 5.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the code for 'early'?

solution.concept: Remove the codes of the shared words
solution.explanation: In sentence 1, today = mi (in sentences 1, 2, 3), train = ra (1 and 3) and leaves = ko (1 and 4). The leftover code ve is 'early'.
steps: today = mi; train = ra; leaves = ko
solution.why_others_wrong: ko is 'leaves', ra is 'train' and mi is 'today'.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which word is coded as 'pu'?

solution.concept: Leftover code of a sentence
solution.explanation: Sentence 4 is 'platform leaves at night' = 'pu sa zo ko'. platform = sa (shared with sentence 2), leaves = ko (shared with 1) and night = zo (shared with 3), so pu = at.
steps: platform = sa; leaves = ko; night = zo
solution.why_others_wrong: platform = sa, leaves = ko and night = zo.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the code for 'night train'?

solution.concept: Two codes, each from a shared pair of sentences
solution.explanation: night is in sentences 3 and 4, whose only common code is zo. train is in sentences 1 and 3, whose common codes are ra and mi; mi is 'today' (also in sentence 2), so train = ra. 'night train' = 'zo ra'.
solution.why_others_wrong: le is 'arrives', mi is 'today' and pu is 'at'.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: For which of the following words can the code NOT be found with certainty?

solution.concept: Words that occur only together cannot be separated
solution.explanation: 'is' and 'crowded' occur only in sentence 2. After today = mi and platform = sa are removed, they are left with 'tu' and 'ne' in an unknown order. early (ve), at (pu) and arrives (le) are each the single leftover of a sentence.
steps: early = ve, at = pu, arrives = le are fixed
solution.why_others_wrong: early, at and arrives each have a fixed code.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, MARKET is written as JDSLZQ and SILVER is written as UDQRHK. How is CORNER written in that code?

solution.concept: Swap the halves, then move each letter
solution.explanation: MARKET → halves MAR | KET → swapped KETMAR → each letter one place back: JDSLZQ. SILVER → VERSIL → UDQRHK. CORNER → NERCOR → MDQBNQ.
solution.why_others_wrong: BNQMDQ shifts without swapping the halves; ODSDPS moves the letters forward; MDQBNR leaves the last R unshifted.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, 5821 is written as 1845 and 7406 is written as 7093. How is 3958 written in that code?

solution.concept: Swap digits in pairs, then add 3
solution.explanation: 5821: swap the 1st–2nd and 3rd–4th digits → 8512, then add 3 to each digit (keeping only the units digit) → 1845. 7406 → 4760 → 7093. 3958 → 9385 → 2618.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6281 adds 3 without swapping; 9385 swaps without adding; 2617 adds only 2 to the last digit.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, PEARL is written as RCCPN. Which word is written as DPCLEF in that code?

solution.concept: Undo the rule letter by letter
solution.explanation: PEARL → RCCPN: the 1st, 3rd and 5th letters move 2 places forward (P→R, A→C, L→N) and the 2nd and 4th move 2 places back (E→C, R→P). To decode, reverse it: D−2 = B, P+2 = R, C−2 = A, L+2 = N, E−2 = C, F+2 = H: BRANCH.
steps: Decode DPCLEF: odd −2, even +2 ⇒ B R A N C H
solution.why_others_wrong: BRUNCH would be coded DPWLEF, BLANCH as DJCLEF and BREACH as DPGYEF.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, COIN is written as OKRG and LAMP is written as QODP. How is STORE written in that code?

solution.concept: Reverse, then shift by place
solution.explanation: COIN reversed is NIOC; then the 1st letter moves 1 place forward, the 2nd 2 places, the 3rd 3 and the 4th 4: O K R G. LAMP → PMAL → Q O D P. STORE → EROTS → E+1 F, R+2 T, O+3 R, T+4 X, S+5 X = FTRXX.
steps: Shift the k-th letter k places forward
solution.why_others_wrong: TVRVJ shifts without reversing; FSPUT moves every letter only one place; FTRXW moves the 5th letter only 4 places.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, DOG is written as 55 and BEE is written as 27. How is LION written in that code?

solution.concept: Each position is multiplied by the letter's place in the word
solution.why_others_wrong: 50 is the plain sum of positions; 119 counts the weights from the right; 137 uses 15 for I.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which element is 6th to the right of the 4th element from the left end?

solution.concept: Add when moving right
solution.explanation: The 4th element is P. Six places to its right is the 10th element: L.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How many letters in the arrangement are immediately followed by a number?

solution.concept: Look at the right neighbour of every letter
solution.explanation: Letter–number pairs: G 4, P 7, L 8, E 2, F 6, W 9, T 5 — 7 in all.
steps: Pairs: G4, P7, L8, E2, F6, W9, T5

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If the whole arrangement is written in reverse order, which element will be 8th from the left end?

solution.concept: Reversing turns left-end positions into right-end positions
solution.explanation: After reversal, the 8th from the left is the 8th from the right of the original arrangement, i.e. the 15th from the left: F.
steps: 8th from the left after reversal = 8th from the right before

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How many odd numbers in the arrangement are immediately followed by a letter?

solution.concept: Check the right neighbour of every odd number
solution.explanation: Odd numbers and their right neighbours: 7 U, 3 M, 9 A, 5 (end). Followed by a letter: 7 U, 3 M, 9 A — 3.
steps: Keep those with a letter on the right (5 is the last element)

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which element is exactly midway between U and W in the arrangement?

solution.concept: Midway = average of the two positions
solution.explanation: U is 6th and W is 18th from the left; (6 + 18) ÷ 2 = 12: %.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Which term should replace the question mark in the series?

B2, E5, I9, N14, ?

solution.concept: Letter and number move together
solution.explanation: Each number is the alphabetical position of its letter, and the letters move forward by 3, 4, 5, … places: B(2) +3 → E(5) +4 → I(9) +5 → N(14). The next move is +6: N(14) → T(20). So the term is T20.
solution.why_others_wrong: S19 adds only 5 again; U21 adds 7; T21 breaks the link between the letter and its position.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If all the vowels are removed from the arrangement and then the 10th to the 20th elements (both inclusive) of the new arrangement are written in reverse order, which element will be 6th from the right end?

solution.concept: Delete, then reverse a block, then count
solution.explanation: Without vowels (24 elements): 7 K # 2 R 9 @ D 4 £ 6 H Q 1 $ 8 B * 3 Z 5 % N 6. Reversing the 10th to 20th gives 7 K # 2 R 9 @ D 4 Z 3 * B 8 $ 1 Q H 6 £ 5 % N 6. The 6th from the right is 6.
steps: Reverse positions 10–20: 7 K # 2 R 9 @ D 4 Z 3 * B 8 $ 1 Q H 6 £ 5 % N 6

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In how many places in the arrangement do three consecutive elements follow the pattern 'number, consonant, symbol'?

solution.concept: Both neighbours must match
solution.explanation: Consonants with a number on the left: 7 K #, 6 H Q, 8 B *, 3 Z O. Of these, followed by a symbol: 7 K #, 8 B * — 2.
steps: Find consonants with a number on the left
Keep those with a symbol on the right

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the sum of all the numbers in the arrangement that are immediately followed by a vowel?

solution.concept: Filter by the right neighbour, then add
solution.explanation: Numbers followed by a vowel: 2 E, 4 U. Sum = 2 + 4 = 6.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other totals leave out one qualifying number or add a number that is followed by a consonant or symbol.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which element is 3rd to the right of the 2nd vowel from the right end?

solution.concept: Locate the reference element first
solution.explanation: Vowels from the right: O (24th), I (18th), U (11th), E (5th). The 2nd from the right is I (18th); three places to its right is the 21st element: *.
steps: 2nd vowel from the right = I, 18th from the left

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If the 1st and 2nd elements interchange their places, the 3rd and 4th interchange theirs, and so on to the end, which element will be 11th from the right end?

solution.concept: Swap in pairs, then count from the right
solution.explanation: After the pairwise swaps: K 7 2 # R E @ 9 4 D £ U H 6 1 Q I $ B 8 3 * O Z % 5 6 N. The 11th from the right is the 18th from the left: $.
steps: Swap each pair: K 7 2 # R E @ 9 4 D £ U H 6 1 Q I $ B 8 3 * O Z % 5 6 N
11th from the right = 18th from the left ⇒ $

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How many letters of the word belong to the first half of the English alphabet (A to M)? Count every occurrence of a letter.

solution.concept: A–M are positions 1 to 13
solution.explanation: Letters with positions 1 to 13: C, A, B, L, A — 5 (A occurs twice).

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If the letters of the word are arranged in alphabetical order from left to right, which letter will be 5th from the right end?

solution.concept: Sort, then count from the right
solution.explanation: Alphabetical order: A A B C L N O R S T U Y. From the right: Y, U, T, S, R — the 5th is R.
steps: Sorted: A A B C L N O R S T U Y
solution.why_others_wrong: S, O and N are 4th, 6th and 7th from the right.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If the first four letters of the word are written in reverse order, then the next four in reverse order, and then the last four in reverse order, which letter will be 5th from the left end?

solution.concept: Reverse each block of four
solution.explanation: CONS → SNOC, TABU → UBAT, LARY → YRAL: SNOCUBATYRAL. The 5th letter from the left is U.
solution.why_others_wrong: T is the 5th letter of the original word; B is 6th and C is 4th in the new arrangement.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

solution.concept: Check every adjacent pair
solution.explanation: Adjacent pairs that are consecutive in the alphabet: ON (O 15, N 14), ST (19, 20) and AB (1, 2) — three.
steps: Adjacent pairs: CO, ON, NS, ST, TA, AB, BU, UL, LA, AR, RY

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: The English alphabet is divided into groups of four letters from the left (ABCD, EFGH, …, with YZ as the last group), and the letters within each group are written in reverse order. Which letter will then be 15th from the left end?

solution.concept: Find the group, then the place inside it
solution.explanation: The 15th place falls in the 4th group (places 13–16), MNOP, which becomes PONM. Places 13, 14, 15 are P, O, N, so the 15th letter is N.
solution.why_others_wrong: O is the 15th letter of the normal alphabet; M and P are the other ends of the reversed group.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If the words PLASTIC, PLANET, PLATFORM, PLANTAIN and PLAZA are arranged in the order in which they appear in an English dictionary, which word will be in the middle?

solution.concept: Compare letter by letter after the common part
solution.explanation: All start with PLA. The 4th letters are S, N, T, N, Z, so the order begins with the two N-words: PLANE-T vs PLANT-AIN differ at the 5th letter (E < T), so PLANET comes first, then PLANTAIN. Then PLASTIC (S), PLATFORM (T) and PLAZA (Z). The middle (3rd) word is PLASTIC.
steps: 4th letters: N, N, S, T, Z
Order: PLANET, PLANTAIN, PLASTIC, PLATFORM, PLAZA
solution.why_others_wrong: PLANTAIN is 2nd, PLATFORM 4th and PLANET 1st.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a row of 36 students facing north, Harsh is 25th from the left end and Ishaan is 22nd from the right end. Ishaan sits to the left of Harsh. How many students sit between Harsh and Ishaan?

solution.concept: Convert both positions to the same end
solution.explanation: Ishaan is 36 − 22 + 1 = 15th from the left. Harsh is 25th from the left, so the students between them are those in places 16 to 24: 25 − 15 − 1 = 9.
solution.why_others_wrong: 11 is 25 + 22 − 36, the overlap that still counts Harsh and Ishaan; 10 forgets to subtract one; 8 subtracts one too many.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Five parcels P, Q, R, S and T have different weights.
- Parcel Q is heavier than parcel R but lighter than parcel T.
- Parcel P is lighter than parcel R.
- Parcel S is heavier than parcel T.

Which parcel is the second lightest?

solution.concept: Join the comparisons into one chain
solution.explanation: T > Q > R and R > P give T > Q > R > P; S is heavier than T. Order from the heaviest: S, T, Q, R, P. The second lightest is R.
steps: Order: S, T, Q, R, P
solution.why_others_wrong: P is the lightest; Q is third from the lightest; T is the second heaviest.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a test, Komal scored 8 marks more than Lata. Mira scored 5 marks less than Komal, and Nalini scored 2 marks more than Mira. Who scored the second highest marks among the four?

solution.concept: Express every score in terms of one person's score
solution.explanation: Take Lata's score as L. Komal = L + 8, Mira = L + 3, Nalini = L + 5. Order: Komal, Nalini, Mira, Lata. The second highest is Nalini.
solution.why_others_wrong: Komal is the highest, Mira third and Lata the lowest.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Twenty-nine children sit in a row facing north. Kabir sits exactly in the middle of the row. Lina sits sixth to the left of Kabir. What is Lina's position from the right end of the row?

solution.concept: Middle of an odd row = (n + 1) ÷ 2
solution.explanation: Kabir is (29 + 1) ÷ 2 = 15th from the left. Lina is six places to his left: 15 − 6 = 9th from the left, so she is 29 − 9 + 1 = 21st from the right.
solution.why_others_wrong: 9th is her place from the left; 20th and 22nd come from dropping or doubling the + 1.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Six ropes U, V, W, X, Y and Z have different lengths.
- Rope U is longer than rope V but shorter than rope W.
- Rope X is shorter than rope V.
- Rope Y is the longest.
- Rope Z is longer than rope W.

How many ropes are shorter than rope U?

solution.concept: Build the chain from the longest
solution.explanation: Y is the longest and Z > W > U > V > X, so the order is Y, Z, W, U, V, X. Two ropes (V and X) are shorter than U.
steps: Order: Y, Z, W, U, V, X
solution.why_others_wrong: One counts only V; Three and Four count ropes longer than U or include U itself.

solution.explanation: Order from the heaviest: Charu, Bimal, Abha, Ekta, Dhruv, Farhan, Gopi. The second heaviest is Bimal.

solution.concept: Count below a fixed place

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: The weights are whole numbers of kilograms, and each person is exactly 4 kg heavier than the next lighter person. If Farhan weighs 51 kg, how much does Bimal weigh?

solution.concept: Equal gaps: weight difference = number of places × gap
solution.explanation: Farhan is 6th and Bimal 2nd from the top, four places apart, so Bimal weighs 51 + 4 × 4 = 67 kg.
solution.why_others_wrong: 63 kg counts three gaps, 71 kg five, and 59 kg two.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Some persons sit in a row facing north. Ojas is 7th from the left end and Pia is 7th from the right end. Exactly four persons sit between Ojas and Pia. Which of the following could be the number of persons in the row?

solution.concept: Two cases: the two persons may or may not cross
solution.explanation: If Pia is to the right of Ojas, the row has 7 + 4 + 7 = 18 persons. If Pia is to the left of Ojas, Pia is 2nd and Ojas 7th from the left with four persons between them, so the row has 8 persons. Only 8 is among the options.
solution.why_others_wrong: 16, 17 and 19 do not leave exactly four persons between them in either arrangement.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Some persons sit in a row facing north. Ravi is 6th from the left end, and Sunil sits fourth to the right of Ravi. Tara is 10th from the right end, and exactly three persons sit between Sunil and Tara. What is the minimum possible number of persons in the row?

solution.concept: Check each case against the seats already taken
solution.explanation: Sunil is 10th from the left. Tara is either 14th or 6th from the left. The 6th seat is Ravi's, so Tara is 14th from the left and 10th from the right: 14 + 10 − 1 = 23 persons. This is the only possible number, so it is also the minimum.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15 puts Tara in Ravi's seat; 22 and 24 come from dropping or doubling the − 1.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
