questions.question_text: Under Section 45ZI of the RBI Act, 1934, who presides over a meeting of the Monetary Policy Committee if the Governor is absent?

options.text: The RBI officer nominated by the Central Board
The Deputy Governor who is a member of the MPC
A member elected by those present

solution.concept: Conduct of MPC meetings
solution.explanation: The Governor presides over MPC meetings; in his absence the Deputy Governor who is a member of the MPC (the Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy) presides. The quorum is four members.
steps: In his absence: the Deputy Governor-member
solution.why_others_wrong: The Act does not give the chair to an external member, to an elected member or to the Board-nominated RBI officer.
solution.final_answer: Option C: The Deputy Governor who is a member of the MPC

fact_checks.claim: The meetings of the Monetary Policy Committee shall be presided over by the Governor and, in his absence, by the Deputy Governor who is the Member of the Monetary Policy Committee (Section 45ZI(6), as summarised on the page).

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: At the October 2026 MPC meeting, Dr. Nagesh Kumar voted for the 25 bps repo rate increase but wanted to retain the neutral stance. What reason did he give in the minutes?

options.text: Continued geopolitical and trade policy uncertainties
Inflation had already fallen below the 4% target
Bank credit growth had slowed sharply
The rupee had appreciated too fast against the dollar

solution.concept: Policy stance and dissent
solution.explanation: The minutes of 5–7 October 2026 show two members, Dr. Nagesh Kumar and Prof. Ram Singh, preferring a neutral stance. Dr. Kumar said a neutral stance remained appropriate in view of continued geopolitical and trade policy uncertainties, which call for flexibility.
steps: Stance: Dr. Kumar preferred neutral, citing uncertainties
solution.why_others_wrong: Inflation was above 4% (4.8% in August), credit growth was strong, and he did not cite the rupee.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Continued geopolitical and trade policy uncertainties

fact_checks.claim: in view of the continued geopolitical and trade policy uncertainties, I feel that a neutral stance remains appropriate

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under Section 45ZE of the RBI Act, 1934, which of the following is a ground on which the Central Government may remove a member of the Monetary Policy Committee?

options.text: Not attending three consecutive MPC meetings without prior leave
Failing to meet the inflation target for three consecutive quarters
Dissenting on the policy stance in the published minutes
Voting against the Governor at two consecutive meetings

solution.concept: Removal of MPC members
solution.explanation: Section 45ZE lists grounds such as insolvency, incapacity, conviction for moral turpitude, undisclosed conflict of interest, abuse of position, and absence from three consecutive MPC meetings without prior leave. Voting or dissent is a member's right; missing the inflation target triggers a report by RBI under Section 45ZN, not removal of a member.
steps: Only absence without leave appears there
solution.why_others_wrong: Votes and dissents are recorded and published as part of the process; target failure leads to a report to the Government, not removal.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Not attending three consecutive MPC meetings without prior leave

fact_checks.claim: does not attend three consecutive meetings of the Monetary Policy Committee without obtaining prior leave

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Prof. Ram Singh supported the 25 bps repo rate increase of October 2026 but opposed changing the stance to 'calibrated tightening'. According to the minutes, why?

options.text: It might signal an extended cycle of rate hikes
He believed the repo rate should have been cut instead
He wanted the stance changed to accommodative
He felt a stance should be announced only in the Monetary Policy Report

solution.concept: Signalling role of the stance
solution.explanation: The stance signals the likely direction of future rate moves. Prof. Ram Singh favoured a mild hike because real rates would turn negative, but said that shifting from neutral to tightening may signal an extended cycle of rate hikes.
steps: Stance: wanted neutral, fearing a signal of prolonged hikes
solution.why_others_wrong: He voted for the hike, not a cut; he did not seek an accommodative stance; the stance is part of the MPC resolution, not an MPR-only item.
solution.final_answer: Option A: It might signal an extended cycle of rate hikes

fact_checks.claim: I do not favour shifting the stance from neutral to tightening mode, as it may signal an extended cycle of rate hikes.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: The Monetary Policy Report of October 2026 lists the baseline assumptions behind RBI's projections. Which set matches it?

options.text: Crude oil US$116 a barrel in H2:2026-27 and US$95 in 2027-28; exchange rate ₹95 per US$
Crude oil US$85 a barrel in H2:2026-27 and US$95 in 2027-28; exchange rate ₹88 per US$
Crude oil US$95 a barrel in H2:2026-27 and US$85 in 2027-28; exchange rate ₹95 per US$
Crude oil US$70 a barrel throughout; exchange rate ₹85 per US$

solution.concept: Assumptions behind the projections
solution.explanation: Table V.2 of the October 2026 MPR assumes the Indian crude basket at US$95 a barrel in H2:2026-27 and US$85 in 2027-28, the rupee at ₹95 per US$ during 2026-27, a below-normal monsoon in 2026-27 and global growth of 3.0% in 2026. Oil and the exchange rate pass through to domestic prices.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other sets reverse the oil path, use the realised September 2026 basket price (about US$116) as if it were the assumption, or give levels the MPR does not use.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Crude oil US$95 a barrel in H2:2026-27 and US$85 in 2027-28; exchange rate ₹95 per US$

fact_checks.claim: US$95 per barrel during H2: 2026-27 and $85 per barrel during 2027-28 ... ₹ 95/US$ during 2026-27 (Table V.2, baseline assumptions)

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: What role does the Central Government have in the deliberations of the Monetary Policy Committee under Section 45ZI of the RBI Act, 1934?

options.text: It may communicate its views to the MPC in writing from time to time
It must approve the MPC's resolution before it is published
It can veto a repo rate change within 14 days
Its nominee attends every meeting and has one vote

solution.concept: Independence of the MPC
solution.explanation: The Government sets the inflation target and appoints three members, but it does not sit in or vote at MPC meetings. Section 45ZI only allows it to send its views to the MPC in writing from time to time; the decision rests with the MPC.
solution.why_others_wrong: No Government official is an MPC member, the resolution is published by RBI without Government approval, and the Act gives no veto.
solution.final_answer: Option A: It may communicate its views to the MPC in writing from time to time

fact_checks.claim: The Central Government may, from time to time, communicate in writing its views to the Monetary Policy Committee (Section 45ZI(9), as summarised on the page).

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
Consider the following statements about the monetary policy provisions of the RBI Act, 1934:
I. RBI must publish the schedule of MPC meetings for a year at least one week before the first meeting of that year.
II. The Secretary to the Monetary Policy Committee is appointed by the Central Government.
III. RBI must publish a document explaining the steps it will take to implement the MPC's decisions.
Which of the above is/are correct?

solution.concept: Chapter IIIF of the RBI Act
solution.explanation: Section 45ZI requires the annual schedule to be published at least a week before the first meeting. Section 45ZG says the Bank (RBI), not the Government, appoints the Secretary to the MPC. Section 45ZJ requires RBI to publish a document explaining the steps to implement MPC decisions.
steps: II: Section 45ZG – Secretary appointed by RBI – false
solution.why_others_wrong: Any option containing II is wrong because the Secretary is appointed by the Bank.
solution.final_answer: Option B: I and III only

fact_checks.claim: The annual schedule must be published at least one week before the year's first meeting (Section 45ZI(2), as summarised on the page).
The Bank shall appoint a Secretary to the Monetary Policy Committee.
The Bank shall publish a document explaining the steps to be taken by it to implement the decisions of the Monetary Policy Committee, including any changes thereto.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
Consider the following statements about Dr. Nagesh Kumar's statement in the minutes of the October 2026 MPC meeting:
I. He noted that gross fixed capital formation was 34.3% in Q1:FY27, about 2.9 percentage points higher than in Q1:FY26.
II. He argued that inflation was being driven mainly by demand-side overheating of the economy.
III. He voted against the increase in the policy repo rate.
Which of the above is/are correct?

solution.concept: Reading MPC minutes
solution.explanation: Dr. Kumar cited GFCF of 34.3% in Q1:FY27 against 31.4% a year earlier (a 2.9 percentage point rise). He said inflation is driven largely by supply-side factors with no sign of overheating, and he voted for the 25 bps hike while preferring a neutral stance.
steps: II: he said supply-side, no overheating – false
III: the hike was unanimous – false
solution.why_others_wrong: II reverses his diagnosis; III is wrong because all six members voted for the increase.

fact_checks.claim: a healthy rate of gross fixed capital formation (GFCF), which was 34.3% in Q1:FY27 compared to 31.4% in Q1:FY26.
inflation is driven largely by supply-side factors and does not show any signs of overheating of the economy

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
Match each member of the MPC with an argument from his or her statement in the minutes of the October 2026 meeting:
1. Shri Saugata Bhattacharya   2. Shri Indranil Bhattacharyya   3. Prof. Ram Singh   4. Dr. Poonam Gupta
P. RBI's September household survey showed 3-month-ahead median inflation expectations jumping to 9.9%
Q. A gap between Indian and G7 interest rates matters for attracting debt capital flows
R. With headline inflation likely to hit the 6% upper tolerance limit, one may not want to wait for definitive evidence of generalisation
S. The weighted median and trimmed mean measures show high momentum of underlying inflation

solution.concept: Members' reasoning in MPC minutes
solution.explanation: Saugata Bhattacharya stressed the India–G7 rate gap and capital flows; Indranil Bhattacharyya pointed to weighted median and trimmed mean measures; Prof. Ram Singh cited the household survey (9.9%); Dr. Poonam Gupta argued against waiting given projections of inflation reaching the upper tolerance limit.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other options swap the household-survey, underlying-inflation and 'not wait' arguments between members.

fact_checks.claim: maintaining a certain gap between India and G7 interest rates is important for attracting debt capital flows.
The momentum of underlying inflation is also high as evident from the weighted median and trimmed mean measures in recent months.
the RBI's September household survey showed the 3-month median inflation expectation jumped to 9.9%
with projections indicating the likelihood of headline inflation hitting the upper tolerance limit of 6 per cent, one may not want to wait for more definitive evidence of generalisation

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: In the minutes of the October 2026 MPC meeting, Prof. Ram Singh backed a mild increase in the repo rate. What did he say the projected inflation trajectory would otherwise do to the real policy rate?

options.text: Make it equal to the SDF rate

solution.concept: Real policy rate
solution.explanation: The real policy rate is roughly the repo rate minus expected inflation. With headline inflation projected to average about 5.8% over the next three quarters against a repo rate of 5.25%, Prof. Ram Singh noted that the real rate would turn negative, which argued for a calibrated hike.
solution.why_others_wrong: A real rate above 3% or of exactly zero is not what he described; the SDF rate is a nominal corridor rate, not a real rate.

fact_checks.claim: the projected inflation trajectory will render the real rate negative

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Explaining her vote for the repo rate increase of October 2026, Dr. Poonam Gupta pointed to projections that headline CPI inflation could hit which level?

options.text: 2 per cent, the lower tolerance limit
6 per cent, the upper tolerance limit
8 per cent, the ceiling set in the RBI Act

solution.concept: Inflation targeting and pre-emptive action
solution.explanation: Under flexible inflation targeting the target is 4% with a 2–6% band. Dr. Gupta said that with projections showing headline inflation likely to hit the 6% upper tolerance limit (6.0% projected for Q3), one may not want to wait, since monetary policy acts with a lag.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4% is the target and 2% the lower limit; the Act sets no 8% ceiling.
solution.final_answer: Option B: 6 per cent, the upper tolerance limit

fact_checks.claim: with projections indicating the likelihood of headline inflation hitting the upper tolerance limit of 6 per cent, one may not want to wait

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: In the October 2026 MPC minutes, Shri Saugata Bhattacharya argued that the pace of tightening must also consider the external sector. Why did he say a gap between Indian and G7 interest rates matters?

options.text: It sets the ceiling of the LAF corridor
It determines the Government's borrowing calendar
It decides the level of the CRR
It is important for attracting debt capital flows

solution.concept: Policy rate and capital flows
solution.explanation: A higher domestic policy rate relative to rates in advanced economies keeps rupee debt attractive to foreign investors. Mr Bhattacharya said maintaining a certain gap between Indian and G7 rates is important for attracting debt capital flows.
steps: Relevant with the rupee under pressure
solution.why_others_wrong: The CRR, the corridor and the borrowing calendar are set domestically and were not linked to the G7 gap.
solution.final_answer: Option D: It is important for attracting debt capital flows

fact_checks.claim: maintaining a certain gap between India and G7 interest rates is important for attracting debt capital flows.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Shri Indranil Bhattacharyya urged the MPC in October 2026 to set aside the 'cautiousness bias' and act pre-emptively. What risk does the term refer to, as explained in the minutes?

options.text: Raising rates too fast causes a sudden fall in bank deposits
Changing the stance too often confuses the bond market
Acting too little lets inflation expectations de-anchor, forcing sharper tightening later
Waiting for the Union Budget delays transmission to lending rates

solution.concept: Pre-emptive monetary policy
solution.explanation: A footnote to his statement explains that the 'cautiousness bias' is the risk that a central bank, by doing too little, allows inflation expectations to de-anchor and then has to tighten more sharply. He therefore favoured a pre-emptive 25 bps increase.
solution.why_others_wrong: The footnote does not relate the term to deposits, the Budget or stance changes.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Acting too little lets inflation expectations de-anchor, forcing sharper tightening later

fact_checks.claim: I feel it is better to set aside the “cautiousness bias” (footnote 4: the risk that acting too little lets inflation expectations de-anchor, forcing sharper tightening later, as summarised).

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: In the October 2026 MPC minutes, Shri Saugata Bhattacharya cited an estimate of the real natural rate of interest of 1.4–1.9%. The repo rate after the meeting is 5.50%, and headline inflation was expected to average about 5.8% over the next three quarters. Taking the real rate as the repo rate minus expected inflation, how does it compare with the natural-rate estimate?

options.text: About +1.5%, within the estimate, so policy is restrictive
About −0.3%, i.e. 1.7 to 2.2 percentage points below the estimate, so policy is still accommodative
About −0.3%, within the estimate, so policy is neutral
About +0.3%, i.e. 1.1 to 1.6 percentage points below the estimate, so policy is neutral

solution.concept: Real policy rate vs natural rate
solution.explanation: Real rate ≈ 5.50 − 5.8 = -0.3%. The natural-rate range is 1.4–1.9%, so the real rate is 1.7–2.2 percentage points below it, which means policy remains accommodative even after the hike. That is why Mr Bhattacharya asked whether policy was 'too accommodative'.
steps: Real rate below natural rate → accommodative
solution.why_others_wrong: +0.3% uses the annual 2026-27 projection (5.2%) instead of the next-three-quarter average; −0.3% is not within 1.4–1.9%; +1.5% has no basis in the stated numbers, and a real rate below the natural rate is accommodative, not restrictive.
solution.final_answer: Option B: About −0.3%, i.e. 1.7 to 2.2 percentage points below the estimate, so policy is still accommodative

fact_checks.claim: The real natural rate of interest (pertaining to Q4 of FY23-24) estimated this to be 1.4-1.9%.
In this context, might the broad monetary policy environment in India now be too accommodative?
Headline inflation averaging about 5.8% over the next three quarters (cited by Prof. Ram Singh and Shri Indranil Bhattacharyya).

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: RBI's money market data for 3 November 2026 show weighted average overnight rates of 5.45% (call money), 5.43% (triparty repo), 5.48% (market repo) and 5.70% (repo in corporate bonds). With the repo rate at 5.50%, SDF at 5.25% and MSF at 5.75%, which statement is correct?

options.text: All four segments traded below the repo rate, between the SDF and the repo rate
Call, triparty and market repo rates were in the lower half of the corridor; the corporate bond repo rate was 20 bps above the repo rate but below the MSF
The corporate bond repo rate was above the MSF rate, the ceiling of the corridor
Triparty repo traded 7 bps above the repo rate, the highest of the government-collateral segments

solution.concept: Overnight rates within the LAF corridor
solution.explanation: The corridor runs from 5.25% (SDF) to 5.75% (MSF) around the 5.50% repo rate. Call (5.45%), triparty (5.43%) and market repo (5.48%) were just below the repo rate. Repo in corporate bonds, backed by riskier collateral, traded at 5.70%: 20 bps above the repo rate but 5 bps under the MSF.
solution.why_others_wrong: The corporate bond repo was above the repo rate; 5.70% is below the 5.75% MSF; triparty was 7 bps below, not above, the repo rate and was the lowest of the three.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Call, triparty and market repo rates were in the lower half of the corridor; the corporate bond repo rate was 20 bps above the repo rate but below the MSF

fact_checks.claim: I. Call Money 11,860.77 5.45; II. Triparty Repo 5,50,320.25 5.43; III. Market Repo 1,86,513.67 5.48; IV. Repo in Corporate Bond 6,311.45 5.70 (Money Market Operations as on November 03, 2026)
MSF 5.75; SDF 5.25 (RBI operations, November 03, 2026)

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: RBI's money market statement for 3 November 2026 shows an outstanding variable rate reverse repo of ₹25,555 crore at 5.49%, auctioned on 8 October 2026 and maturing on 6 November 2026. What was its tenor?

solution.concept: Term VRRR operations
solution.explanation: A variable rate reverse repo (VRRR) absorbs surplus funds from banks for a fixed period. The operation auctioned on Thursday 8 October 2026 had a 29-day tenor, maturing on Friday 6 November 2026.
steps: Tenor shown in the statement: 29 days
solution.why_others_wrong: 14 and 7 days are standard tenors but not this one's; 1 day is the overnight VRRR.

fact_checks.claim: 2(b). Variable Rate: Reverse Repo – Auction date Thu, 08/10/2026 – Tenor 29 – Maturity Fri, 06/11/2026 – 25,555.00 – 5.49 (Outstanding Operations)

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: In RBI's overnight VRRR auction of 4 November 2026 (notified ₹50,000 crore), offers of ₹73,907 crore were received and ₹50,015 crore was accepted at a cut-off rate of 5.49%, with 'partial acceptance of offers received at cut-off rate' of 67.64%. What does the 67.64% mean?

options.text: 67.64% of all offers received in the auction were accepted
Banks were paid 67.64% of the cut-off rate as interest
Only that share of the amount offered exactly at the cut-off rate was accepted, as offers exceeded the notified amount
67.64% of the notified amount was left unsubscribed

solution.concept: Allotment in variable rate auctions
solution.explanation: In a VRRR, offers at rates up to the cut-off are accepted. When the offers at the marginal (cut-off) rate are more than what is needed to fill the notified amount, they are accepted only in part; here 67.64% of the offers at 5.49% were accepted. Overall, about 68% of total offers (50,015 of 73,907) were taken, but the figure in the result refers only to offers at the cut-off.
steps: Bids at the cut-off pro-rated at 67.64%
solution.why_others_wrong: The percentage applies to offers at the cut-off rate, not all offers; interest is paid at the bid rate; the auction was oversubscribed, so nothing was left unsubscribed.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Only that share of the amount offered exactly at the cut-off rate was accepted, as offers exceeded the notified amount

fact_checks.claim: Notified Amount 50,000; Total amount of offers received 73,907; Amount accepted 50,015; Cut off Rate 5.49; Partial Acceptance Percentage of offers received at cut off rate 67.64

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: According to RBI's Monetary Policy Report of October 2026, how many variable rate repo (VRR) and variable rate reverse repo (VRRR) auctions did RBI conduct in H1 (April–September) 2026-27?

solution.concept: Fine-tuning operations
solution.explanation: The MPR says RBI conducted 36 VRR (injection) and 51 VRRR (absorption) auctions in H1:2026-27, as liquidity swung into large surplus. Average daily net absorption under the LAF rose to ₹3.21 lakh crore from ₹1.43 lakh crore in H2:2025-26.
solution.why_others_wrong: 51/36 reverses the two; '55 and 2' mixes up the Governor's count of VRRR auctions (incl. 2 term) since August; 12/87 has no basis.

fact_checks.claim: Overall, the RBI conducted a total of 36 VRR and 51 VRRR auctions in H1.
average daily absorption under the LAF increased to ₹3.21 lakh crore in H1:2026–27 from ₹1.43 lakh crore in H2:2025–26

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: On 3 November 2026 RBI absorbed ₹23,905 crore through an overnight VRRR at 5.49% and ₹1,74,812 crore under the SDF at 5.25%, and lent ₹5,765 crore under the MSF. Approximately what share of the day's absorption came through the SDF, and what was the net liquidity effect of the day's operations?

solution.concept: SDF as the floor absorption window
solution.explanation: Total absorption = 23,905 + 1,74,812 = ₹198,717 crore, of which the SDF was 1,74,812/1,98,717 ≈ 88%. Net = MSF 5,765 − 1,98,717 = ₹192,952 crore absorbed. Even though the VRRR paid 24 bps more, most surplus went to the standing SDF because the VRRR amount is capped by the auction while the SDF has no ceiling.
solution.why_others_wrong: 12% is the VRRR share; ₹1,98,717 crore ignores the MSF injection; the day's operations absorbed, not injected, liquidity.
solution.final_answer: Option A: About 88%; net absorption of ₹1,92,952 crore

fact_checks.claim: 2(b). Variable Rate: Reverse Repo 1 day 23,905.00 5.49; 3. MSF 5,765.00 5.75; 4. SDF 1,74,812.00 5.25; 5. Net liquidity injected from today's operations [injection (+)/absorption (-)]: -1,92,952.00

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: According to RBI's description of its monetary policy instruments, how is the percentage of net demand and time liabilities that a bank must keep as the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) prescribed?

options.text: By a resolution of the Monetary Policy Committee
Through an amendment to the RBI Act each time
Through the Union Budget each year
By notification in the Gazette of India, from time to time

solution.concept: Legal basis of the CRR
solution.explanation: RBI defines the CRR as the average daily balance a bank must keep with it as a per cent of its NDTL that the Reserve Bank may notify from time to time in the Official Gazette (the power comes from Section 42 of the RBI Act). The MPC decides only the policy repo rate.
steps: CRR is set by RBI, not by Parliament or the MPC
solution.why_others_wrong: The Budget and Act amendments are not used to set the CRR; the MPC's remit is the repo rate.
solution.final_answer: Option D: By notification in the Gazette of India, from time to time

fact_checks.claim: Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR): The average daily balance that a bank is required to maintain with the Reserve Bank as a per cent of its net demand and time liabilities (NDTL) ... that the Reserve Bank may notify from time to time in the Official Gazette.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Which provision of the RBI Act, 1934 allows RBI to require scheduled banks to keep an additional cash balance on the increase in their liabilities over a specified date (an 'incremental CRR')?

solution.concept: Incremental CRR
solution.explanation: Section 42(1A) lets RBI direct scheduled banks to keep, in addition to the normal CRR balance, an additional average daily balance calculated on the excess of their liabilities over those on a date RBI specifies; the additional balance can never exceed that excess.
solution.why_others_wrong: Section 17 lists RBI's business; Section 45ZA deals with the inflation target; Section 49 with the Bank Rate.

fact_checks.claim: Under Section 42(1A) the Bank may require an additional average daily balance ... provided that the additional balance shall, in no case, be more than such excess.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: The Monetary Policy Report of October 2026 says reserve money grew 8.5% (y-o-y) as on 15 September 2026, but 11.9% after adjusting for the first-round impact of the CRR change. Why is the adjusted figure higher?

options.text: The CRR cut increased currency held by the public, which is excluded from reserve money
The adjustment adds the SLR holdings released by the CRR cut
CRR balances earn interest, which is deducted from reserve money
The CRR cut reduced banks' required balances with RBI, which are part of reserve money

solution.concept: CRR and reserve money
solution.explanation: Reserve money includes banks' deposits with RBI, most of which are CRR balances. A CRR cut (to 3% of NDTL by November 2025) mechanically shrinks these balances, depressing measured reserve money growth. Stripping out this first-round effect gives a higher underlying growth of 11.9%.
steps: Reserve money = currency + bankers' deposits with RBI + other deposits
solution.why_others_wrong: Currency with the public is part of reserve money; RBI pays no interest on CRR balances; SLR securities are not part of reserve money.
solution.final_answer: Option D: The CRR cut reduced banks' required balances with RBI, which are part of reserve money

fact_checks.claim: Adjusted for the first-round impact of CRR change, growth in reserve money stood at 11.9 per cent (9.4 per cent a year ago).
As on September 15, 2026, reserve money expanded by 8.5 per cent (y-o-y) as against 5.6 per cent a year ago.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: RBI's money market statement for 3 November 2026 puts the average daily cash reserve requirement of banks for the fortnight ending 15 November 2026 at ₹8,16,655 crore. Assuming a uniform CRR of 3% of NDTL and the current rule that CRR is maintained on NDTL as on the last day of the second preceding fortnight, on which date's NDTL is this based, and what NDTL does it imply?

solution.concept: CRR arithmetic with the new fortnight
solution.explanation: Fortnights now run 1–15 and 16–end of month. For 1–15 November, the preceding fortnight is 16–31 October and the second preceding is 1–15 October, so NDTL as on 15 October 2026 applies. Implied NDTL = 8,16,655 ÷ 0.03 ≈ ₹27,221,833 crore ≈ ₹272 lakh crore.
steps: Second preceding fortnight of 1–15 Nov = 1–15 Oct → 15 Oct
solution.why_others_wrong: 31 October is the end of the immediately preceding fortnight; ₹24.5 lakh crore and ₹245 lakh crore come from misplacing the decimal or dividing by 3.33%; 30 September is not a fortnight-end used for this period.
solution.final_answer: Option A: 15 October 2026; about ₹272 lakh crore

fact_checks.claim: G(ii). Average daily cash reserve requirement for the fortnight ending November 15, 2026: 8,16,655.00

the period from the first day to the fifteenth day of each calendar month and sixteenth day to the last day of each calendar month ... based on the NDTL as on the last day of the second preceding fortnight

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: After RBI's amendment of the CRR and SLR Directions effective 15 December 2025, in which return do scheduled commercial banks report their SLR maintenance, and how often?

options.text: Form VIII, weekly, by e-mail to the regional office
Form A, fortnightly, in hard copy
Form VIII, monthly, on RBI's CIMS portal
Form X, quarterly, with the audited balance sheet

solution.concept: SLR reporting
solution.explanation: The December 2025 amendment says CRR and SLR maintenance are reported in Form A and Form VIII respectively. Banks file a fortnightly Form A and a monthly Form VIII electronically on the Centralised Information Management System (CIMS); paper returns are not accepted.
solution.why_others_wrong: Form A is the CRR return and is no longer filed on paper; Form VIII is monthly, not weekly; Form X is not the SLR return.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Form VIII, monthly, on RBI's CIMS portal

fact_checks.claim: the CRR and SLR maintenance and reporting in their returns i.e., Form A and Form VIII respectively ... The banks are required to submit fortnightly Form A return from December 15, 2025 and monthly Form VIII return
Form A and Form VIII are not to be submitted in hard copy / paper returns by Scheduled Commercial banks.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A scheduled commercial bank's required CRR balance for a fortnight is ₹1,200 crore. Both CRR and SLR are computed on the same NDTL. At the current CRR and SLR, what is its SLR requirement?

solution.concept: SLR as a multiple of CRR
solution.explanation: CRR is 3% and SLR 18% of NDTL, so the SLR requirement is 18/3 = 6 times the CRR requirement: 6 × 1,200 = ₹7,200 crore (NDTL = 1,200 ÷ 0.03 = ₹40,000 crore).
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹6,000 crore uses a 15% SLR; ₹21,600 crore multiplies by 18 instead of 6; ₹40,000 crore is the NDTL itself.

fact_checks.claim: CRR: 3.00%; SLR: 18.00% (current rates panel)
the CRR and SLR maintenance and reporting ... based on the NDTL as on the last day of the second preceding fortnight

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under the transition arrangements in RBI's CRR and SLR Amendment Directions of 11 December 2025, banks maintained CRR and SLR during 13–15 December 2025 and 16–31 December 2025 on NDTL as on 28 November 2025, and during 1–15 January 2026 on NDTL as on 15 December 2025. For how many consecutive days was the 28 November NDTL used, and what applied from 16 January 2026?

options.text: 19 days; NDTL as on the last day of the second preceding fortnight
19 days; NDTL as on the last Friday of the second preceding fortnight
16 days; NDTL as on the last day of the preceding fortnight
34 days; NDTL as on the first day of the current fortnight

solution.concept: Transition to calendar fortnights
solution.explanation: 13–15 December is 3 days and 16–31 December is 16 days, so the 28 November NDTL was used for 19 consecutive days. From 16 January 2026 maintenance is based on NDTL as on the last day of the second preceding fortnight; Friday-based references were replaced by calendar fortnights.
steps: From 16 Jan 2026: last day of second preceding fortnight
solution.why_others_wrong: 16 days omits the three transition days; the 'last Friday' rule was replaced in December 2025; 34 days wrongly adds 1–15 January, which used the 15 December NDTL.
solution.final_answer: Option A: 19 days; NDTL as on the last day of the second preceding fortnight

fact_checks.claim: During the transition period of three days i.e., December 13-15, 2025, the maintenance of CRR and SLR is to be done by the banks, based on the Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL) as on November 28, 2025.

for December 16-31, 2025 and January 1-15, 2026, maintenance is based on the NDTL as on November 28, 2025 and December 15, 2025, respectively; from January 16, 2026, based on the NDTL as on the last day of the second preceding fortnight

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Section 49 of the RBI Act, 1934 requires RBI to make public the rate at which it is prepared to buy or rediscount bills of exchange. What does the section call this rate?

solution.concept: Statutory basis of the Bank Rate
solution.explanation: Section 49, headed 'Publication of Bank rate', requires RBI to publish from time to time the standard rate at which it will buy or rediscount eligible bills of exchange or commercial paper. Today the Bank Rate is aligned with the MSF rate.
steps: Section 49 heading: Publication of Bank rate
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Policy rate' refers to the repo rate set by the MPC; 'marginal' and 'reference' rate are not the Act's terms.

fact_checks.claim: The Bank shall make public from time to time the standard rate at which it is prepared to buy or re-discount bills of exchange or other commercial paper eligible for purchase under this Act.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: On 3 November 2026 banks borrowed ₹5,765 crore overnight under the Marginal Standing Facility. The October 2026 MPR says MSF recourse averaged ₹0.01 lakh crore a day in H1:2026-27. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The day's MSF borrowing was about 5.8 times the H1 average and cost 5.25%, the SDF rate
The day's MSF borrowing was about 58 times the H1 average and cost 5.50%, the repo rate
The day's MSF borrowing was below the H1 average and cost 6.00%
The day's MSF borrowing was about 5.8 times the H1 average and cost 5.75%, the same as the Bank Rate

solution.concept: MSF and the Bank Rate
solution.explanation: ₹0.01 lakh crore = ₹1,000 crore, so 5,765 ÷ 1,000 ≈ 5.8 times. MSF funds are priced at 25 bps above the repo rate, i.e. 5.75%, and the Bank Rate is aligned with the MSF rate.
solution.why_others_wrong: 58 times misreads ₹0.01 lakh crore as ₹100 crore; 5.50% and 5.25% are the repo and SDF rates; borrowing was well above, not below, the average, and 6.00% is no current rate.
solution.final_answer: Option D: The day's MSF borrowing was about 5.8 times the H1 average and cost 5.75%, the same as the Bank Rate

fact_checks.claim: banks' recourse to the marginal standing facility (MSF) averaged ₹0.01 lakh crore during H1:2026-27

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: After the Bank Rate was raised to 5.75% on 7 October 2026, RBI revised the penal interest rates on shortfalls in CRR and SLR requirements, which are linked to the Bank Rate and depend on how long the shortfall lasts. What are the two revised rates?

options.text: 8.75% at first, rising to 10.75% if the default continues

solution.concept: Bank Rate as the penal reference rate
solution.explanation: RBI's circular of 7 October 2026 revised the penal rates to Bank Rate plus 3.0 percentage points (5.75 + 3 = 8.75%) or Bank Rate plus 5.0 percentage points (10.75%), the higher rate applying when the shortfall continues. This is why the Bank Rate still matters even though it is no longer a policy signal.
solution.why_others_wrong: 7.75%/9.75% use +2/+4; a flat 8.75% ignores the escalation; 6.75%/8.75% use +1/+3.
solution.final_answer: Option C: 8.75% at first, rising to 10.75% if the default continues

fact_checks.claim: the Bank Rate is revised upwards by 25 basis points from 5.50 per cent to 5.75 per cent with immediate effect. Accordingly, all penal interest rates on shortfall in CRR and SLR requirements, which are specifically linked to the Bank Rate, also stand revised as under: Bank Rate plus 3.0 percentage points (8.75 per cent) or Bank Rate plus 5.0 percentage points (10.75 per cent)

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: According to MoSPI's CPI (base 2024=100) release for September 2026, which division recorded the highest year-on-year inflation at the all-India combined level?

options.text: Personal care, social protection and miscellaneous goods and services

solution.concept: Division-wise CPI inflation
solution.explanation: In September 2026, the 'personal care, social protection and miscellaneous goods and services' division (which includes gold and silver jewellery) had inflation of 13.75%, ahead of restaurants and accommodation services (9.36%), food and beverages (7.36%) and transport (5.01%).
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three divisions were high but lower: 9.36%, 7.36% and 5.01%.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Personal care, social protection and miscellaneous goods and services

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: In the WPI data for September 2026 (headline WPI inflation 11.39%), which major group recorded the highest annual inflation rate?

solution.concept: Components of WPI
solution.explanation: Fuel and power inflation rose to 25.85% in September 2026 from 22.93% in August, driven by mineral oils and crude petroleum and natural gas. Primary articles were at 8.67%, manufactured products at 9.76% and the food index at 8.66%.
solution.why_others_wrong: Primary articles (8.67%), manufactured products (9.76%) and the food index (8.66%) were all far below 25.85%.

fact_checks.claim: Fuel and Power recorded the highest annual inflation rate at 25.85 per cent in September, compared to 22.93 per cent in August.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Among the key items in MoSPI's CPI release for September 2026, which item recorded the highest year-on-year inflation at the all-India combined level?

solution.concept: Item-level CPI inflation
solution.explanation: Onion inflation more than doubled from 48.78% in August to 108.09% in September 2026, overtaking silver jewellery (87.80%, down from 106.81%), ginger (62.85%) and garlic (54.62%).
solution.why_others_wrong: Silver jewellery led in August but eased to 87.80% in September; ginger and garlic were third and fourth.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: According to MoSPI's CPI release for September 2026, which of the major States (population above 50 lakh) recorded the highest headline inflation?

solution.concept: State-level CPI inflation
solution.explanation: Among States with population above 50 lakh, Tamil Nadu had the highest headline inflation at 6.81% in September 2026, followed by Odisha (6.70%), Madhya Pradesh (6.68%), Telangana (6.64%) and Andhra Pradesh (6.29%). All-India inflation was 5.54%.
solution.why_others_wrong: Odisha, Madhya Pradesh and Telangana were second, third and fourth.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: According to the Monetary Policy Report of October 2026, what was urban households' one-year-ahead inflation expectation in RBI's September 2026 survey?

solution.concept: Inflation expectations
solution.explanation: Urban households' three-month-ahead and one-year-ahead expectations rose by 70 bps and 60 bps to 9.9% and 10.0% respectively. Anchoring such expectations is central to inflation targeting and was one reason for the October 2026 hike.
solution.why_others_wrong: 9.9% is the three-month-ahead figure; 7.9% is rural households' one-year-ahead expectation; 6.8% is rural households' current perception.

fact_checks.claim: Urban households' inflation expectations for the next three months as well as one year ahead rose by 70 bps and 60 bps to 9.9 and 10.0 per cent, respectively
rural ... increased by 70 bps to 6.8 per cent in September 2026 ... one-year-ahead expectations also rose by 50 bps to 7.9 per cent

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
The October 2026 MPR gives 50% and 70% confidence intervals for headline CPI inflation in Q4:2027-28 of 3.1–6.1% and 2.3–6.9% respectively. Consider:
I. The upper end of the 50% interval lies above the upper tolerance limit of the inflation target.
II. The lower end of the 70% interval lies below the lower tolerance limit.
III. The 70% interval is 1.6 percentage points wider than the 50% interval.
Which of the above is/are correct?

solution.concept: Fan charts and the tolerance band
solution.explanation: The tolerance band is 2–6%. I: 6.1 > 6 – true. II: 2.3 > 2 – false. III: widths are 3.0 and 4.6 points, a difference of 1.6 – true. Wider intervals reflect greater uncertainty at higher confidence.
solution.why_others_wrong: Any option with II is wrong because 2.3% is above the 2% lower limit.
solution.final_answer: Option B: I and III only

fact_checks.claim: The 50 per cent and the 70 per cent confidence intervals for headline inflation in Q4:2027-28 are 3.1-6.1 per cent and 2.3-6.9 per cent, respectively.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: In the October 2026 MPC minutes, Shri Indranil Bhattacharyya noted that trimmed mean measures (5%, 10% and 25%) of CPI inflation rose from a range of 2.2–2.7% in March 2026 to 3.7–4.2% in August, and the weighted median from 2% to 3.5%. Which inference is correct?

options.text: The measures fell, showing the rise in headline inflation came from a few volatile items
Each measure rose by about 1.5 percentage points, pointing to broad-based momentum in underlying inflation
The trimmed means rose by 1.5 points but the weighted median by only 1.0 point, so pressure was narrow
All measures rose about 0.5 point, so underlying inflation was stable

solution.concept: Exclusion-based measures of underlying inflation
solution.explanation: Trimmed means drop the most extreme price changes and the weighted median takes the middle one, so they capture underlying inflation. Both ends of the trimmed-mean range rose from 2.2–2.7% to 3.7–4.2% (+1.5 points) and the weighted median from 2% to 3.5% (+1.5 points), a broad-based rise that supported a pre-emptive hike.
solution.why_others_wrong: The weighted median also rose 1.5 points, not 1.0; a 0.5-point rise or a fall contradicts the data.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Each measure rose by about 1.5 percentage points, pointing to broad-based momentum in underlying inflation

fact_checks.claim: Various measures of trimmed mean (5%, 10% and 25%) suggest that it has increased from the range 2.2-2.7 per cent ... the weighted median has increased from 2 per cent to 3.5 per cent over the same period.
Table IV.2 (August 2026, y-o-y): 5% trimmed mean 4.2; 10% trimmed mean 4.0; 25% trimmed mean 3.7; weighted median 3.5

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
For September 2026: CPI headline inflation 5.54% and CFPI (food) 7.74%; WPI fuel and power 25.85%, WPI food index 8.66%, WPI primary articles 8.67% and WPI manufactured products 9.76%. Consider:
I. WPI fuel and power inflation was more than four times CPI headline inflation.
II. WPI food index inflation exceeded CFPI inflation by about 0.9 percentage point.
III. WPI primary articles inflation exceeded manufactured products inflation.
Which of the above is/are correct?

solution.concept: Comparing CPI and WPI
solution.explanation: I: 4 × 5.54 = 22.16 < 25.85 – true. II: 8.66 − 7.74 = 0.92 – true. III: 8.67 < 9.76 – false. WPI is far above CPI because it gives more weight to fuel and intermediate goods, where the oil shock hit hardest; CPI has a large services share.
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing III are wrong because manufactured products inflation was higher than primary articles.
solution.final_answer: Option B: I and II only

fact_checks.claim: Primary Articles inflation also accelerated to 8.67 per cent in September ... Inflation in Manufactured Products increased to 9.76 per cent ... [the Food Index] recorded an annual inflation rate of 8.66 per cent in September
Fuel and Power recorded the highest annual inflation rate at 25.85 per cent in September
Retail inflation based on Consumer Price Index in September, 2026 is 5.54% ... food inflation, based on Consumer Food Price Index, in September, 2026 is 7.74%

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: The pre-packaged insolvency resolution process (PPIRP), introduced into the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code by the Amendment Ordinance of April 2021, is available for which borrowers?

options.text: Large corporate borrowers with bank exposure above ₹1,500 crore
Financial service providers such as NBFCs and housing finance companies
Individuals and partnership firms with debts below ₹1 crore
Corporate debtors classified as micro, small and medium enterprises

solution.concept: Pre-packaged insolvency (PPIRP)
solution.explanation: The IBC (Amendment) Ordinance, 2021, promulgated on 4 April 2021, provided a pre-packaged insolvency resolution process for corporate debtors classified as MSMEs. IBBI notified the PPIRP Regulations on 9 April 2021 to operationalise it, covering matters such as the base resolution plan and its competition with the best resolution plan.
steps: PPIRP = insolvency route under the IBC
Eligible debtors: corporate debtors that are MSMEs
solution.why_others_wrong: Individuals and partnership firms are not corporate debtors; PPIRP is not meant for large corporates; financial service providers are outside the corporate insolvency process of the IBC.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Corporate debtors classified as micro, small and medium enterprises

fact_checks.claim: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Ordinance, 2021 promulgated on 4th April, 2021 provides for pre-packaged insolvency resolution process (PPIRP) for corporate debtors classified as micro, small and medium enterprises.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: After receiving a demand notice under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act, a borrower sends a representation objecting to it. If the secured creditor does not accept the objection, within what time must it communicate the reasons for non-acceptance under Section 13(3A)?

options.text: Within 60 days of receipt of the representation
Within 15 days of receipt of the representation
Within 7 days of receipt of the representation
Within 30 days of receipt of the representation

solution.concept: Section 13(3A) of SARFAESI
solution.explanation: Section 13(3A) requires the secured creditor to consider the borrower's representation or objection and, if it is not acceptable, communicate the reasons for non-acceptance within fifteen days of receipt. Non-compliance can later be raised when the borrower challenges the creditor's measures before the DRT under Section 17.
steps: Creditor must reply with reasons within 15 days
solution.why_others_wrong: Seven and 30 days are not the statutory period; 60 days is the notice period given to the borrower under Section 13(2), not the creditor's reply period.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Within 15 days of receipt of the representation

fact_checks.claim: Where a borrower objects, the creditor must consider the objection and 'communicate the reasons for non-acceptance within fifteen days of receipt'.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's Commercial Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025, a resolution plan involving restructuring is proposed for a borrower to whom the lenders' aggregate exposure is ₹650 crore. What independent credit evaluation (ICE) of the residual debt is required?

options.text: One ICE, by the lead bank's statutory auditor
No ICE, because only accounts above ₹1,000 crore need one
Two ICEs, by credit rating agencies specifically authorised by RBI
One ICE, by any SEBI-registered credit rating agency

solution.concept: Independent credit evaluation under the prudential framework
solution.explanation: Restructuring or change-in-ownership plans for accounts where the lenders' aggregate exposure is ₹100 crore or more need an independent credit evaluation of the residual debt by credit rating agencies specifically authorised by RBI. Accounts of ₹500 crore and above need two such evaluations; others need one. ₹650 crore is above ₹500 crore, so two ICEs are needed.
steps: ₹650 crore ≥ ₹500 crore → two ICEs by RBI-authorised CRAs
solution.why_others_wrong: One ICE applies only between ₹100 crore and ₹500 crore, and must come from RBI-authorised CRAs, not any agency or an auditor; the threshold for needing an ICE is ₹100 crore, not ₹1,000 crore.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Two ICEs, by credit rating agencies specifically authorised by RBI

fact_checks.claim: Plans involving restructuring or change in ownership where the aggregate exposure is ₹100 crore or more 'shall require independent credit evaluation of the residual debt by credit rating agencies' specifically authorised by the Reserve Bank (para 32).
'accounts with aggregate exposure of ₹500 crore and above shall require two such independent credit evaluations' (para 34).

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025, the 'specified period' after a resolution plan is implemented (relevant for upgrading a restructured account) runs from the date of implementation until at least what share of the outstanding principal under the plan (plus any capitalised interest) is repaid?

solution.concept: Specified period and monitoring period
solution.explanation: The Directions define two periods from the date of implementation of the resolution plan: the 'monitoring period' runs until at least 10% of the outstanding principal (plus sanctioned interest capitalisation) is repaid, and the 'specified period' runs until at least 20% is repaid. An account can be upgraded only if it performs satisfactorily during the specified period.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10% defines the monitoring period, not the specified period; 25% and 50% are not used in either definition.

fact_checks.claim: 'specified period' shall mean the period from the date of implementation of resolution plan up to the date by which at least 20 per cent of the outstanding principal debt as per the resolution plan and interest capitalisation sanctioned as part of the restructuring, if any, is repaid (para 6(16)); the 'monitoring period' uses a 10 per cent threshold (para 6(8)).

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Lenders' aggregate exposure to Company X is ₹900 crore. Its restructuring plan gets credit opinions on the residual debt of RP3 from one RBI-authorised credit rating agency and RP5 from another. Under RBI's Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025, what is the position?

options.text: The plan cannot be implemented, since both required opinions must be RP4 or better
The plan can be implemented, since the better opinion (RP3) is above RP4
The plan can be implemented, since the average of RP3 and RP5 is RP4
The plan can be implemented if 75% of lenders by value approve it despite the RP5 opinion

solution.concept: RP symbols and plan eligibility
solution.explanation: An exposure of ₹900 crore (≥ ₹500 crore) needs two independent credit evaluations. Only plans that receive a credit opinion of RP4 (moderate degree of safety) or better for the residual debt from the required number of agencies can be implemented. RP5 signals a moderate risk of default, so one of the two required opinions fails the test.
steps: Each required opinion must be RP4 or better
RP5 is worse than RP4 → plan not eligible
solution.why_others_wrong: The rule is not satisfied by the better opinion or by an 'average' rating; lender approval cannot override the ICE condition.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The plan cannot be implemented, since both required opinions must be RP4 or better

fact_checks.claim: 'Only such resolution plans which receive a credit opinion of RP4 or better for the residual debt' from the required number of credit rating agencies shall be considered for implementation (para 35); RP4 denotes a moderate degree of safety and RP5 a moderate risk of default (para 33).
'accounts with aggregate exposure of ₹500 crore and above shall require two such independent credit evaluations' (para 34).

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025, the Chapter IV timelines for implementing a resolution plan apply from a reference date that depends on the lenders' aggregate exposure. Consider three borrowers: P (aggregate exposure ₹2,400 crore), Q (₹1,600 crore) and R (₹1,200 crore). Which is correct?

options.text: P from 7 June 2019 and Q from 1 January 2020; R is not subject to Chapter IV
P, Q and R all from 7 June 2019
Only P, from 7 June 2019; Q and R are not subject to Chapter IV
P from 1 January 2020 and Q from 7 June 2019; R from 1 April 2020

solution.concept: Reference dates under the prudential framework
solution.explanation: The table of reference dates sets 7 June 2019 for accounts with aggregate exposure of ₹2,000 crore and above, and 1 January 2020 for ₹1,500 crore and above but below ₹2,000 crore; for accounts below ₹1,500 crore the date is to be announced, and such accounts are not subject to the Chapter IV requirements.
steps: R: below ₹1,500 crore → not subject to Chapter IV
solution.why_others_wrong: The dates are tiered, not uniform; they are not reversed; and Q (above ₹1,500 crore) is covered.
solution.final_answer: Option A: P from 7 June 2019 and Q from 1 January 2020; R is not subject to Chapter IV

fact_checks.claim: Reference dates (para 42): aggregate exposure of ₹2,000 crore and above – June 07, 2019; ₹1,500 crore and above but less than ₹2,000 crore – January 1, 2020; less than ₹1,500 crore – to be announced. Accounts with aggregate exposure below ₹1,500 crore are not subject to the Chapter IV requirements (para 43).

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
Consider the following statements about remedies against measures taken under the SARFAESI Act:
I. Any person aggrieved, including the borrower, may apply to the Debts Recovery Tribunal within 45 days of the date on which the measure was taken.
II. An appeal against the DRT's order lies to the Appellate Tribunal within 30 days of receipt of the order.
III. A borrower's appeal is entertained only on deposit of 75% of the debt due, which the Appellate Tribunal may reduce to not less than 50%.
Which of the above is/are correct?

solution.concept: Sections 17 and 18 of SARFAESI
solution.explanation: Under Section 17, any person aggrieved by a measure under Section 13(4), including the borrower, can apply to the DRT within 45 days of the date the measure was taken. Under Section 18, an appeal lies to the Appellate Tribunal within 30 days of receipt of the DRT's order; a borrower must deposit 50% of the debt due, which the Appellate Tribunal may reduce, for reasons recorded, to not less than 25%.
steps: S.17: DRT within 45 days of the measure → I correct
S.18: appeal within 30 days → II correct
Pre-deposit is 50%, reducible to 25% (not 75%/50%) → III wrong
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement III misstates the pre-deposit (75% was the DRT pre-deposit struck down in Mardia Chemicals), so any option containing III is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option D: I and II only

fact_checks.claim: Section 17(1): 'any person aggrieved, including the borrower' may apply 'to apply to the Tribunal within forty five days of the date on which the measure was taken'.

An appeal may be filed 'within thirty days of receipt of the order', and 'no appeal by a borrower is entertained unless it deposits fifty per cent of the amount of debt due', reducible to 'not less than twenty five per cent'.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: After reviewing the Counter-Cyclical Capital Buffer (CCyB) framework in May 2026, what did RBI decide?

options.text: Not to activate the CCyB at that time, with the credit-to-GDP gap as the main indicator
To activate the CCyB at 1% of risk-weighted assets, based on the gross NPA ratio
To replace the CCyB with a higher capital conservation buffer of 3.5%
To activate the CCyB at 0.5% of risk-weighted assets, based on the credit-to-GDP gap

solution.concept: Counter-cyclical capital buffer
solution.explanation: The CCyB is a Basel III buffer built up in good times for use in a downturn. In its review of 18 May 2026, RBI said, based on empirical analysis of CCyB indicators, that it was not necessary to activate the CCyB at that point. The framework uses the credit-to-GDP gap as the main indicator, with supplementary indicators.
solution.why_others_wrong: RBI did not activate the buffer at any rate, the GNPA ratio is not the main indicator, and the capital conservation buffer was not changed.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Not to activate the CCyB at that time, with the credit-to-GDP gap as the main indicator

fact_checks.claim: Review of Requirement of Counter-Cyclical Capital Buffer: 'it has been decided that it is not necessary to activate CCyB at this point in time'; the framework uses the 'credit-to-GDP gap as the main indicator'.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio standard, Level 2 assets can make up at most what share of a bank's stock of high-quality liquid assets (HQLA)?

solution.concept: Composition of HQLA
solution.explanation: HQLA consists of Level 1 assets, which can be included without limit, and Level 2 assets, which cannot exceed 40% of the liquidity reserve. Within Level 2, the riskier Level 2B assets cannot exceed 15% of the HQLA stock.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15% is the cap on Level 2B alone; 25% and 60% are not Basel caps (60% was the initial LCR phase-in level).

fact_checks.claim: 'Level 1 assets, which can be included without limit' and 'Level 2 assets, which cannot exceed 40% of the liquidity reserve'.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: From which date did the Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) become a Basel minimum standard for internationally active banks?

solution.concept: NSFR implementation
solution.explanation: The NSFR, which requires available stable funding to at least equal required stable funding (a ratio of at least 100%), became a minimum standard for all internationally active banks on a consolidated basis on 1 January 2018.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2015 was when the LCR began its phase-in at 60%; 2019 was when the LCR reached 100%; 2023 is not the NSFR date.

fact_checks.claim: 'The NSFR became a minimum standard applicable to all internationally active banks on a consolidated basis on 1 January 2018'.
LCR phase-in: 'the requirement set at 60% and rising by 10 percentage points annually to reach 100% on 1 January 2019'.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's capital adequacy amendment directions of 7 October 2026, what risk weight applies to a commercial bank's trade exposure to a qualifying central counterparty (QCCP) when it acts as a clearing member for its own purposes, in OTC derivatives, exchange-traded derivatives and securities financing transactions?

solution.concept: Exposures to central counterparties
solution.explanation: The Twelfth Amendment Directions revised the treatment of clearing member banks to align with international standards: a 2% risk weight applies to the bank's trade exposure to a QCCP for OTC derivatives, exchange-traded derivatives and SFTs. The same 2% applies where the bank, offering client clearing, must reimburse clients for losses if the QCCP defaults. Parallel amendments were issued for SFBs, payments banks and AIFIs the same day.
steps: Bank = clearing member of a QCCP (own purposes)
Trade exposure (OTC, ETD, SFT) → 2% risk weight
solution.why_others_wrong: QCCP trade exposures are not risk-free (0%), and 20% and 100% are far above the prescribed weight.

fact_checks.claim: 'Where a bank acts as a clearing member of a QCCP for its own purposes, a risk weight of 2 per cent shall be applied' to the bank's trade exposure to the QCCP in respect of OTC derivatives transactions, exchange traded derivatives transactions, and SFTs.
SFB amendment of the same date: trade exposure to a QCCP from OTC derivatives, exchange-traded derivatives and SFTs carries a 2% risk weight.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio standard, which statement about Level 2A and Level 2B assets is correct?

options.text: Level 2A assets take no haircut; Level 2B assets take a 15% haircut and cannot exceed 40% of HQLA
Level 2A assets take a 50% haircut; Level 2B assets cannot be included in HQLA at all
Both take a 15% haircut, and together they cannot exceed 15% of HQLA
Level 2A assets take a 15% haircut; Level 2B assets take higher haircuts and cannot exceed 15% of HQLA

solution.concept: HQLA haircuts and caps
solution.explanation: Level 2A assets are subject to a 15% haircut. Level 2B assets carry higher haircuts and cannot exceed 15% of the stock of HQLA. All Level 2 assets together cannot exceed 40%.
steps: Level 2B: higher haircuts, cap 15% of HQLA
solution.why_others_wrong: Level 2A does take a haircut; Level 2B can be included (within its cap); the 15% cap is on Level 2B only, while all Level 2 assets are capped at 40%.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Level 2A assets take a 15% haircut; Level 2B assets take higher haircuts and cannot exceed 15% of HQLA

fact_checks.claim: 'Level 2A assets, whose value is subject to a 15% haircut' and 'Level 2B assets, which are subject to higher haircuts but cannot exceed 15% of the stock of HQLA'.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's amended leverage ratio framework (directions of 23 October 2026, effective 1 April 2027), a bank's derivative netting set has a replacement cost of ₹20 crore and an aggregate add-on of ₹30 crore, and the bank has received collateral of ₹15 crore from the counterparty. Applying the framework's formula for derivative exposures (with the alpha it prescribes and the PFE multiplier fixed at one), what is the leverage ratio exposure for this netting set?

solution.concept: Derivative exposures in the leverage ratio (SA-CCR)
solution.explanation: For the leverage ratio, derivative exposure = alpha × (RC + PFE), with alpha = 1.4 and the PFE multiplier fixed at one, so PFE equals the aggregate add-on. Collateral received from the counterparty does not reduce the exposure measure. Exposure = 1.4 × (20 + 30) = ₹70 crore.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹49 crore wrongly deducts the collateral; ₹50 crore omits the alpha of 1.4; ₹62 crore applies alpha only to the add-on.

fact_checks.claim: 'Exposure measure = alpha * (RC + PFE)', where 'alpha is 1.4'; 'For the purposes of the leverage ratio framework, the multiplier is fixed at one.'
'a bank shall not reduce the leverage ratio exposure measure amount by any collateral received from the counterparty.'

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's Commercial Banks – Minimum Capital Requirements for Market Risk Directions, 2026 (effective 1 April 2027), a bank's capital requirement for market risk computed under the simplified standardised approach is ₹240 crore. What are its risk-weighted assets for market risk?

solution.concept: Converting a capital charge into RWAs
solution.explanation: Banks must use the simplified standardised approach (SSA) for market risk, and the risk-weighted assets are obtained by multiplying the capital requirement by 12.5 (the reciprocal of 8%). So RWA = 240 × 12.5 = ₹3,000 crore.
solution.why_others_wrong: Multiplying by 10, dividing by 9% (the minimum CRAR) or multiplying by 8 are not the prescribed conversion.

fact_checks.claim: 'A bank shall use the simplified standardised approach (SSA) for computing risk-weighted assets for market risk', by 'multiplying the capital requirements calculated as set out in paragraph 40 by a factor of 12.5.' These Directions shall come into effect from April 1, 2027.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under the Basel III LCR standard, a bank holds Level 1 assets of ₹450 crore and Level 2A assets with a market value of ₹480 crore; it has no Level 2B assets. Its total net cash outflows over the next 30 days are ₹700 crore. Applying the Level 2A haircut and the cap on Level 2 assets, what is its LCR?

options.text: About 75.6%; it falls short of the 100% minimum

solution.concept: Applying HQLA haircuts and caps
solution.explanation: Level 2A after the 15% haircut = 480 × 0.85 = ₹408 crore. Level 2 can be at most 40% of HQLA, i.e. at most 40/60 of Level 1 = 300. So eligible Level 2A = ₹300 crore and HQLA = 450 + 300 = ₹750 crore. LCR = 750 ÷ 700 ≈ 107.1%.
solution.shortcut: A 40% cap on Level 2 means Level 2 can be at most two-thirds of Level 1.
solution.why_others_wrong: 122.6% ignores the 40% cap; 113.3% wrongly takes 40% of the uncapped total; 75.6% applies the 15% Level 2B cap to Level 2A assets.
solution.final_answer: Option B: About 107.1%; it meets the 100% minimum

fact_checks.claim: 'Level 2 assets, which cannot exceed 40% of the liquidity reserve'; 'Level 2A assets, whose value is subject to a 15% haircut'.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's PSL Directions, 2025, what is the total priority sector lending target for Primary (Urban) Co-operative Banks?

options.text: 75% of ANBC or CEOBSE, whichever is higher
40% of ANBC or CEOBSE, whichever is higher
50% of ANBC or CEOBSE, whichever is higher
60% of ANBC or CEOBSE, whichever is higher

solution.concept: PSL targets for UCBs
solution.explanation: Paragraph 7.2 of the PSL Directions sets UCB targets as a percentage of ANBC or CEOBSE, whichever is higher: total priority sector 60%, micro enterprises 7.5% and advances to weaker sections 12%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 40% is the target for domestic commercial banks, 75% for RRBs, and 50% is not a prescribed PSL target.
solution.final_answer: Option D: 60% of ANBC or CEOBSE, whichever is higher

fact_checks.claim: 'The priority sector lending targets for UCBs shall be as follows': Total Priority Sector 60%; Micro Enterprises 7.5%; Advances to Weaker Sections 12% (targets as a percentage of ANBC or CEOBSE, whichever is higher).

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under the PSL Directions, 2025, what is the sub-target for advances to weaker sections for Regional Rural Banks?

options.text: 15 per cent of ANBC or CEOBSE, whichever is higher
10 per cent of ANBC or CEOBSE, whichever is higher
12 per cent of ANBC or CEOBSE, whichever is higher
18 per cent of ANBC or CEOBSE, whichever is higher

solution.concept: Weaker sections sub-target by bank type
solution.explanation: The weaker sections sub-target is 12% for domestic commercial banks (and foreign banks with 20 or more branches) and for SFBs, but RRBs, with their rural focus, have a higher sub-target of 15%. It does not apply to foreign banks with fewer than 20 branches.
solution.why_others_wrong: 12% is for commercial banks and SFBs; 10% is the small and marginal farmers sub-target; 18% is the agriculture target.
solution.final_answer: Option A: 15 per cent of ANBC or CEOBSE, whichever is higher

fact_checks.claim: Advances to Weaker Sections: Domestic Commercial Banks & Foreign Banks with 20 branches and above – '12 percent of ANBC or CEOBSE, whichever is higher'; Regional Rural Banks – '15 per cent of ANBC or CEOBSE, whichever is higher'; Small Finance Banks – 12 percent.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Can a bank use its export credit portfolio as the underlying for issuing 'PSLC – General', according to RBI's PSL FAQs?

options.text: Yes, without any condition, since all export credit is priority sector
Yes, provided the export credit is eligible for PSL classification under the criteria for domestic banks
No, export credit can back only PSLCs issued by foreign banks with fewer than 20 branches
No, PSLC – General can be backed only by agriculture and micro enterprise loans

solution.concept: Underlying assets for PSLCs
solution.explanation: RBI's FAQs say export credit can be used as the underlying for PSLC – General, but the issuing bank must ensure that the export credit portfolio is eligible for priority sector classification under the criteria applicable to domestic banks.
steps: PSLC – General counts towards the overall PSL target
Export credit may back it if PSL-eligible
solution.why_others_wrong: Export credit is not restricted to foreign banks' PSLCs; PSLC – General is not limited to agriculture or micro-enterprise loans; and export credit qualifies only if it meets the PSL criteria.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Yes, provided the export credit is eligible for PSL classification under the criteria for domestic banks

fact_checks.claim: Export credit can be the underlying for PSLC – General, provided the bank ensures that the export credit portfolio 'is eligible for priority sector classification' as per the criteria for domestic banks.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: On RBI's e-Kuber portal, a bank places a buy order for PSLCs of ₹100 lakh at a premium of up to 2%. Sale offers were placed in this order of time: ₹50 lakh at 2.0%, ₹25 lakh at 1.5% and ₹50 lakh at 1.8%. Following RBI's matching rule, what total premium will the buyer pay?

solution.concept: Order matching for PSLCs
solution.explanation: Orders are matched at the lowest sale offer first, and only then by time (FIFO). So ₹25 lakh is bought at 1.5% (₹0.375 lakh), ₹50 lakh at 1.8% (₹0.90 lakh) and the remaining ₹25 lakh at 2.0% (₹0.50 lakh): total ₹1.775 lakh.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹2.000 lakh assumes the buyer's own 2% bid applies throughout; ₹1.825 lakh matches in order of time instead of price; ₹1.767 lakh uses a simple average of the three rates.

fact_checks.claim: Matching follows the lowest sale offer first, then first-in-first-out; in the FAQ's example of a buyer at 2% with sellers at 1.5%, 1.8% and 2%, 'the portal will first match with the sale deal at 1.5%', then moves to 1.8% and 2% for remaining units.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
RBI gives higher or lower weights to incremental priority sector credit depending on the district's per capita PSL. Consider the following statements, according to RBI's PSL FAQs:
I. If a bank's credit in a district declines, the weighted incremental credit for that district is taken as zero.
II. Loans bought through Inter Bank Participation Certificates (IBPCs) from another bank in a low-credit district earn the higher weight.
III. Credit is mapped to a district on the basis of its place of utilisation.
Which of the above is/are correct?

solution.concept: District-wise weights in PSL achievement
solution.explanation: Incremental credit in lower-credit districts gets a 125% weight and in higher-credit districts 90%. Only organic credit (disbursed directly, with borrower details on the bank's books) counts; routes such as securitised assets, direct assignment, IBPCs, PSLCs and on-lending through NBFCs, MFIs or HFCs are excluded. A decline gives a weighted incremental credit of zero, and credit is mapped by place of utilisation.
steps: II: IBPCs excluded from weights → wrong
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II is wrong because IBPCs are one of the seven indirect routes excluded from the weighting, so any option containing II is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: I and III only

fact_checks.claim: 'If there is a decline in credit, the weighted incremental credit will be zero (0).' Credit is mapped to a district based on its place of utilization.
Only organic credit counts for incremental weights; excluded routes include 'Inter Bank Participation Certificates (IBPCs)' and 'Priority Sector Lending Certificates (PSLCs)'.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A bank has two education loans to individuals. Loan A was sanctioned for ₹25 lakh, but accrued interest during the repayment moratorium has taken the outstanding to ₹26.4 lakh. Loan B was sanctioned for ₹22 lakh and has ₹21 lakh outstanding. Applying RBI's PSL FAQ on education loans whose outstanding exceeds the limit because of interest accrued during the moratorium, how much of the two outstandings together counts as priority sector?

solution.concept: Education loans under PSL
solution.explanation: Education loans to individuals qualify up to ₹25 lakh. When the sanctioned limit is within ₹25 lakh, the entire outstanding counts as PSL even if accrued moratorium interest pushes it above ₹25 lakh. Both loans are within the limit, so 26.4 + 21 = ₹47.4 lakh counts.
steps: Loan A: limit ₹25 lakh (within cap) → full ₹26.4 lakh counts
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹46.0 lakh wrongly caps Loan A at ₹25 lakh; ₹21.0 lakh wrongly excludes Loan A; ₹47.0 lakh uses Loan B's sanctioned amount instead of its outstanding.

fact_checks.claim: Outstanding may exceed ₹25 lakh due to 'accrued interest due to moratorium on repayment during the study period'; if the sanctioned limit is within ₹25 lakh, the full outstanding counts toward PSL.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Two borrowers take bank loans for PSL-eligible activities: a partnership firm in which three of its five partners belong to a specified minority community, and a company in which three of its five directors belong to that community. According to RBI's PSL FAQs, which can be counted as advances to specified minority communities (a weaker sections category)?

options.text: Both loans, since the majority test is met in each
Neither loan, since only individuals can be counted

solution.concept: Minority community advances
solution.explanation: A partnership firm whose majority partners belong to a specified minority community can be treated as an advance to minority communities. A company is a separate legal entity, so advances to it cannot be classified as advances to specified minority communities, whoever its directors are.
steps: Partnership firm: majority partners from minority → eligible
Company: separate legal entity → not eligible
solution.why_others_wrong: The company does not qualify, so options including it are wrong; firms are not excluded, as RBI expressly allows partnership firms with majority minority partners.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Only the partnership firm's loan

fact_checks.claim: A partnership firm whose majority partners belong to a specified minority community can be treated as a minority-community advance; however, 'A company has a separate legal entity', so its advances 'cannot be classified as advances to the specified minority communities.'

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
Consider the following statements about trading of Priority Sector Lending Certificates on RBI's e-Kuber portal, according to RBI's PSL FAQs:
I. The premium is settled in real time by debiting/crediting the banks' current accounts with RBI, with no separate RTGS transaction.
II. The portal levies a transaction charge on each lot traded.
III. The tax treatment of PSLC trading is left to banks to determine under the applicable tax laws.
Which of the above is/are correct?

solution.concept: Settlement of PSLC trades
solution.explanation: Premiums on matched PSLC deals are settled in real time through the banks' current accounts with RBI, so no separate RTGS is needed. There are no transaction charges on the e-Kuber PSLC module, and RBI leaves the tax treatment to banks under the applicable tax laws.
steps: I: real-time settlement via RBI current accounts → correct
III: tax treatment left to banks → correct
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II is false, so options with II are wrong; 'I only' omits the correct statement III.
solution.final_answer: Option A: I and III only

fact_checks.claim: Premiums are settled in real time; the participating banks' RBI current accounts are debited or credited by the matched premium, so no separate RTGS transaction is needed.
There are no transaction charges for the e-Kuber PSLC module; tax treatment is for banks to determine 'in accordance with the applicable tax laws'.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RB-IOS, 2026, callers to RBI's Contact Centre (toll-free 14448) can speak to its personnel in English, Hindi and how many regional languages?

solution.concept: RBI Contact Centre
solution.explanation: The Contact Centre guides complainants on the grievance redress mechanism and complaint status. Its personnel are available in English, Hindi and ten regional languages (Assamese, Bengali, Gujarati, Kannada, Marathi, Malayalam, Odia, Punjabi, Telugu and Tamil).
solution.why_others_wrong: Eight and twelve are wrong counts; 22 is the number of languages in the Eighth Schedule, not the Contact Centre's languages.

fact_checks.claim: The facility to connect to Contact Center personnel is available ... 'in English, Hindi and ten regional languages' (Assamese, Bengali, Gujarati, Kannada, Marathi, Malayalam, Odia, Punjabi, Telugu, Tamil).

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RB-IOS, 2026, the RBI Ombudsman or Deputy Ombudsman may help the complainant and the regulated entity reach a mutually acceptable settlement. By which means can this be done, according to RBI's FAQs?

options.text: Negotiation through a Lok Adalat or a civil court
Conciliation only, in a meeting held in person

solution.concept: Modes of resolving complaints
